text: Ficino's Neoplatonism holds that creation is the overflowing of the One, which is source of being and yet beyond being; the first-born of the One is mind.
Pico was so immersed in Aristotle and the Scholastics that he can be regarded as a late Scholastic rather than a Platonist, and Ficino called him an eminent Aristotelian in a preface.

Allen says Pico's De ente et uno takes the Aristotelian side that the One coincides with being, on a basically Thomist basis, dismisses the Parmenides and Sophist as dialectical games, and annoyed Ficino, who called this temerity.
q: On Being and the One is a brief position paper examining whether the One is prior to being, as the Neoplatonists had taught, or coincident with it, as Aristotle had argued. Pico della Mirandola takes the Aristotelian side, utilizing a …

text: Allen says Pico's commentary on a friend's Italian love lyric (the Commento) was used to attack Ficino's understanding of the Symposium, with insights on a par with Ficino's and deeply indebted to them.
Allen says some of Pico's disagreements with Ficino are curtly phrased, in the ... manner of an aristocrat trained by French Scholastics to score in argument.
Allen says Pico, unlike Ficino, scorned astrological prediction, and that this scorn was not itself Platonic or Aristotelian but sceptical in ancestry.
Allen says Pico, in the Oration, champions a Socratic rather than Neoplatonic view of human independence, at odds with the Timaean subordination of humankind beneath star-gods and spiritual beings.
Allen says Pico's youthful anthropology is starkly at odds with Savonarola's jeremiads, to whose influence he later succumbed.
Allen says a curial commission asked Pico to reconsider just thirteen of the nine hundred propositions, and that his refusal provoked condemnation of the whole enterprise.
Allen says the Heptaplus explains many biblical terms and images by way of Neoplatonic metaphysics, and nods perhaps rashly toward the Kabbalah.
Allen says Pico would probably have relished being known as Ficino's fellow Platonist despite considerable differences between them.

Allen proposes to examine Pico's debts in the Oration to later Platonic dialogues as interpreted by the Neoplatonists and as Pico probably met them in Ficino's commentaries, the same dialogues Pico adduces in an anti-Ficinian thesis in De ente et uno.
loc: oration | opening; De ente et uno

text: Allen reports that an older minority view holds Pico a Neoplatonist, while the majority view since Garin's 1937 study is that he was an eclectic committed to the Scholastics and through them to Aristotle and Averroes.

Allen states that Pico scholars have failed to understand the subtlety of Ficino's analyses of the Parmenides and Sophist and hence Ficino's role in generating the De ente et uno and the reaction to it.
q: Pico scholars have failed to understand the subtlety of Ficino analyses of the Parmenides and Sophist and therefore his role in the generation of and reaction to the De ente et uno. See my The second Ficino-Pico controversy: Parmenidean poetry, …

text: Allen says that Ficino in his Philebus commentary and Pico briefly in the Commento both argue on Aristotelian grounds that the Platonic indeterminate is potentiality for the determination which is act.

Allen says Ficino, glossing Parmenides, argues that the ideal unities, for all their diversity, are in one something, Mind the second hypostasis, and that Pico in the Commento equates the son of the Good with this Mind, in which the highest father, the One, has established this universal world.
Allen cites Pico's Commento as saying that the 'son of God' of the Platonists is to be compared to the first and noblest angel created by God, and not to the Son of the theologians.
q: «Secondo e’ Platonici da Dio immediatamente non proviene altra creatura che questa prima mente

text: Allen says both Ficino and Pico were aware that the ancient Platonists' 'son' could not be equated with the Son of God.

Allen argues against Valcke that the 'better Platonists' of Commento 1.4-5 are not also directed against Ficino, since Commento 1.4 explicitly sets Ficino apart from them on God's direct creation of human souls.
Allen questions the view of Cassirer, Garin, Kristeller, Trinkaus and Buck that Pico propounds a notably different view of man from Ficino's.
Allen reports Kristeller's view that Pico places man outside the hierarchy of beings with unlimited freedom, a step toward dissolving the great chain of being.

Allen argues, hedging that it seems to him, that in Pico's account the first man moves within the universal hierarchy rather than outside it, with freedom but not unlimited freedom, in accord with Neoplatonic procession and return.

Allen reads the choice in Pico's opening speech as one of hypostatic level: the first man can dwell in the sensual or animate realms, enter the realm of pure angelic intellects, or reach the solitary darkness of the Father.
Allen says Pico's Commento, like Ficino's De amore, treats a state of potentiality as a chaos awaiting transition into a cosmos, as the Penia of the Symposium longing for Plenty.

Allen suggests the Oration's vision of man is indebted not only to the Philebus and Sophist but especially to the Timaeus and Phaedrus myths and to the Timaeus and Parmenides on the universal paradigm and the Idea of Man.
Allen says the Timaeus is second only to the Phaedrus in supplying Pico with Platonic material for the 900 Conclusions and is the palimpsest of the Heptaplus.

Allen notes that in the second proem of the Heptaplus man is the fourth world after angelic, celestial and sublunar worlds, but that Heptaplus 5.6 qualifies this by calling man the link or bond of the other three.
Allen says Heptaplus 3.7 lets man serve as the terminus of the angelic world and the beginning of corruptible nature.
Allen says Pico declares in Heptaplus 3.7 that man is lower than the angels yet, perfected in Christ, is raised above them or at least to fellowship with them.

Allen says the Heptaplus adds Johannine and Pauline Christological themes absent from the Oration, and that what began as a Hermetic moment in the Oration becomes an orthodox Christological cosmology.

Allen judges that the most significant difference between Pico and Ficino lies in Pico's dual Neoplatonic and anthropocentric orientation, which fastens attention on the Idea of Man almost exclusively.
Allen argues that in a Christocentric system Man becomes the prime Idea and Christ, the Idea of Man, is the perfection of the Platonic theory of Ideas.
Allen states in a note that both Pico and Ficino rejected metempsychosis, held to be Plotinus's one great error.
Allen says the transfer by Christian Platonists of attributes of the Plotinian hypostases of Soul, Mind and the One to God, the Trinity, its persons and the angels was beset with difficulties.
Allen reports Valcke's view that Pico moved from youthful scholastic Aristotelianism to Orphism, Plotinus and poetry, and from the De ente et uno of 1491 returned to Aristotle and the Scholastics.
Allen says Ficino and Pico inherited from Proclus and others the conception of a line of ancient theologians stemming from Zoroaster and Hermes Trismegistus and culminating in Plato.
Allen notes that Ficino accepts an Idea of Man in his commentary on the Parmenides, while Pico in the Commento 1.6 refers to the Idea of men as being in the hypostasis Mind.
Allen notes that Pico in Heptaplus proem 1 claimed Philolaus rather than Pythagoras as author of the Pythagorean dicta translated by Ficino.
Allen contrasts Pico's anthropocentric focus on the Genesis myths, stressing the uniqueness of man, with Ficino's more unitary, panentheistic vision.

Allen says Ficino believed apophatic theology began with the Parmenides and reached its peak with the Areopagite, whom he took as the authentic Athenian disciple of St. Paul, whereas Allen adds that the Areopagite was in fact a late fifth-century disciple of Proclus.
q: The other is its role in the development of the via negativa, the apophaticism which Ficino believed began with the Parmenides and reached its apogee with the works of the Areopagite, for him the authentic Athenian disciple of St. Paul …

text: Allen suggests that scholars have often stressed Pico's originality by focusing too exclusively on the rhetorical and Hermetic excursus on man in the Oration, and that Kristeller did not do this for Ficino.

Allen says Ficino never entirely went along with Pico's attack on the key assumptions of astrology, preserved in a posthumous work of 1496, though he was a knowledgeable if circumspect theorist of astrology.
Allen presents Ficino as saying, in a passage comparing the soul with the triangle, that above the soul the angelic mind needs no inferior powers within itself and is pure, whole and sufficient.

Allen cites Ficino's account in which divine light poured into the angel becomes an intellectual light understood intuitively, and when poured into the soul becomes rational light understood also discursively.

Allen says thirteen of Pico's 900 propositions were found questionable by a committee of the Roman Curia, and that Pico's defence of them was followed by the committee's condemnation of them as heretical; they included items on the real presence, Christ's descent into hell, worship of the Cross and the role of the Cabala in Christology.

Allen says Ficino believed the Proclus-inspired writings now attributed to Pseudo-Dionysius of the late fifth century were composed by the Dionysius of Acts 17:34, converted by Paul, and so a thinker of the first century.

Allen says one Dionysian treatise is a negative theology inspired by the second part of Plato's Parmenides as interpreted by Plutarch of Athens, Syrianus and Proclus, and that Ficino's early dating thus moved Proclus's late Neoplatonism back to the first century.

Allen says Ficino read Proclus's distinctions back into Plotinus and Plato and thereby created an ancient Platonic but in effect heretical Proclan theology perfected in Plato, the Christian Dionysius and Plotinus, a fabric built on mistakes of attribution and dating that his contemporaries shared.
Allen says Ficino held that only two passages in Plato's Letters were interpretable as Trinitarian, in an elliptical way, since the full Trinitarian revelation came only through Christ.
Allen says the Neoplatonic framework of the primacy of the One and the descent of being was potentially read as an Arian system because of its series of subordinations.
Allen reports that Ficino settled on six gentile sages, Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Aglaophemus, Pythagoras and Plato, omitting Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides and Empedocles.
Allen says Ficino identified the highest order or chorus of demons in ancient theology with the angels of Christianity, and inherited a hierarchy of lower demons.
Allen cites Ficino's Platonic Theology as making Saturn the supreme intellect among the angels, whose rays illuminate souls more than the angels.
Allen says that in Origen and Augustine the angels have aethereal bodies, which Aquinas denied by taking them as subsistent forms, while Scotus argued for their composite nature.

Allen says Christian angelology, especially Scotist, opened the possibility for Ficino of accommodating the ancient star vehicle or body of light to the theology of man's return to the angelic choirs.
Allen cites Ficino's Platonic Theology 13.4.12 as saying that a person entirely committed to God's inspiration ceases to be a soul and becomes a son of God, an angel.
Allen says one might well argue that Ficino's whole Platonic endeavour was heretical, since its goals were to become a sage, a magus and a choiring angel.
Allen notes that for the Areopagite God is also the Father of darkness, or rather of what is beyond light and darkness.

Allen says that on Ficino's first method of allegorizing the gods, Saturn is the son of the Good and the One, identified with the First Intellect, first to emanate from the One and the dyad of thinking and thought, which Plotinus and later Neoplatonists made the second hypostasis, Mind.

Allen says that although Mind was identifiable in Christian metaphysics, at least in its Arian version, with the Son, Latin usage of Jupiter for the Deity and Saturn's negative associations worked against it, and Christian philosophers coopted aspects of the Plotinian Mind for aspects of God and of the angel, God's first creature.
Allen says Ficino read the god's castration of his father Uranus allegorically as a mythical description of the radical nature of Mind's descent or procession from the One.

Allen says Ficino, on the enigma of Plato's Sixth Letter, takes Saturn as intellect and cause of Jupiter, with the Good as lord and father of both, and that Saturn is the first principle to issue from and return to the One.

Allen reports Ficino (XV.1.16), setting out the Averroists' argument that forms wholly free of matter are the angels or pure intellects, as adducing on Thomist grounds that there are as many angelic species as there are individual angels.

Allen says Ficino devoted all of Book XV of the Platonic Theology to refuting Averroes's unity of the intellect, an anathema to him ethically, psychologically and intellectually, and that for Ficino the answer to whether there is one intellect for all men is a resounding No.
Allen suggests that Averroes's unitary intellect resembled the Plotinian nous so closely that Ficino needed to discredit it, an explanation he offers as a hypothesis.
Allen says Ficino's whole lifetime endeavour was focused on a Plotinian-Christian metaphysics centred on nous and noes: nous in God, in the angels and in souls.

Allen says Ficino revered Plotinus as a virtual Church Father and supposed him acquainted with the apophatic theology of Dionysius the Pseudo-Areopagite, described as Proclus's disciple, which was possible only because Ficino mistakenly took the works for those of Paul's Athenian convert.
q: He revered Plotinus, moreover, as one of the first and greatest of the Church Fathers in all but name, supposing him acquainted not only with Johannine and Pauline theology, but, confusingly, with the apophatic theology of Proclus’ great sixth century …

text: Allen states in a note that Dionysius the Areopagite, in On the Celestial Hierarchy 11.3, suggests that the more rebarbative the myth, the profounder its core.

Allen reports that Ficino's Philebus commentary describes the Seraphim triad as a single divine intelligence with head, breast and thigh, whose head gazes to the Good, breast to its own beauty and thigh to creating lower things.

Allen reports that Ficino's second triad applies, following Dionysius's De divinis nominibus 4.8, to all the angels, who are declared to have three motions: circular in returning to God, straight in extending power to lower things, and spiral in attending to themselves.

Allen reports that Ficino's third triad makes the ray of the Good triple in any intelligence: Saturn when striving toward the Good, Jupiter when reverting to itself, Prometheus when turning to lower things, with three corresponding powers in the soul.

Allen says that in the last decade of his life Ficino translated and commented on two works of Dionysius, whom Allen calls a sixth-century Neoplatonist confused by the medieval tradition with the Dionysius converted by Paul and with the patron saint of France.
Allen says Ficino's commentary on Dionysius's Mystical Theology describes a sevenfold ascent by subtraction that ends at the absolute Unity, God, concealed beneath the soul's particular unity.
q: Ficino suggests a sevenfold contemplative ascent by way of subtraction. It is imperative that first we banish body from our soul; second, banish corporeal passions from this same soul; third, banish imagination’s images from its reason; fourth, banish reasons discursive …

text: Allen says Ficino derives from the Second Letter's enigma Plato's core metaphysical system with its apex in the One and emanation into Mind and then Soul, in a subordinationist scheme that is Plotinian rather than strictly Platonic, and later tried to accommodate it to Trinitarian formulae.

Allen says that Pico, in his gloss on Benivieni's fourth stanza in Commento III, argued that Orpheus was unwilling to die for his beloved because his music had made him soft and weak, that he descended to Hades for an imaginary Eurydice, and should instead have sent his intellect to heaven to gaze on the true Eurydice among the intelligible Ideas.
q: The interpretation of Pico is equally unexpected. In his gloss on Benivieni’s fourth stanza in the third book of his Commento,64 he went so far as to argue that Orpheus had been unwilling to die in order to pursue his …

text: Allen says Pico complains that no one, Ficino included, had understood the subtle and profound mystery, which occurred to Pico the first time he read the Symposium.

Allen argues that Pico was simply responding to Ficino's brief remark in the Symposium commentary 1.4 that for the moment he did not intend to delve into the allegorical meaning of Orpheus or Alcestis, and that Plotinus's twin Herakles was as familiar to Pico as to Ficino.

Allen notes that in the Commento Pico never seems to refer to anything of Ficino's except the De amore, and that only intermittently, though Ficino had by the mid 1480s produced a great body of translation, analysis and commentary.
Allen says the Plotinian exegesis of the double Herakles served as a guide for Ficino, and presumably for a Neoplatonizing Pico also, in reading Platonic figures in a double, antithetical way.
Allen notes that Angelo Poliziano, in a complimentary reference to Ficino at the end of the Miscellanea, glossed Eurydice as the Platonic wisdom of judgment at its amplest.
Allen says that Lorenzo and other Medicean poets read the authentic Eurydice as dwelling among the gods, and that the false Orpheus is the pusillanimous singer of Plato's, Lorenzo's and Pico's scorn.

Allen says the later Neoplatonists read the Parmenides as the repository of Plato's highest mysteries concerning the One, taking its first five positive hypotheses as the five hypostases: the One, mind, soul, Forms in matter, and matter.

Allen says that in Christian eyes Parmenides had anticipated the apophatic theology of Pseudo-Dionysius, a thinker revered in the Renaissance as Paul's first Athenian convert but later exposed as a late fifth- or early sixth-century follower of Proclus.
Allen says Proclus's Parmenides commentary was translated by William of Moerbeke for a few medieval readers, and that Ficino was the first in the West since antiquity to master Proclus's works.
Allen names Copenhaver's work on the Oration and the Cabala as the most important recent work on the Oration.
Allen characterises Pico as an Aristotelian by training and an eclectic by conviction, not a devout Neoplatonist like Ficino.
q: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463-94) was the wunderkind among Italian Renaissance philosophers and a key figure, along with Cusanus, Bessarion, and Ficino, in the revival of Platonic metaphysics, though he was not a devout Neoplatonist like Ficino but rather an …

text: Allen reports that Pico sent a draft of the Commento to Ficino, who found off-the-cuff attacks on his own views and wrote marginalia on it before returning it.
Allen holds that the disagreement over the Commento did not become a feud or estrangement, though Pico took only partial account of Ficino's corrections.
Allen reports that Pico asserted at the end of Commento 2.2 that Marsilio had made mistakes on every subject in every part of his De amore.
Allen infers that Benivieni, Gianfrancesco and friends concealed Pico's disagreements with Ficino, and that Benivieni's expurgated version omitted the references to Ficino.
Allen reports that Ficino regarded the Commento notes as full of youthful errors whose publication would not enhance Pico's reputation, citing a letter to Ganay.
Allen says the Commento does not always persuade in Pico's disputes with Ficino, and that its combative style belongs to the conventions of Renaissance scholarly disagreement.
Allen says that when writing the Commento Pico was not yet well acquainted with the Phaedrus and Hermias's commentary on it, the Charmides, or sections of the Enneads.
Allen says the real concern of the Commento is metaphysics, conceived as a dimension of theology and read in Greco-Roman myth and less in Egyptian and Chaldean myth, rather than love theory.

Allen presents Pico's ecstasy as two deaths: in the first the soul's lower powers cease but the intellect gazes on the heavenly Venus, in the second the body falls away and the soul unites with her in a kiss.
loc: commento | Death of the Kiss (Allen's account)

text: Allen reports Pico saying that Cabalist wise men held many ancient fathers to have died in intellectual rapture, and that the Cabalists call this death binsica, death from kissing.
q: Since the Cabalist wise men believe that many of the ancient fathers died in this kind of rapture of the intellect, you will find the Cabalists saying that those fathers died of binsica which in our language means death from …

text: Allen reports that Pico says Solomon longs for the death of the kiss in a verse of Canticles, and Plato too in speaking of the kisses of Agathon.
Allen holds that for Pico union with intelligible Beauty means passing from human to intellectual existence and being transformed into an angel, as the Cabalists say Enoch became Metatron.
loc: commento | gloss on Da lui el foco

text: Allen says that through the kiss-death we cease to be human and become angels, the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's vision.
q: To attain such a gift, the soul separates from the body, but, even more importantly, the body drops away entirely from the soul. We cease to be humans and become angels - the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's great vision.

text: Allen finds it unclear whether Pico means Orpheus should have died the second death or only the first, and asks whether he has thought the situation through.
Allen reports that Pico says God does not love us because love in God would be an imperfection, and reads this as aimed at Ficino, who held that God loves us.
loc: commento | gloss on Per lui el fonte immortale

text: Allen reports that Pico denies there is beauty in God, according to the Platonists, because of infinite simplicity, so God must be loved in himself and not as author of ideal beauty.
loc: commento | gloss on Che poi che in se

text: Allen says Pico's Commento presents Platonic psychology keyed to being rather than, as in Ficino, to unity, though Pico is indebted to the third book of Ficino's Platonic Theology.
Allen says the Commento begins by distinguishing causal, formal and participated being, defining God as cause of being and of all intellect rather than as being or intellect per se.
Allen reports that Pico challenges a great Platonist's amazement at Plotinus's saying that God understands nothing, explaining that understanding exists in God in causal, not formal, being.
q: This leads Pico from the onset to challenge the reaction of amazement by "un gran platonico" (clearly Ficino) to a passage in Plotinus's Enneads (5.6.3 or 6.7.37) in which God is said to understand nothing and to castigate him for …

text: Allen argues that Ficino, versed in negative theology, if amazed at all as Pico claimed, must have been amazed not at the notion that God does not understand as we or the angels do, but at its role in the Plotinus passage.

Allen argues that Pico's account of the three hypostases, identifying the second, which the ancient Neoplatonists called Mind, with Angel or Angelic Mind, is one of his most interesting contributions in the Commento.

Allen says some Neoplatonists put a host of intelligible and intellectual creatures, whom Christians call angels, between the first hypostasis and the World Soul, and that this shows Pico's medievalism since Plotinus spoke simply of Soul.

Allen reports that for the view of an angelic order between the first and third hypostases Pico cites Proclus, Hermias and Syrianus, together with the Areopagite and other Christian theologians, probably alluding to Scotus and Giles of Viterbo.

Allen says Pico's terminology certainly draws on Iamblichean and Proclian distinctions between the Ideas and the highest spiritual beings contemplating them, midway between the intelligibles and the intellectual beings below.

Allen reports that the 'more perfect Platonists' whom Pico twice names, among them Plotinus and Porphyry, held that between the first and third hypostases there is only one Mind, called the son of the father, and that Pico prefers this view as closer to Aristotle.
q: However, those Pico twice calls the "more perfect Platonists," Plotinus and Porphyry among them, had maintained that between the first and third hypostases there is only one Mind, not many minds, and they had even referred to it as the …

text: Allen says that in the Commento God creates a single Mind from eternity, a perfect effect of a perfect cause and God's sole immediate creation.

Allen reports that Pico attacks Ficino for holding, presumably in De amore 4.4, that according to Plato human souls are also created directly by God, a view held by neither Plotinus nor Proclus nor their followers.
Allen argues that Pico ignores the Timaeus's Demiurge, who creates human souls directly and the World Soul, and that Pico is either precipitate or radically simplifying.
Allen says that Pico argues the Platonic Word should not be identified with the Christian Son of God, whereas Ficino does identify them, convinced that Plato foresaw the mystery of the Trinity.

Allen says Pico gives two grounds for not identifying the second hypostasis with the Christian Son: the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and the Son is a creator whereas the second Platonic hypostasis is a creature, identified with the first and noblest angel; God creates Mind as Angel.

Allen says that for the Neoplatonists the first emanation from the One is the emergence of thought, and that God has created the Ideas in the first Mind, giving the intelligible world of which the sensible world is an image.

Allen reports Pico saying the ancient theologians equated God with Uranus, Mind with Cronus (Saturn), and the World Soul with Jupiter, Uranus standing for preeminence, Saturn for intellectuality, Jupiter for active rule over inferiors.
Allen says the triple principle of Uranus, Cronus and Zeus derives from etymologies in Plato's Cratylus, and that Ficino sets out the same arguments in his Phaedrus commentary.

Allen says both Florentines accept Proclian-inspired equations letting Saturn exercise a Uranian or Jovian power, but Pico breaks with Ficino in denying that Uranus can exercise a Saturnian power because he transcends the intellect entirely.

Allen says these equations presuppose that any deity can exercise all these powers, since each deity is in its way all the others, a monotheistic system concealed beneath a polytheistic rind, so that readings of a deity or its daemons must be careful and may run in parallel.

Allen says Pico identifies the Platonic Mind as the first and noblest angel and as the intelligible world within it, the Ideas of all things later created, a creature as perfect as a created thing can be.

Allen says Pico, thinking in an Aristotelian way, treats Angel or Mind as compounded of potency and act, equating potency with the unlimited of the Philebus and a kind of matter, and act with the limit and form.

Allen says Mind, identified with Saturn, has three functions: contemplation of higher things (which Ficino was to call Uranian), self-contemplation (which Ficino was to call self-regarding), and a Jovian downward providential regard of the universe it creates.
q: But Mind, identified hypostatically with Saturn, nonetheless has three functions - a Saturnian contemplation of (Ficino was to call this, more logically, a Uranian regarding of) things higher than itself (but such can only be God); a Saturnian contemplation "that …

text: Allen argues that Pico's attribution of Mind's upward regard to act, self-regard to act and potency and downward regard to potency is a sleight of hand that becomes untenable given his own identification of potency with matter and act with form.

Allen says Mind, as first one-and-many and first angel and the plenitude of the Ideas, is the first unitary composite and first beautiful thing, the composite universal beauty that Ficino would call the splendor of the Ideas.
q: Moreover, since Mind is the first one-and-many and exists both as the first angel and as the plenitude of the Ideas, it is the first unitary composite and therefore the first beautiful thing: not so much the absolute, exemplary unique …

text: Allen reports Pico's definition in Commento 2.8 of such beauty as a friendly enmity or harmonious discord, backed by Heraclitus and Empedocles, and that only God is without contrariety while Angel and Beauty are composed of potency and act.

Allen believes the lemmata about Love's birth on the birth day of Venus, when Porus had joined Penia in the gardens of Jupiter, are the greatest mystery of the Symposium for Pico and occasioned some of his most fertile ideas as a Platonizing hermeneut.
Allen reports that in Commento 2.13 Pico asserts an unformed substance trailed after God, originally prime matter, which when given form by God became Angel-Mind.

Allen says that the Ideas have causal being in God, formal being in Mind, which is counselled by God, and participated being in rational Soul, and that Pico's arguments about the unformed substance look at first self-contradictory.
Allen says the Commento exposes a real and enduring problem in the Neoplatonic emanatory system: Mind without the Ideas must have been unformed, in potency, and quasi-matter.

Allen reports that in Pico's account angelic Mind, once it holds the Ideas' imperfectly seen beauty, comes to desire them in perfect form; Allen adds that this desire is the first instance of love though Pico never says so.

Allen says that in the reading he gives Pico, Love is born when Porus, the multitude of the Ideas in Mind, unites with Penia, the unformed deficient Jovian state of that essence, an act-potency union that gives rise to Mind as Paradise.

Allen says Pico stumbles in declaring that desire was born from the union of the perfect state of the Ideas, signified by Porus, son of Counsel that is of God, and their imperfect state, signified by Penia; and reports the birthday of Venus as the day when the beauty of the Ideas first descended into Angelic Mind.
Allen says Pico lost interest in the Commento project but did extract some formulations from it in preparing the Heptaplus.
Allen reports that in Pico's account Love, once born, turns Mind to God, which receives from him the perfecting of the beauty of the Ideas, and only then does Venus become a fully grown goddess.
Allen reports that Pico takes the gods seated at the banquet, in the Pythagorean-Parmenidean manner, to mean the Ideas, which precede Venus since she is the beauty that results from all the Ideas.

Allen says Pico takes Porus drunk with nectar to signify the sheer multiplicity of the Ideas, and that Pico concludes 2.13 by saying the Ideas of other things existed in the Angelic Mind but were not welcomed to the banquet since immortality was not granted them.
q: Pico takes Plato's description of Porus as drunk with nectar to signify "the sheer multiplicity of the Ideas" (l'affluenzia universale d'esse idee), presumably the Ideas of all the other things that were there in Mind, or possibly all the Ideas …

text: Allen reports that Pico resolves the paradox of Love as oldest and youngest god by holding that Love existed before the other gods, the Ideas, who achieved perfected being only after Love caused Mind to return to the One, yet is the youngest because the other gods existed before him joined to the unformed substance of Mind.

Allen says Love is a mysterious paidogeron, a child-father, whose birth in the unformed substance of angelic Mind from the mixing of Porus and Penia coincides with the birth of his still infant mother Venus, though Pico does not pursue the paradox.

Allen says Ficino had confronted the same conundrums in De amore 5.10 and 1.3, and that both thinkers are struck by the Orphic bosom of chaos and argue that Mind was in a sense a chaos waiting to be a cosmos.
Allen reports that Pico, citing Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22, says Mind could rightly be called a chaos when first filled with all the Ideas, still imperfect, indistinct and confused.
q: Pico adduces the Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22 and observes that Mind could "rightly be called a chaos" when it was first filled with all the Ideas and the Ideas were still "imperfect, indistinct as it were, and confused."

text: Allen says that in Pico's account Mind, to perfect the Ideas, must revert to God and unite with him, completing what Pico calls the first circle, and then possesses the beauty of the Ideas in perfection so that Venus becomes a sovereign goddess in Mind.
q: Since the Ideas can be perfected only when they are separated from what is alien to them, separated in effect from the as yet unformed chaos of Mind and returned to their source in the One, Mind must itself revert …

text: Allen says that despite this circle Mind eventually succumbs to time in what seems the onset of a Saturnian aging, being overthrown by its youngest son Jupiter, the World Soul, who escapes being swallowed by being replaced with a stone.

Allen says that for both Pico and Ficino the succession myth expresses the violence of hypostatic succession and Soul's emergence from Mind, but that it no longer seems to accommodate Pico's initial account of Love and Beauty.

Allen says Pico turned to another Venus of the Symposium, the heavenly Venus, daughter of Uranus, who was born a perfect nymph from the sea's foam when Uranus's sperm cast by Saturn fell into the waves of matter.

Allen says Pico knew that Proclus and other antique interpreters taught that all traditional myths were theological at heart, and that Dionysius the Areopagite had stressed in On the Celestial Hierarchy that the more repellent the myth the more profound its hidden mystery.
q: particularly when we recall that he was well aware that Proclus and other antique interpreters had taught, following the lead of the mythological passages in Plato's dialogues, that all the traditional myths were theological at heart and that one had …

text: Allen says the myth of the Anadyomene spurred Pico to suggest that the sea was the unformed substance first found in Mind, the primal Oceanus or Neptune as certain Platonists maintained, and that Venus was in this sense united with Mind.

Allen says that since Uranus as God creates only the first angel, whom the Platonists call Mind and the poets Saturn, God is figuratively sterile once he has created Mind, having been in a way castrated by Mind.

Allen says Pico avoids reconciling Saturn as castrator with Saturn as himself the foam-flecked sea, the unformed substance of Mind impregnated by Uranus's sperm, which Pico allegorizes as the plenitude of the Ideas.

Allen says Pico identifies the unformed substance of Mind with the Necessity of the Timaeus, so that the Ideas first came into Mind in the reign of Necessity, only becoming perfected in the reign of Love when Mind turned to God.
q: Moreover, since he also identifies this substance with the Necessity of the Timaeus (47Eff.), he can argue that the Ideas first came into Mind during the reign of Necessity and were thus not yet in their perfect state; only in …

text: Allen says Pico in these arguments treads a tightrope between inherited mythological contradictions and Neoplatonic attempts to distinguish stages in the emanation of being.
Allen thinks that behind the Neoplatonic allegoresis of the Commento there looms for Pico, much more than for Ficino, the authority and ever presence of Genesis.

Allen reports that in the proem to the second exposition of the Heptaplus Pico declares Genesis to excel all other progeny of the human mind in doctrine, eloquence and genius, though Moses speaks with a veiled face.

Allen says the Heptaplus of 1489 gives a sevenfold interpretation of the six days of creation and the seventh day of rest, with an appendix on the Bible's opening phrase, approaching Genesis by way of Christology and Neoplatonic metaphysics.

Allen argues that for Pico, unlike for Ficino with the Timaeus, Moses's first book took precedence and became the most profound of Platonic texts, letting him look beyond the Platonic dialogues as the Parmenides let Proclus and his successors.

Allen reports that in the Heptaplus proem to Lorenzo de' Medici Pico says Moses philosophizes on the emanation of all things from God and on the grade, number and order of the parts of the world, beneath the rough bark of its words.

Allen reports that Pico asserts Genesis requires a self-consistent and coherent course of interpretation, interpreting the whole creation continuously and without confusion in seven senses, and asserts nothing alien to nature or to the truths ascertained by the better philosophers.

Allen reports that in the proem to the second exposition Pico defines Moses's aim as arranging discourse so that the same words, context and order are suitable for symbolizing the secrets of all the worlds and of the whole of nature.

Allen reports that in the second general proem Pico outlines the ancient philosophers' doctrine of the three worlds: the supercelestial world, which the theologians call the angelic and the philosophers the intelligible world, the celestial, and the sublunary.

Allen reports Pico assigning eternal life and unchanging activity to the first world, stable life with changing activity to the second, and alternation of life and death to the third, the third moved by the second and the second governed by the first.
Allen reports Pico saying that the three worlds are one world since whatever is in all the worlds together is also contained in each separately.

Allen says Pico is surely invoking two Neoplatonic formulas, that the whole is in the part according to the part's capacity and that all things are in all things, each in its own way, which Proclus had refined as keys to the unity of the world.

Allen reports that Pico says whatever is in the lower world is in the higher ones in better form, and that the supercelestial world has the Idea of heat, apparently the love of the seraphic intellects, and the understanding of the cherubic intellects corresponds to water.

Allen reports that Pico correlates the nine orders of angels, presided over by God's unmoving unity, with the nine heavenly spheres presided over by the unmoving empyrean, and these with nine spheres of corruptible forms founded on prime matter.

Allen reports Pico saying that the worlds, bound by the chains of concord, exchange natures and names with mutual liberality, and infers from this that Nature is an allegory full of 'hidden alliances and affinities' open to an enlightened interpreter.
Allen says an Empedoclean vision of nature riven by discord seems foreign to Pico, perhaps because it is too dualistic, the intelligible realm being governed by the concord of Castor and Pollux.
Allen says Pico wants to postulate a separate fourth world for man, in whom are found all the things of the sublunar, celestial and supercelestial worlds.

Allen says that because Moses's scripture is the exact image of the world each word must be interpreted in terms of the four worlds, with a fifth exposition on discordant concord, a sixth on fifteen ways things are joined, and a sabbatical exposition on the return of creatures to God.

Allen says that because Moses treats all worlds in the same words, each reading must pertain both to sublunar nature and translunar heavens and be consonant with a theological account of the angelic realm and the realm of Mind.

Allen says the method of the Heptaplus implies that natural science, theology and anthropology share one methodology and hermeneutics, a reading in one being keyed by isomorphic analogies to a parallel reading in another.
Allen says that, like other medieval and ancient texts and like Pico's own Commento, the Heptaplus's central engagement is with another authoritative text, here the opening verses of the Bible.

Allen says the Heptaplus is original in turning to the Cabala and in making Genesis a Christological, anthropocentric text, the seventh chapter of each of the seven expositions turning to the Son of Man as the definitive law and first and final cause.

Allen says the Heptaplus is a summa of a cosmology of harmony, correspondence and consonance, drawing on Plato's Pythagorean themes and the Neoplatonists, including Dionysius the Areopagite, whom Pico still took to be the Athenian disciple of St. Paul.

Allen says that in the Oration other creatures, including the planetary souls and the angelic intellects above them, have natures confining them to a realm of being, whereas the first man can sculpt himself into a beast or a seraph.

Allen reports that in Commento 1.12 Pico defines human nature as the tie and knot of the world and correlates man's parts with the world: body with the material realm, vegetative part with plants, sensitive part with animals, intellectual part with the angels, unity with God.
Allen says Pico seems to suggest in Commento 2.6 that the world is the great man, the macroanthropos, and that this is for Pico a Mosaic trope as his gematria-based epilogue on Bereshit shows.
Allen reports that in the Heptaplus man is not even a fourth world but the bond and union of the other three, containing all things as their centre as God contains them as their origin.
loc: heptaplus | man as bond of the three worlds

text: Allen says that if Mosaic man is angelic only allegorically, since scripture uses man to represent angelic and rational creatures as the end and terminus of the angelic world, then Christ as man is more eminent than the first angel and perfects the angels.
Allen says Christ enables us to become more than the angels, not just image and likeness but sons of God, as Paul says in Hebrews.

Allen says Ficino, drawn to man's standing on the middle rung, worked with a pentadic scheme of hypostases inherited from Proclus, the One, Mind, Soul, Quality and Body, in which Soul mediates between Mind and the corporeal.

Allen says Ficino's emphasis on Soul directs attention to life and the whole reflected in the part, whereas Pico's Platonic anthropocentrism and Genesis commitment underscore the uniqueness of man, of man in Christ and of Christ as the Idea of Man.
Allen says Ficino's vision may be more unitary and panentheistic, attuned to harmony and to ratio and proportion.

Allen says Pico's speculations on the principles of the emanative process are rich but not internally consistent, and that many of his problems are intrinsic to Neoplatonism and to Plotinus's attempts to probe the first flowing out of the One.
q: Pico's contribution, however, is interesting for different reasons. He has given us a rich, if not an internally consistent, set of speculations concerning the principles of the emanative process itself: the principles that underlie the birth of thought, of the …

text: Allen argues that for Pico and Ficino the fascination with the origin of existence is the fundamental allure of Plotinian Platonism, and concludes that Pico should still be thought of as Ficino's fellow Neoplatonist, who joined him, however contentiously, in celebrating the birthday of Venus.

Allen cites in his endnotes Commento 1.3 (edition pages 464-5, translation page 79) for the discussion of a host of intermediate creatures called angels, and Commento 2.13 (502 and 108) for a later passage.
Allen cites in his endnotes Commento 1.3 (464-5) for the one-mind view, 1.4 (465-6) for the sole direct creation, and 1.5 (466-7) for the names of the first creature and for the creature Son.
Allen cites in his endnotes Commento 1.6 for the intelligible world within the first creature, 1.8 for the poetic veils, and 1.8 (470-1) for the triple principle of the mythological equations.

Allen cites in his endnotes Commento 1.9 (472-3, translation 85-6) for the potency, act and three functions of the first creature, 2.13 (503) for its composite beauty, and 2.8 (495-6) for the definition of beauty.
Allen notes that the lemmata on the birth of love also intrigued Ficino, as his De amore 6.7 shows, but leaves that for another occasion.
Allen's endnotes cite Commento 2.13 (501 [107]), noting that Pico himself refers to 1.9, and Commento 2.21 (513 [117]) on Porus the son of counsel, with a see-reference to Wind, Pagan Mysteries.
A note at the gloss of Porus as son of Counsel, that is of God, cites Isaiah 9:6 and Proverbs 8:14.

Allen reports that Jayne judges the sentence in Commento 2.13 about the Ideas of other things not welcomed to the banquet clearly a mistake, since Pico had just said all the Ideas are immortal, and that Pico deleted the passage in his own manuscript.
Allen notes that of the surviving manuscripts of the Commento none is a Pico autograph, and that Marsilio's name is omitted at one place in most manuscripts, on a note by the translator.
Allen notes that in the passage on a cabalistic account of a transformation into an angel Pico spells the angel's name Matatron.
loc: commento | gloss on Da lui el foco

text: Allen cites in his endnotes Commento particulare 557 (translation 150) for the first death and 557-8 for the binsica passage, and identifies the kisses of Agathon as Plato's first epigram to Agathon in Diogenes Laertius.
A note refers the reader to chapter 1 of an earlier Icastes, titled The Ficinian Sophist and the Controversy with Pico.
Allen says that Crofton Black's study of the Heptaplus treats patristic, Neoplatonic, scholastic and cabbalistic sources but not Ficino, whose influence on Pico Allen would argue was pervasive.
Allen reports that Black's study underscores the Heptaplus's debt to the Pseudo-Areopagite.

Allen cites in his endnotes Heptaplus 2.6, 4.7 and 3.7 in turn for the statements that man stands for angelic creatures, that the newest Adam is more eminent than the first angel, and that Christ perfects the angels.

Black presents the Heptaplus as containing a theory of allegory that departs from mainstream medieval and Renaissance exegesis and is tied to contemporary debate on the nature and action of the intellect.

Black argues that the theory of allegory of the second proem derives largely from the Neoplatonic tradition, especially the Dionysian corpus, and that the parallels with Pseudo-Dionysius lead to the question of intellectual ascent (anagogy).
The first proem justifies a hidden non-literal meaning in the Bible, and its argument rests on a semiotic and social distinction between esoteric and exoteric meaning.
Black proposes that the Heptaplus should be viewed as an expression of the role of the intellect in man's progress to felicitas.

Black argues that the seven-fold structure of the Heptaplus reflects the forty-nine gates of understanding through which, according to texts Pico read, Moses ascended and whose knowledge he concealed in the Genesis account.
Black holds that Pico's engagement with the debate on the intellect was influenced by the Jewish tradition, in its application to hermeneutics rather than in the details of epistemology.
In Florence Pico made the acquaintance of Poliziano, Benivieni and Ficino among others, and around this time took up the project of reconciling Plato and Aristotle.
The lifelong reconciliation project never took written form as such; De ente et uno represents a part of it and the Conclusiones give intimations of the intended method.
The Commento, written around 1485-1486, is a commentary strongly influenced by Platonism and Neoplatonism on a love poem by Benivieni that is itself based on Ficino's commentary on Plato's Symposium.

Black says Ficino's interpretation of Plato was tendentious: he wished to establish Platonism as the philosophy of choice for Christians against a scholastic Aristotelianism he thought mired in heresy about the soul.

Black says Pico's own position was less partisan than Ficino's, as seen in his reply of 9 June 1485 to Barbaro's attack on scholastic barbarism, defending scholasticism on the ground that truth alone matters.

Black sees no reason to doubt Pico's sincerity in the earlier defence of scholasticism, since Pico followed that path in practice, having spent time among the Averroists of Padua and then going to Paris.
Pico planned to debate nine hundred conclusions in Rome in the manner of Parisian disputation, and published them on 7 November.
Black describes the Conclusiones as formally far from the Heptaplus: a miscellaneous collection of bare bones that, despite commentators' efforts, do not form a coherent body.
A papal committee scrutinised the Conclusiones for several months and found fault first with seven, then thirteen of them; the debate never took place, so Pico's position on most of them is unknown.
Pico's Apologia responded to the censure as a preamble to the debate and a defence of the thirteen condemned propositions, blaming the committee for misreading his words.
Innocent VIII issued a bull dated 8 August 1487 banning the book, not promulgated until 15 December; by then Pico had fled toward Paris and been captured and arrested on the way.

Lorenzo de' Medici helped secure Pico's release and offered him hospitality in Florence; Black reads this as a pragmatic solution keeping Pico's doctrines within Florentine libraries and Lorenzo's circle.

Black says the Roman affair produced the Conclusiones, the Apologia and the Oratio, and that the Oratio is essentially a version of the first part of the Apologia presented as an introductory speech to the debate.
Black notes that Copenhaver argues the subtitle 'On the Dignity of Man' misrepresents the work's content.
After returning to Florence Pico turned to biblical commentary, the pre-eminent result being the Heptaplus, contemporary with an incomplete series of Psalm commentaries begun in 1488.

Lorenzo wrote in June 1489 that Pico lived like a monk in theological work; Black reads the letter as an effort at rehabilitation, which failed, since Lanfredini reported that the pope found Pico's theology intolerable and preferred poetry.

Black says that as far as the pope was concerned the Heptaplus continued the heretical tendencies of the Conclusiones, and that Lorenzo again defended Pico's work; several intellectuals, including Barbaro, wrote to admire it.
De ente et uno, published in 1490, is all Pico managed to write of his proposed Concordia Platonis et Aristotelis.
Gianfrancesco Pico's Vita stresses Pico's orthodoxy and holiness, dismisses the Roman affair as youthful folly, and largely overlooks his interest in kabbalah.

Black says the Hebrew literary tradition presented Pico with both biblical exegesis and philosophy, and was one of his points of entry into the Arabic tradition, notably through otherwise untranslated works of or on Averroes.
Black names three scholars who made Jewish and Arabic works available to Pico, orally or textually: Elijah Delmedigo, Flavius Mithridates and Johanan Alemanno.

Delmedigo's two treatises on the intellect were first composed in Latin at Pico's request, and the original Latin versions are not extant, so the surviving Hebrew versions cannot be a sure guide to what he wrote for Pico.

Black reports that Delmedigo, in a long letter to Pico, gives bibliographies of writers said to help prove that the first principle is separate from matter, a doctrine he says they received by revelation and which must therefore be believed.
Delmedigo's letter to Pico lists under 'Kabbalah' the Zohar, a work by Recanati, Gikatilla's Sha'arei orah, and other works, adding that he cannot recall further names.
Black argues that Delmedigo's letter to Pico, addressed to him in Rome, must date from late November 1486 at the earliest, and that it shows Pico's kabbalah studies already well under way.

Black reports it has been demonstrated (citing Wirszubski) that Mithridates's translation of Recanati's Pentateuch commentary was the single most influential source for Pico's interpretation of kabbalah in the Conclusiones, so Pico had read it before November 1486.
The lost Latin translation of Recanati's Pentateuch commentary cannot be shown to have been sent by Delmedigo, since no volume of Recanati is identifiable in Pico's library inventory.
Black says Delmedigo was not involved with biblical exegesis, unlike Mithridates and Alemanno, but was a conduit for Averroes and important to Pico's Hebrew studies.
Around 1486 Mithridates translated for Pico a substantial corpus of Hebrew texts into Latin, of which the surviving part amounts to over 3,500 pages in five Vatican manuscripts.
q: Documentation of their working relationship begins in 1486. Around this time, as has already been mentioned, Mithridates translated a substantial corpus of Hebrew texts into Latin specifically for Pico. Some of these are no longer extant. What survives, in five …

text: Links between the translations and the Conclusiones show that part of the corpus, certainly Vat. Ebr. 190 and the lost Recanati manuscript, had been completed and read by Pico by November 1486, while Vat. Ebr. 189 postdates it.
The translated corpus omits the Sefer Ye.zirah and the Zohar, but Pico knew they existed.

Black says the translated corpus includes more than one strand of kabbalah, but Pico understood kabbalah as handed down orally from Moses, so the places and dates of composition mattered little to him.

Marginal markings in the translated manuscripts against passages used, sometimes almost verbatim, in the Conclusiones show that Pico read, marked and reused them; Black adds that several concern exegesis and are potentially important background to the Heptaplus.
Mithridates's translations contain interpolations: some clarify letter-number passages, some add a Christian veneer, and some add references to kabbalah and kabbalists absent from the original.
Pico's association with Mithridates apparently ended before March 1489 for reasons that remain unclear.
q: Some time before March 1489, Pico's association with Mithridates apparently came to an end, for reasons that remain unclear.

text: Around 1488 Pico met the Jewish scholar Alemanno, whose Song of Songs commentary was written apparently at Pico's request and who was composing a Genesis commentary at about the time of the Heptaplus.

Black finds a shared interest of Alemanno and Pico in exegesis and intellectual ascent easy to make out but concrete links between their texts hard to show, and there is no evidence that Pico read the Einei ha-edah.

Black cautions against taking literally, given epistolary convention, Pico's attribution of his interest in Genesis to Lorenzo de' Medici in the Heptaplus introduction (and Alemanno's attribution of his commentary to Pico).

Black says information probably passed between Pico and Alemanno in conversation, so Alemanno may have introduced other works and broadened Pico's grasp of the textual bases of doctrines Mithridates had introduced.
Pico accumulated a sizeable collection of Hebrew books not represented in the translated corpus and used some in his biblical commentaries, though the details are obscure.

Pico replied to a letter from Ficino of 8 September 1486, writing that he had spent a whole month at Hebrew day and night and could now compose a letter not yet worthy of praise but without fault; Black says how much Hebrew this was is hard to say.

Black argues that the Psalm expositions show Pico had enough Hebrew to draw on commentators for individual words in philological sections, but this does not necessarily imply he could read whole treatises by Recanati, Abulafia, Gikatilla or Alemanno.

Black hypothesises that Pico and Mithridates jointly began translating Job through Gersonides, with Mithridates continuing in Pico's absence after chapter 10, and that the manuscript reflects a teacher-pupil relationship.

Black argues that the unusual Jewish exegetical terminology in Pico's Apologia, matching Bahya ben Asher, reached Pico by oral transmission from Mithridates or another Jewish associate, since the note in Pico's hand is in a manuscript of another work that does not contain it.

Black warns that oral contact cannot be assumed to be a full conduit: information would not necessarily have been shared fully, Mithridates distorted texts in a Christianizing manner, and Delmedigo deliberately withheld information about kabbalah from works produced for Pico, who was his patron.

Black concludes that, given the limits of the evidence, one cannot assume Pico could read complete kabbalistic treatises unaided even in 1489; he was a pioneer in his area of interest, kabbalah, rather than in linguistic ability, and approached it through the translated corpus and oral contact.
q: On balance, given these limitations, we cannot assume that, even in 1489, he would have been able to read complete kabbalistic treatises unaided

text: Black states that he generally seeks the origins of Jewish influence on the Heptaplus in works known to be available to Pico in Latin, printed or in Mithridates's corpus, while citing Alemanno and Delmedigo as evidence of contemporary Jewish thought in Pico's circle.

The Heptaplus is titled as a sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis for Lorenzo de' Medici; Roberto Salviati saw it into print at his own expense in a dedicatory epistle calling the subject physical and divine mysteries.
Black suggests that describing the Heptaplus as Pico's first fruits perhaps shows a deliberate wish to overlook the recent scandal.

Black summarises the first proem as mostly a justification, by pagan and Christian examples, of an esoteric reading of the Bible distinguishing literal 'shell' from non-literal 'kernel', with the claim that the secrets of the whole of nature lie in the six days.

Black summarises the second proem as describing a theory of allegory related to a cosmic model of three worlds, the sublunary, the celestial and the angelic or intellectual, each of the seven expositions except the last treating an aspect of these worlds separately or in combination, in seven chapters each.
The Genesis text quoted after the proems runs from verse 1 to verse 27 in the Vulgate, ending with the creation of man on the sixth day and omitting the seventh day of Genesis 2.1.

At the start of each exposition Pico defines a body of knowledge, such as Aristotelian physics or the angelic metaphysics of Pseudo-Dionysius, and then derives information about it from the Genesis narrative by allegorical reading.
The frame of reference of the first exposition is natural philosophy and the world of generation and corruption; it opens with the doctrines of natural philosophers, not with the Bible.

Black says the frame of reference of the second exposition is the nature and function of the ten heavenly spheres, an ascent from the first exposition, in which 'heaven' is the empyrean and the eight lower spheres are 'earth'.
In the second exposition Pico invokes his first-proem principle that Moses must not be made to look as if he had left anything out, to explain why four planets go unmentioned.

Black says Pico credits an unnamed 'ancient Hebrew' doctrine, held to be a deeper mystery, that Jupiter and Mars are included in the sun and Venus and Mercury in the moon; the Hebrews give no reasons, so Pico supplies reason himself.
Pico says that whether one follows the authority of Aristotle, Avicenna or Averroes on celestial influence, their words, correctly interpreted, accord with those of Moses.

Black reports that the second exposition ends with Pico's warning that our souls, on the authority of Plato and unnamed theologians, were mixed in the same bowl as the heavenly bodies, so we should not fear, love and honour them rather than Christ.

Black says that in the Third Exposition Pico had initially intended two expositions of the angelic world, one on Jewish teaching and one on Pseudo-Dionysius, but for lack of space and time concentrates on Dionysius alone, planning another book on the Jewish doctrine in which he will separate what accords with Catholic faith from what does not.
q: From consideration of the celestial spheres Pico ascends to contemplation of the intellectual world above them. He had initially intended to provide two expositions of the angelic world, one based on the teachings of the Jews, the other on Pseudo-Dionysius, …

text: Black notes that Pico says he follows the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather of Paul and Hierotheus whom Dionysius followed, and that the existence of Hierotheus, whom Pseudo-Dionysius calls his teacher, has been doubted.

Black says the third exposition begins by analysing the relationship of unity and number, applied to God and creation as a Pythagorean technique, and holds that as number depends on unity so angels depend on God.
Black identifies the third exposition as treating angels as numbers: an angel is not unity itself, for it would then be God, so it must be number.

Black says Pico defines every number as imperfect as a multiplicity and perfect as a unity, and uses this interplay of perfection through participation in unity and imperfection through multiplicity as the definition of the nature of angels in general.

Black states that an angel is imperfect in two respects: in essence, since it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and in cognition, since it is not intellection itself but understanding happens to it.

Black reads the first day in the third exposition as the drama of the angel overcoming its double imperfection: earth is its rough, unformed essence and heaven the acting of its essence and participation of unity in multiplicity, that is its connection to ipsum esse.

Black explains that in the third exposition the angel has an intellectual capacity but must be given intelligible forms, represented by light, which are accidents of its intellect and not part of its essence.

Black reports that Pico's exegesis of 'one day' says the bond between forms and the angelic mind is stronger than that between forms and the human intellect, citing Averroes and Maimonides for the point and adding his own reason that the forms are joined to the angelic mind indivisibly.
Black says Pico follows Pseudo-Dionysius in dividing the angelic hierarchy into three groups, which he represents by the two groups of waters and the firmament.

In Black's outline the lowest angelic group assists man, the middle group administers the celestial spheres, and the highest is engaged only in contemplation; the final chapter says Christ, though a man, was superior to the angels.
Black points to Proclus's Elements of Theology, Proposition 1, for the idea that every number participates unity.
Black notes that another Dionysian discussion of the dependency of all creation on God, in De caelesti hierarchia, comes immediately before the discussion of the angelic hierarchies.
The Fourth Exposition begins by asserting that every detail of the creation narrative related to the three worlds can also be read as referring to man himself.
Black reports that in the fourth exposition, above the rational soul lies 'intelligence', shared with angels, and below it a 'sensual part' shared with animals.

Black says the Spirit of God moving over the upper waters is identified in the fourth exposition with a greater and more divine intellect that illuminates the human intellect; Pico leaves open whether this is God or a mind close and akin to man.
q: The Spirit of God, which moves over the upper waters, is identified with 'a greater and more divine intellect' which illuminates the human intellect.

text: Black says that in the fourth chapter of the Fourth Exposition Pico refers to a great controversy with unnamed recent philosophers, denying that sun and moon stand for the actual and potential intellect, and takes them to name two aspects of the one human intellect, turned up toward the greater intellect or down toward the sensual powers.

Black says that at the start of the fifth exposition Pico dedicates the first day's section to the angelic world and the other parts to the other worlds in succession, and that the first four expositions gave self-contained bodies of knowledge whereas the fifth turns to the vertical hierarchy of the cosmos as a whole, the golden chain of Homer.

Black reports that the Fifth Exposition opens with angelic cognition, holding that the angelic nature is pure intellect, that minds are like eyes, and that angelic cognition involves some combination of actuality and potentiality represented by heaven and earth.
Black says the whole sixth chapter of the fifth exposition is reminiscent of the Oratio, noting especially the placing of man at the midpoint of the world and the Hermetic citation.
Pico argues that man's likeness to God cannot rest on the action of mind, because in that respect angels have a closer affinity to God than man does.

Black says Pico locates the unique affinity of man and God in the way man's substance itself holds the substances of all natures, unlike angels and other intelligent creatures, which contain things only accidentally by knowing them.

Black says God contains all things as their principium and in better quality than in themselves, while man contains them as their medium, holding higher things in an inferior quality and lower things in a superior one.
In the seventh chapter of the fifth exposition, Black says, man's moral behaviour is held to affect the cosmos as a whole, which with God will avenge itself on him if he neglects his obligations.

Black observes that the Sixth Exposition has two readings of the Genesis narrative and suggests a threefold division of the Heptaplus into the first five expositions, the sixth and the seventh, which takes its cue from Pico's understanding of the Trinity.

Black reports that the Sixth Exposition opens by defining God as unity divided into three, and finds three aspects of unity in each created thing: with itself, with another, and with its maker; these are mirrored in the structure of the Heptaplus, with expositions one to five, six and seven presenting them in turn.
Black says the sixth exposition is built on the notion of 'copulare', the first part concerning knowledge and the second morality, a connection he takes up in Chapter 6.

Black notes that the first part of the sixth exposition sets out a universal taxonomy of relationships between entities, at most fifteen according to Pico, and that Pico stretches the Genesis text, which never mentions bodies, to fit his allegorical reading.

Black reports that in the sixth chapter of the sixth exposition Pico alludes to a deeper mystery: the eventual union of the part of intellectual light in us with the first mind, where all understanding is complete.
Black says that in the seventh chapter of the Sixth Exposition union with God is possible only through Christ, the mean who unites man and God, which binds the two halves of the exposition together.
Black says the Seventh Exposition distinguishes natural felicitas, in which something attains God in itself, from supernatural felicitas, in which it attains God in Himself.

Black reports that Pico says no philosophical school takes man back to his beginning or end, which only theology offers; a footnote quotes Pico grouping several philosophers who place our reason in the intellect in act or in a higher one akin to us.
Black says that in the seventh exposition the capacity for supernatural felicitas is limited to man and angels, and neither can reach it without the help of Christ.

Black says the Seventh Exposition presents the progress to supernatural felicitas as a journey of all humanity through sacred history, its central fourth chapter arguing from Jewish sources that Christ is the Messiah.

Black says the final section of the Heptaplus returns to the word bereshit and abandons allegory for a technique of letter combination derived from kabbalistic exegetical works, producing a sentence that summarises the Heptaplus and confirms Pico's claim that everything can be found in Moses's text.
q: At this point the main body of the Heptaplus is complete. There follows, however, a final section in which Pico returns to the first word of the Bible bereshit in Hebrew which he has until now neglected. He also turns …

text: Black concludes that the Heptaplus is an array of allegorical identifications between things in the Genesis account and things or concepts in various philosophical disciplines, the choice of disciplines fixed by the three-world model, and built from previous example (auctoritas) or ratio, meaning analogies of structure.
Black distinguishes the Heptaplus's practice of allegorical reading from its theory of allegory, the relation of which to the work's form and content and to other theories is his subject of study.
Black says Pico tells his audience that his work is unprecedented and not derived from previous commentators, thereby framing the Heptaplus in opposition to preceding commentary traditions.

Black says the medieval fourfold method of literal, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses remained dominant in the fifteenth century, and that Pico himself in the Apologia recognised it as the normal Christian way of reading the Bible.

Black observes that Nicholas of Lyra's stricter definition of the spiritual senses was copied almost verbatim from Aquinas at the start of the Summa theologiae, which the quoted passage grounds partly in Dionysius on the new law as figure of future glory.
q: Nor did the stricter definition given in the Postilla originate from the pen of Nicholas of Lyra: he copied, almost

text: Black says Pico's phrase 'apud nos' comes in his defence of kabbalah in the Apologia, where he argues that the Jews have a fourfold scheme parallel to the Christian one, with Pesat, Midras, Sechel and Cabala as the literal, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses.

Black argues that aligning the fourfold methods of the two traditions was meant to make kabbalah less alien to Christian readers, so that Pico's argument depends on readers taking the fourfold method as the norm.

Black thinks Pico's Apologia matching of terms to senses contains a mistake, since Sechel as practised by Gersonides, Maimonides and Ibn Ezra would more accurately be the allegorical and Midras the tropological, perhaps from haste in writing the Apologia.
Black notes that the survey of incunable biblical commentary shows no printed commentaries solely and specifically on Genesis, though Genesis commentaries may have existed in manuscript.

Black sums up that the survey presents the norms for biblical interpretation in the late fifteenth century, against which Pico's own comment on which authors bear on the Genesis narrative is largely antithetical.

Black says that in the first proem Pico, to substantiate the claim that his method is new, lists authorities he will not imitate, and that this list shows what Pico himself regarded as significant in biblical commentary.
q: Before telling his readers what the Heptaplus is, Pico informs them of what it is not. He claims that his method of interpretation is new. To substantiate this claim, he gives a list of authorities 'robust minds' in the field …

text: Black says the Heptaplus is explicitly defined by its author against a background of exegesis in four languages and two faiths, stretching from well-known Latin exegetes into an uncertain twilight of Greek and Hebrew figures unrepresentative of fifteenth-century Christian commentary.

Black identifies Pico's listed exegetes guided by Pico's phrase 'super hoc libro', meaning works specifically on Genesis, and by Pico's library inventories and other collections, noting that Pico's own access to the Vatican appears to have ended in March 1487.
Black notes that both Albertus and Aegidius figure in the Conclusiones, Aegidius with eleven conclusions and Albertus with sixteen.
Black says Pico was particularly interested in Origen, whose orthodoxy Pico defends in the Apologia, and that Origen's work on Genesis probably reached him in the Latin translation of Rufinus.

Black argues that Pico's only access to Didymus's lost Genesis commentary must have been through the Genesis catena, and that Pico's mention of an author, as with Didymus, does not imply that the author's works were directly available to him.

Black proposes that Pico's 'Eusebius' is Eusebius of Emesa because the works by another Eusebius in Pico's library contain no interpretation of Genesis whereas Emesa's commentary on the Octateuch was among the most cited in the Genesis catena.
Black leaves open which of two authors Pico's 'Theodoretus' means, since the catena labels excerpts from 'Theodorus' variously.

Black concludes, leaving some names unresolved, that many of Pico's listed authors may have reached him only as names and fragments, and that the catena played a decisive role in forming his list whether or not it played any role in his actual exegesis.

Black says Pico's 'Chaldeans' Anchelos and Ionethes are traditional names for two Aramaic Targumim, and that Pico possessed a 1482 Pentateuch containing the Targum Onkelos with the commentary of Rashi.
Black thinks it likely that Pico's 'Simeon' the Chaldean is Simeon bar Yohai, but says that what in fact lies behind the reference is the Zohar, attributed to him.

Black says Pico knew of the Zohar but named it only once and there is no evidence he had the work itself; his knowledge appears to have come from intermediaries, notably Recanati's Pentateuch commentary, which quotes it extensively.

Black says Pico regarded Maimonides as a kabbalist, being particularly influenced by Abulafia's commentary on the Guide (Sitrei Torah), which Mithridates translated as De secretis legis and which played a formative role in Pico's conception of kabbalah.

Black observes that the chapter headings of Abulafia's work include creation topics, suggesting Pico would have regarded it as a source on the Genesis narrative, and thinks it conceivable that Pico's 'Abraam' refers to Abulafia.

Black says Pico owned a printed Nahmanides Pentateuch commentary and mentions Nahmanides in the Apologia, the Psalms expositions and the Heptaplus, but the Heptaplus reference could have come from Recanati's quotation of him, so it is unclear how much Pico read Nahmanides.

Black says Gersonides exercised an undeniable influence on Pico's concept of exegesis, seen in the Job manuscript and in Pico's annotated Mithridates translation of Gersonides on the Song of Songs, though it is unclear that Pico read Gersonides on the Pentateuch.
q: Levi ben Gershom (otherwise known as Gersonides), on the other hand, exercised an undeniable influence on Pico's concept of exegesis. In the first place, this is evident from Pico's Job manuscript, which bears the imprint of Gersonides's own commentary on …

text: Black says Recanati's Pentateuch commentary was Pico's principal point of entry to the Zohar, was translated for him by Mithridates in 1486, and was an influential source for his interpretation of kabbalah in the 900 Conclusiones.

Black sums up that the Hebrew exegetes in Pico's list are a cross-section of the best-known medieval Jewish exegetes, that Pico had access to their works though often only in Hebrew, and that the Psalm citations show he could draw on untranslated works such as Ibn Ezra and Rashi.

Black says 'Neonias' probably refers to Nehunya ben Ha-Kanah, to whom the Bahir was attributed; the Bahir opens with a quotation from him, Pico read it in Mithridates's version and used it in the Conclusiones.

Black notes that the Bahir cites a Rabbi Johanan on Genesis 1, that Eleazar, Abba and Isaac are cited in the Zohar and so in Recanati, and that these names also occur in Bereshit Rabbah, of which Pico owned an untranslated copy; other sources may have existed.

Black argues that one essential function of Pico's list of rejected authorities is to impress the reader with his acquaintance with a wide range of commentaries, and that formulating the list negatively doubles its rhetorical impact.
q: What can we conclude from this analysis? Clearly, one essential function of the list is to impress the reader. While not neglecting a representative sample of canonical works, it serves to emphasize Pico's acquaintance with a remarkably wide range of …

text: Black warns that knowing an author's name does not imply knowing the text: many 'ancient Hebrews' were known through intermediaries such as the Bahir and Recanati, and many early Greek exegetes through fragments in the catena.
Black concludes that despite these doubts the list shows Pico's frame of reference was broad compared with contemporary norms and his exegetical toolkit better stocked than most.

Black says the attention Pico gives to Genesis in the Heptaplus differs fundamentally from his other exegetical works; the Heptaplus relies on the Vulgate text of Genesis 1.1-27, whereas the Job manuscript and Psalms commentaries scrutinise translation.

Black reports that in a 1489 letter to Andrea Corneo Pico described a new work undertaken with the encouragement of Lorenzo de' Medici, to interpret the Psalms at length and to defend the Septuagint against the Jews.

Black says the double aim of the Psalm expositions, interpretation and defence of a translation, was repeated at the beginning of the Heptaplus, showing that philology's purpose was polemical rather than merely scholarly.

Black concludes from soundings that Pico's philological sections compare four versions of the Psalms, give the Septuagint precedence and correct Hebrew exegetes by reference to textual transmission; defending the Septuagint also defends the standard Gallician Psalter, making Pico a more conservative philologist than Valla or Manetti.
The Heptaplus abandons the fourfold senses of Scripture and sets up a new, explicitly theorised concept of allegory, which Pico claims is unique to his work.
The Heptaplus shows no interest in philology as such; when Pico cites the Hebrew or the Septuagint his aim is interpretative, not textual.
In the second proem Pico derives the Hebrew word he transcribes asciamaim from words for fire and water, symbolising the highest and lowest worlds, to show that the heavens hold a median position.
In Black's account, Pico's exposition of Psalm 47 reads the city of God as the spiritual world and the kings of the earth as corporeal spheres separated from corruption.
loc: expositiones in psalmos | Psalm 47, expositio physica

text: The first proem does not chiefly justify Pico's allegorical theory but his attitude to Moses's text, through two arguments: aligning Moses with ancient philosophy, and then claiming a concealed layer of meaning in the Bible.

Black locates the same esoteric attitude in two non-Christian traditions, the Neoplatonic, reaching Christianity through Pseudo-Dionysius, and the kabbalistic, known to Pico through translations made for him by Mithridates and through contacts in the Italian Jewish community.

In the Heptaplus Pico deliberately removed references to the word kabbalah; Black argues this expurgation is more apparent than substantial, though several typical kabbalistic approaches to the biblical text are absent.
