Pico's argument that Moses was a master of all learning rests on evidence including a book called Sapientia, the testimony of Luke and Philo, Numenius's phrase 'Attic Moses', and Hermippus on Pythagoras.
The first proem's argument is aimed at unidentified opponents who separate Moses's text from the philosophers and find Moses rough and popular by comparison.

To explain the disparity between the apparent simplicity of Moses's book and the complexity proper to great philosophy, Pico invokes esotericism: the custom of ancient wise men not to write of divine things, or to write of them in a concealed fashion.

A substantial part of the first proem's argument for esotericism repeats historical and thematic references from the Commento, the Apologia and the Oratio, the last being essentially a verbatim transcript of the Apologia at this point.
The esoteric hermeneutic stance of the Heptaplus was for the most part already developed by 1486; the Heptaplus version expands earlier versions without substantial deviation.

Pico's historical examples share the idea of a demarcation between initiated and uninitiated, which he equates with a division of reading into exoteric or literal for the multitude and esoteric or non-literal for the elite, whom he calls the perfect.
Black holds that esotericism of Pico's kind was not typical of Christianity throughout its history but arose at a particular time for particular reasons and was later superseded.
Pico regarded Pseudo-Dionysius as a convert of Paul and so a first-century figure, but Black thinks the direct sources of Pico's idea of esotericism were probably later.

The elements of Pico's esotericism were current in late second and early third century Christian exegesis and found their fullest expression in Clement of Alexandria's Stromata, and much later Christian hermeneutics withdrew from Clement's position.
Clement held that gnosis is an esoteric accomplishment open to very few and is facilitated by non-literal reading of Scripture and by oral transmission of secret doctrine.

Origen made less of the dichotomy between those who can and cannot understand the mysteries than Clement did; the difference is quantitative rather than qualitative, so that Origen appears a watered-down version of Clement.

Black finds a tension in early Christian exegetes, who kept esoteric exclusivity for part of their knowledge while criticising the heretical esotericism of the gnostics, so that the line between masses and elite is somewhat blurred.

Basil, in his third homily on Genesis, rejected as a pernicious mixture of dreams and old wives' tales the allegorical view that the waters above the heavens signify spiritual and incorporeal powers, and would think of water as water.
The compilers of the Greek catenae favoured literal exegesis and, in their selection, tended to exercise an anti-allegorical stance, so much of the early Greek allegorical tradition did not pass on.
Black judges it highly unlikely that Clement of Alexandria was Pico's direct source for esotericism, although his approach to non-literal reading resembles Pico's.
The only surviving manuscript of Clement's Stromata was in the Medici library and was consulted by Poliziano, but a record of purchase shows it did not arrive there until 1492.

In the early 1490s Lorenzo de' Medici was making a concerted effort to procure rare early Greek Christian texts, and Pico accompanied Poliziano on research and buying missions to this end, notably in the summer of 1491.

Pico does not mention Clement in the Heptaplus, and his only specific citation of the Stromata is in the Disputationes, which Black takes as further support for the view that no copy of the Stromata was available before 1492.

Black reduces the Greek allegorical exegesis of Genesis actually available to Pico to a core of Origen, in Rufinus's translation, and Philo, a narrower range than the roll-call of authors in the previous chapter suggests.
Christian interpretation from late antiquity to the late Middle Ages sought to define the literal and non-literal ever more strictly not to separate them but to unite them more closely.

For Augustine the purpose of interpretation is to promote unity among believers and between believers and God, and a secret language comprehensible only to a few, subverting the community, was the defining feature of magic.
Gregory the Great presents the historical and spiritual senses as two ends of a continuum, and his hierarchy of believers was pedagogic rather than elitist.
Black holds that medieval non-literal reading, even where the senses were most rigorously delimited, was directed at a mass audience and was not elitist in practice or theory.

Black argues that the Christian tradition overcame the dichotomy between audiences and text, while the opposition of initiate and uninitiate as a basis for allegory persisted in two traditions, one widely known in the Latin West and one almost unknown there.
Of the Neoplatonic authors, Macrobius and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite stand out from the perspective of the Latin Middle Ages.

The Pseudo-Dionysian corpus, by an unknown late fifth or early sixth century author heavily influenced by later Neoplatonists, was taken in the Middle Ages to date from the first century and to comprise four treatises and ten letters, including the Celestial Hierarchy.
q: The Pseudo-Dionysian corpus, a group of religious works written in Greek by an unknown author in the late fifth or early sixth century and heavily influenced by the later Neoplatonists, was attributed (at its first recorded appearance in 532) to …

text: The Dionysian corpus was very widely received in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, in at least six Latin translations, many manuscripts and nine printed editions before 1500, and was absorbed into scholastic theology by Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas.

Black holds that the Dionysian corpus is thoroughly infused with the same form of esotericism found in Clement, citing injunctions to guard holy things from the uninitiated and to keep them from the multitude.

It is unclear whether Pico came across Valla's 1457 doubts about the Areopagite authorship of the Dionysian corpus, since the Adnotationes did not achieve significant circulation in the fifteenth century.

In 1489 Dionysius was still by and large regarded as the Areopagite, Valla's criticism having yet to take effect, and Ficino was about to produce his own translations of part of the corpus, the second produced in Florence in the fifteenth century.
q: In any case, in 1489 Dionysius was still, by and large, the Areopagite; the criticism of Valla had yet to take effect; and Marsilio Ficino was about to produce his own translations of part of the corpus—the second translation produced …

text: Pico's admiration for Pseudo-Dionysius is clear in the Commento, where he calls him prince of Christian theologians, and Black defers to a later chapter Dionysius's role as a model for Pico's interpretative theory.

The kabbalistic tradition is missing from Pico's account of esotericism in the first proem, although only a couple of years earlier he had made it central to corresponding accounts in the Commento and the Apologia.

In the Commento Pico introduces kabbalah as one among many examples of esoteric transmission, in order to justify his reading of Girolamo Benivieni's canzone as presenting metaphysical truths in a veiled manner.

Black cites Pico's Commento as saying that Dionysius, expounding the names of God and the angelic and ecclesiastical hierarchy, commanded Timothy to keep the book hidden from all but the few who were worthy.

In the Apologia kabbalah is the overall subject of the esoteric argument, and Pico aims to align it with less alien traditions so as to make it acceptable to a Christian audience, saying it is nothing other than this same esoteric tradition.

Pico's definition of kabbalah occurs in his defence of the ninth of the magical conclusions according to his own opinion, which was the fifth of the condemned conclusions: no science makes us more certain of Christ's divinity than Magic and Kabbalah.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: In Pico's defence of that conclusion, kabbalah is the true exposition of the Pentateuch handed to Moses on Sinai alongside the written law, a double law, one literal and written, one spiritual and communicated orally.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: Pico holds that the books of kabbalah recorded the mysteries and were never corrupted, so that almost everything in them confirms Christianity, and he cites Esdras, Paul, Origen, Hilary and Matthew as witnesses.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: In Black's summary of the Apologia, Pico argues that, because the patristic authors cite Jewish doctrine with approval and only the kabbalists predate them among three Jewish sects, they can only mean the kabbalists, the true revelation to Moses.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: Pico distinguishes the senses of the word kabbalah: a primary and proper sense, a usurped sense for any secret science, and two transumptive senses, the letter-combinatory ars combinandi and a science of the powers of superlunary things.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: Black holds that Pico's division of the word's senses diverts blame from the phenomenon of kabbalah to the word, presenting the censure as a misunderstanding from insufficiently defined terms.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: When Pico rewrote the offending conclusions at the end of the Apologia, the reference to kabbalah in the ninth magical conclusion was replaced by a formulation about the Gospel doctrine and Christian theology, which Black says is what he meant by true kabbalah, with the offending word removed.
loc: apologia | defence of the ninth magical conclusion

text: Black draws three points from the Apologia for the Heptaplus: the word kabbalah never occurs there; the first proem really discusses kabbalah as Pico sees it, a spiritual interpretation embodying a secret tradition going back to Moses; and it rests on two earlier redactions with the word excised.

Black thinks Pico probably deleted the kabbalah passages from his final account of esoteric transmission out of prudence, since the bull condemning the Conclusiones, issued by Innocent VIII on 15 December 1487, remained in force until 18 June 1493.
q: We are faced with a deliberate rhetorical strategy. It seems likely that when Pico produced this final revision of his account of esoteric transmission, he consciously deleted the passages referring to kabbalah for reasons of prudence. The bull, which Innocent …

text: Black says the pope was displeased by the Heptaplus as a continuation of the errors of the Conclusiones but it did not undergo the same scrutiny, so Pico's calculation proved correct; he had not lost interest in kabbalah but decided not to emphasise it.

Black holds that Pico, unlike most Christian contemporaries, was well informed about kabbalistic ideas of esoteric transmission, which had contemporary resonance because the sharp dichotomy of masses and elite and of literal and non-literal reading was constant in medieval Jewish tradition.

Alemanno's Hay ha-olamim was not written for Pico and was not finished until 1503, but since Alemanno had worked on it since 1470 and was a colleague or in some respects teacher of Pico, dissemination of parts of it to Pico cannot be discounted.
In Alemanno's account the masses and the elite correspond to the narrative and speculative parts of a text, which must be kept separate, and he follows the distinction with an exegesis of Genesis 1.

Delmedigo's Behinat ha-dat, written after his return to Crete in 1490, cannot be a direct textual influence on the Heptaplus, but together with Alemanno's it shows the centrality of the elite/masses idea in Jewish tradition and suggests a shared source.

Black traces the terms of Alemanno's and Delmedigo's discussions to Averroes's Decisive Treatise, which distinguishes interpreters of demonstration, of dialectic, and the multitude who understand only rhetoric.

Maimonides identified the Work of the Beginning (Genesis 1) with physics and the Work of the Chariot (Ezekiel 1) with metaphysics and, following rabbinic injunctions, restricted their audiences, so these matters are taught in parables and allegories.

Black notes that Pico in the first proem gave an injunction, attributed to Jerome, that the creation not be approached before mature age, whereas Jerome wrote thirty years; Black presumes Pico, then about 26, deliberately rephrased it vaguely.
In Maimonides, if Plato and other philosophers concealed teachings on form, matter and privation, then a fortiori Moses must have.

Abulafia's commentary on the Guide, called De secretis legis in Mithridates's translation for Pico, repeats Nahmanides that the whole Torah is full of the names of God, in the Latin extended to the angels of the sacred celestial order.

Abulafia distinguishes two ways of knowing Moses's law, by the literal sense and by the divine names and secrets handed down orally, and says the two types of people to whom these correspond are inseparable from these two readings.

The exegetical works of the kabbalists that Mithridates translated for Pico offered several radical methods of reading which undermine the grammar and syntax of the biblical text in search of the non-literal sense.

The sefirot are ten hierarchical emanations of divine power connecting the inmost aspect of God to the created universe; the word means numbers, Mithridates renders it numerationes, and each is named after an attribute of God.
q: The metaphysical structure of the sefirot is one of the most central (and controversial) features of kabbalah in general, although some schools of thought emphasized it, while others neglected it. The Hebrew word sefirot (singular: sefirah) literally means “numbers”; in …

text: Because the sefirot were considered the vessels through which the universe was drawn from non-being to being, the kabbalists linked the creation narrative to them, as in the Mysterium operis Geneseos translated for Pico by Mithridates, where words of Genesis 1.1 are equated with sefirot such as wisdom, understanding and clemency.

Black identifies nine of the ten Latin attributes in that passage as Latin terms for sefirot in one translation system known to Pico, and antiquus dierum with the first sefirah Keter, though he has not found Pico's direct source for that wording.
Sefirotic exegesis, prominent in the texts available to Pico and in many Conclusiones, has no place in the Heptaplus, where the sefirot as a metaphysical system are entirely absent.

Black notes that some commentators have tried to relate Pico's cosmic structure to the sefirot; in his own opinion such links can be inferred from the Conclusiones but are not explicit in the Heptaplus and do not contribute to understanding it.
q: Some commentators have attempted to relate the cosmic structure proposed by Pico to the sefirot. I shall discuss this in Ch. 5, section 1.2. My own opinion is that, although such links can be inferred from the Conclusiones, they are …

text: Because Hebrew letters are also numbers, exegetes linked concepts by numerical sums; this occurs throughout the texts translated for Pico, notably Abulafia's, and is entirely absent from the Heptaplus.
q: As each letter of the Hebrew alphabet is also a number, every word has a numerical sum. Some exegetes made use of this to link apparently unconnected concepts or scriptural passages.

text: The ars combinandi appears in the Heptaplus only in the final untitled chapter, where Pico recombines the letters of bereshit, and there he avoids the word kabbalah, calling it another method of interpretation.

Black argues that the other kabbalistic forms of reading do not occur in the Heptaplus, but the hermeneutic idea behind them, that literal and non-literal senses suit two distinct bodies of people, is fundamental to it.

Black concludes that Pico's hermeneutic stance has more affinity with early Greek Christian interpreters than later Latin ones, but limits on circulation of that material make it likely that his direct sources were later authors, and source assignments need caution.
Black notes that a list of Greeks who learnt from the Egyptians, as in Pico's first proem, appears in Iamblichus's De mysteriis, which Ficino translated.

Black notes that Numenius's phrase Plato as Attic Moses is transmitted in Eusebius's Preparatio evangelica, and that no precise source is located for the book Sapientia attributed to Solomon, although Nahmanides refers to such a work and a Hebrew copy of his commentary was in Pico's library.

On Black's analysis the sources of the first proem's esoteric examples are, apart from the Bible, later compilers such as Eusebius, Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch, and Neoplatonic sources Pico had ready access to: Porphyry, Iamblichus and Pseudo-Dionysius.

Black concludes that the same esoteric stance flourished in the Jewish tradition with methods that undermine grammar and syntax; Pico knew these but used most of them nowhere in the Heptaplus, developing instead his own theory of allegory.
The first proem justifies esoteric reading of Genesis in general terms, while the second proem shows in detail how the reading is to be carried out.

The second proem has three main subjects, the structure of the cosmos, the theory of allegory and the arrangement of the Heptaplus, and Pico argues that both the theory of allegory and the arrangement of the whole book grow out of the cosmic structure.
Black says his chapter will deepen the grounding of the Heptaplus in late Neoplatonism, specifically Proclus and, in a Christian context, Pseudo-Dionysius.
Pico devotes about a third of the second proem to the structure of the cosmos, which has two central aspects: the division of the cosmos into three worlds and the relationship between those worlds.

Pico's three worlds are arranged hierarchically: the topmost is the angelic or intellectual world, in the terms of theologians and philosophers respectively, then the celestial world, then the sublunar and elemental world.

The highest world is characterised by light, fire, perpetual life and stability, the lowest is its opposite in every respect, the middle is a mixture of fire and water, light and shadow, and the third world is moved by the second and the second by the first.
q: These three worlds are inter-related primarily by comparison. The highest world is characterized by light, fire, perpetual life and stability. The lowest world is its opposite in every respect, a place of darkness, watery instability, and the vicissitude of life …

text: In Black's account the individual characteristics of the three worlds are the subjects of the first three expositions of the Heptaplus, and the fifth and sixth expositions examine the interconnections between them.

Pico espouses a geocentric universe of ten concentric spheres, the empyrean, the primum mobile, the sphere of the fixed stars and the seven planets, following one version of contemporary astronomical orthodoxy that echoes Sacrobosco and Aquinas, though there was no consensus in his time.

The empyrean is chiefly a theological concept, the abode of the angels, which Pico says is only believed to exist, since it does not follow from the Aristotelian model of the universe he and his contemporaries adopted.

Black identifies an inconsistency in Pico's scheme: although the philosophical division into angelic, celestial and terrestrial would lead one to equate the empyrean with the angelic world, Pico treats it as the foremost celestial sphere, leader of the other nine, the monad filling the denary.
q: At this point we should note an inconsistency in Pico’s scheme. Given that his ‘philosophical’ taxonomy of the universe breaks down into angelic, celestial and terrestrial, we would naturally expect the empyrean to be equated with the first of these …

text: Black suggests that the numerological significance of the structure led Pico to overlook this inconsistency, since it gave a symmetrical correspondence: God and nine ranks of angels in the first world, the empyrean and nine heavenly spheres in the second, prime matter and nine categories of corruptible forms in the third.

In Pico's own words as quoted by Black, God, the first unity, presides over nine orders of angels as over so many spheres and, himself unmoved, moves them all to himself; in the middle world the empyrean presides over nine celestial spheres, and in the elemental world there are nine spheres of corruptible forms after prime matter.

Black holds that the nature of the Heptaplus as a whole suggests that this numerological consideration, rather than any astronomical school, led Pico to articulate the cosmic structure as he did, and that Pico was not overly concerned with the minutiae of contemporary astronomy.

Black notes that the three-world structure is embedded in several of Pico's works and that the Oratio describes God decorating the super-celestial region with minds, the heavenly spheres with eternal souls and the lowest world with animals.

In the Commento Pico attributes to the Platonists a division of all creatures into three levels: corporeal and visible things, wholly incorporeal separate intellectual nature which our theologians call angelic, and between them the rational soul, which is subject to the angelic and in charge of the corporeal.

Pico gives no source for the threefold structure beyond the unnamed Platonists in the Commento and simply antiquity in the Heptaplus, and the Neoplatonic character of the model, emphatic in the Commento and still visible in the Oratio, is less evident in the Heptaplus.

Black traces a transformation of the threefold model: the Commento gives a Plotinian conception of Soul as a hypostasis in a psychological context; the Oratio keeps the hypostasis terminology but links Soul to the celestial spheres, moving toward cosmogony; and the Heptaplus abandons the Neoplatonic terminology but keeps the threefold schema.

Black argues that the Plotinian hypostases One, Mind and Soul do not correspond well with Pico's three worlds: Mind must be the angelic or intellectual world but Pico has placed God, the One, there too, blurring the first two hypostases, while Soul correlates with the celestial spheres and nothing corresponds to sublunar life.

Black notes that the three divisions of the universe in Macrobius's Somnium Scipionis, two twofold and one threefold, none agrees with Pico's cosmic model, and Pico owned Macrobius's work and Proclus's commentary on the Timaeus.
Black finds little evidence that Platonists structured the cosmos as Pico does, and notes that Proclus's threefold cosmic model in the Elements of Theology is not consonant with Pico's.
q: Despite the connection between Platonism and the threefold model of the universe set out in the Commento, there is little evidence that Platonists tended to structure the cosmos in the way Pico proposes.23 Proclus himself, in the Elements of Theology, …

text: Black holds that what mattered to Pico about the threefold model was agreement with, or at least no direct contradiction by, a spectrum of cosmological systems, and that it seems likely he abandoned the specifically Platonizing terminology of his earlier work to assist this syncretistic effort.

Kristeller, as quoted by Black, held that presenting the angels, stars and elementary spheres as a sequence of three worlds is quite unusual in the Greek and Latin traditions, a combination of two dualistic schemes, and concluded that Pico probably took it from Hebrew, probably cabalistic, sources.
Black states that Kristeller's conclusion that the three-world model derives from Jewish sources agrees with his own discussion.

Black argues that the model of the Heptaplus is in accordance with Aristotle's ontology at the start of Metaphysics XII, of sensible perishable, sensible eternal and immovable substance, matching Pico's sublunar, celestial and intellectual worlds, though he thinks a direct link implausible without later developments in the Aristotelian tradition.
q: Although the shift from the psychological model of the Commento to the ontological model of the Heptaplus creates problems for a Platonist reading, it has other advantages. First among these is that the model of the Heptaplus is in accordance …

text: The closest formulation to Pico's three worlds that Black has found in any tradition is in Maimonides's Guide of the Perplexed, where all entities but the creator are divided into separate intellect, heavenly bodies with eternal forms, and bodies subject to generation and corruption.

Samuel ibn Tibbon's commentary on Ecclesiastes states that beings fall into three species, lowest matter and its products, celestial bodies, and above them incorporeal intelligences, which Black cites as showing the idea was a commonplace in that tradition.

Black concludes that the Maimonides passage and Ibn Tibbon's widely circulated Hebrew work suggest the threefold division was unexceptional and was frequently met in the Jewish tradition in an Aristotelian rather than Platonic context.

In the Conclusiones Pico identified the three parts of particular philosophy, on divine, intermediate and sensible natures, with the triple Merkavah, and in the Heptaplus he linked the threefold division of worlds to the tabernacle and to man.

Black assumes Pico regarded the triple world division as related to kabbalah because he viewed Maimonides as a kabbalist, and notes that in the Conclusiones Pico drew a correspondence between the ten spheres and the ten sefirot.

Black argues that the link between the sefirot and the spheres is one of shared structure only, that the sefirotic names and attributes are absent from the Heptaplus and only the number ten remains, and that the threefold structure needs no kabbalistic reading and would probably be distorted by sefirotic metaphysics.
q: It seems likely that these ideas remained in his mind during the writing of the Heptaplus, just as I have argued, in Chapter 4, that the aspect of kabbalah as an example of esoteric tradition remained in his mind while …

text: Wirszubski argues, from evidence in the fiftieth Conclusion, that the three worlds, equated with the triple merkavah, are equivalent to a triadic grouping of the sefirot; Black finds this entirely possible for the Conclusiones but cannot detect any use of this symbolism in the Heptaplus.
q: Wirszubski, Pico’s Encounter, 136–138, argues that the three worlds, said in Conclusiones cabalisticae … secundum opinionem propriam, 2, to be equivalent to the triple merkavah, are (on evidence drawn from the fiftieth Conclusion) therefore equivalent to a triadic grouping of …

text: Black distinguishes kabbalistic analogies of the threefold structure from a kabbalistic source, and notes that Alemanno's introduction to his Genesis commentary raises a question that seems to involve a threefold cosmos: whether the Torah's words refer to the world of change, the world of motion or the world of sefirot.

Black allows that Alemanno may have helped Pico develop the frame of reference for the triple cosmic division, but notes Pico was refining the idea since 1486 if not earlier and did not appear to meet Alemanno until 1488, so this untranslated passage cannot be inferred to be his source.

Black aims to redress the balance towards a broadly Judeo-Aristotelian perspective on the threefold cosmos, not overly beholden to Platonism or kabbalah, and thinks a single source neither possible nor desirable, this being Pico's syncretism in choosing a model linkable to Aristotelian, Platonic or Jewish ideas according to context.
q: My aim is simply to redress the balance towards a broadly Judeo-Aristotelian perspective on the threefold cosmos, not overly beholden either to Platonism or kabbalah. I do not think identification of a single source is possible, or even desirable: this …

text: The structure of the Heptaplus relies on there being three worlds, but for analysing Pico's allegorical method what matters is the sympathetic affinities between the worlds, not their number.

Pico gives two reasons repeating the first proem and adds that Moses uses a wondrous and unknown art so that the same words, context and series of the whole Scripture appropriately represent the secrets of all the worlds, so the same words can express the account of all three worlds.

Pico says the art makes Moses's book pre-eminent over the writings of the gentiles, constitutes the novelty of his own book, and makes Moses the archetype of writers because his words rest on the cosmic correspondences and comprehend all things in very few words.

Pico compares the Mosaic text's ability to comprehend all things in very few words to the way, according to Dionysius and Thomas, the angelic minds that grasp with the fewest forms are superior to lower minds needing many; a marginal note in the first edition says the Mosaic text emulates the angelic intelligence.

Black plans to explore mutual containment of the worlds as the foundation of Pico's allegorical theory, then the assertion that the Mosaic text parallels angelic intelligence and its words are analogous to forms, hoping to show the two strands are closely connected and yield a model of Pico's allegorical theory.

Black holds that the doctrine that things in the lower worlds mirror those in the upper in a worse condition, and the reverse, rests on a Neoplatonic commonplace, since emanation and causation as the Neoplatonists conceived them require mirror imaging; Pico's emphasis is that the same things occur in each world.
Although Pico ascribes the principle of mutual containment to the Presocratic Anaxagoras, Black says the particular expression of the cosmic structure is found in later Neoplatonism.
q: Although Pico claims that this idea originates with the Presocratic philosopher Anaxagoras, it is in later Neoplatonism that this particular expression of the cosmic structure is to be found.

text: Garin, for Pico's mention of Anaxagoras, refers the reader to Simplicius's commentary on Aristotle's Physics, where the saying that there is a part of everything in everything is attributed to Anaxagoras.

Proclus systematised Plotinus in the Elements of Theology; his system passed into Arabic and then into Latin as the Liber de causis, attributed to Aristotle until the thirteenth century, until William of Moerbeke's 1268 translation of the Elements let Thomas Aquinas see that the Liber de causis was based on it.
q: systematized the thought of Plotinus, with particular reference to the mechanics of causation and emanation. Proclus’s system passed into Arabic in the ninth century. From there, it was translated into Latin in the second half of the twelfth century, in …

text: A Greek manuscript of Proclus's Elements of Theology dated 1358, formerly in Pico's possession, is in the Bodleian library, Oxford.

Black starts with Proposition 103 of Proclus's Elements of Theology, that all things are in all things but properly in each, and notes that Pico included the idea in his Conclusiones in the section on Proclus, saying divine hierarchies are distinct but everything is in all things in its own mode.
q: In mapping the lines of thought which led to Pico’s position in the Heptaplus, we should start with Proposition 103 of Proclus’s Elements of Theology: All things are in all things, but properly in each

text: Black notes that the idea also occurs in Syrianus's commentary on the Metaphysics, which Pico probably owned, and in Julian's Hymn to King Helios, certainly read by Pico, but that none of these articulates it in an exegetical context.

Black holds that the ideas of mutual containment entered the Christian tradition soon after Proclus through Pseudo-Dionysius, and that both the original On the Divine Names and Aquinas's commentary on it develop the idea.
q: Soon after their formulation by Proclus these ideas entered the Christian tradition via the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whom we encountered briefly in the previous chapter.

text: Black cites Dionysius, On the Divine Names 4, on the communions of all things in all things according to the property of each, and Aquinas's comment that all things are in all things in different ways, the higher in the lower by participation and the lower in the higher in an outstanding manner.

Black argues that the chain of reception of mutual containment from its Greek roots to the Latin West runs through the two names Pico brackets together at the end of his second discussion of allegory, auctore Dionysio et divo Thoma, and that Pico could read the Greek sources but was aware of their scholastic reception.

In the Neoplatonic hierarchical cosmos underlying the Heptaplus, the condition of things degenerates as one moves down, in direct relation to number, since things further from unity take part more in multiplicity, and the order is reversible, as in Proposition 21 of Proclus's Elements of Theology.

According to Pico, as Black reports, Dionysius and Thomas both hold that angelic intelligence is superior to human because it comprehends with fewer forms, and in the Heptaplus Pico says intelligible forms are accidental to an angel's intellect yet bound to it indivisibly and perpetually, but only loosely to the human intellect.
q: According to Pico, Dionysius and Thomas Aquinas both argue that the intelligence of angels is superior to that of humans because it comprehends with fewer forms, whereas human intelligence, situated lower down the hierarchy (and therefore more subject to multiplicity …

text: Black says the precise nature of intelligible forms or species was controversial and Pico has little to say about it, but for the argument only the relative paucity or plenitude of forms in angelic or human minds matters.

Black says Dionysius in On the Divine Names VII holds that angels have simple and blessed conceptions, gather knowledge of God neither from divisible things, sense perception nor discursive reasoning, and think the intelligible things of God without matter and in a single form, while human souls travel discursively and in a circle yet can roll up the many into the one.

Black notes that Garin refers to Dionysius's De caelesti hierarchia 7 for this point, but the specific subject of the perception of simple forms by the angelic intellect is not present in that chapter, the passage being in On the Divine Names.
q: Garin, 222, refers rather to De caelesti hierarchia, 7, but the specific subject of the perception of simple forms by the angelic intellect is not present in that chapter.

text: Aquinas in the Summa theologiae holds that in all intellectual substances the light of understanding is one and simple in the first principle and more divided the further creatures are from it, so higher intellectual beings understand through fewer, more universal forms and lower ones need more numerous, less universal forms; the human intellect is at the lowest end.
Black says Thomas's theory bears the imprint of the Liber de causis, and that by Thomas's own account the common root of these speculations is Proposition 177 of the Elements of Theology.

Black describes the account of knowledge as part of the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, passed through the scholastics to Pico in an unbroken chain, with the golden chain of Homer in the fifth exposition alluding to it, and lists Albertus Magnus, Henry of Ghent, Aegidius Romanus, Bessarion and Ficino among its exponents.

On this ontology, which Black says originates with Plotinus, the universe has a twofold dynamic, the procession of all things from God or the One (proodos) and the reversion of things back to it (epistrophe), and this model influences Pico's theory of allegory.

Black says Pico believed language mirrors the cosmic structure, since the three worlds exchange names as well as natures, so that divine things may be represented by things of the lower worlds, now by stars, now by wheels and animals, now by elements.

Black notes that Dionysius's De caelesti hierarchia closes with a long discussion of how the Bible depicts angels through fire, animals and wheels, mostly from Ezekiel, and thinks the consonance with Pico's account stronger than a shared reading of Ezekiel.

Black argues that the opening of the last chapter of On the Celestial Hierarchy restates, from the exegete's standpoint, the link between the hierarchy of being and cognition: the exegete is not tied to the human plane but can rise through biblical symbols to the simplicity that underlies the images.

At the start of chapter 2 of On the Celestial Hierarchy Dionysius warns against reading literally the biblical passages that make angels seem shaped like lions, oxen, birds or wheels, saying the word of God used poetic imagery for the formless intelligences to provide a method of uplifting suited to our own mind.

Black says Dionysius allows language from the material domain to refer to the immaterial through analogy, understanding similar things dissimilarly, as with anger, irrational among lower beings but rational among higher, and desire, sensory among lower and conceptual among higher; this is the epistrophe from the exegete's standpoint.

Black believes the connection between Pico and Dionysius is sealed by the Ninth Letter, where Dionysius, after citing Paul in Romans 1.20, shows how the one word fire is read at different levels of the hierarchy of being, in a way strikingly similar to Pico's example of fire and water.

In the Ninth Letter Dionysius says the word fire, applied to God above conception, to his intelligible providence or to angels, must be understood differently each time: as a cause, as a substance, as participation, and in other ways as the contemplation requires.

Black says the comparison of Dionysius with the Heptaplus shows both are exegesis but differ in form and scope: Dionysius plucks words from many biblical places in a thematic commentary and concentrates on the upper levels, the ranks of angels and God, whereas Pico follows one chapter of Genesis sequentially and treats the whole cosmic taxonomy below God.
q: The comparison of Dionysius’s On the Divine Names and On the Celestial Hierarchy, on the one hand, and the Heptaplus, on the other, illuminates similarities and differences.

text: Pico claimed his mode of reading was new and untried; Black argues its seeds lie in Neoplatonic metaphysics, especially Proclus and the Liber de causis, but that the clear expression of the idea as a means of exegesis originates in the Dionysian corpus.

Black holds that Pico used the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius to develop a theory of exegesis that was anagogical in the Dionysian sense, leading the reader upward toward God, unlike the anagogy of the fourfold senses, where it was a property of a word's signification.
Black proposes that Pico's theory of allegory be viewed as an expression of this type of anagogy and understood in the context of intellectual ascent, the subject of the next two chapters.

In the first exposition Pico's use of a traditional Jewish reading of the Hebrew words tohu and bohu, probably drawn from the Sefer Bahir, serves an allegorical identification with a philosophical doctrine about the reception of form by matter.

Black hopes to show, against Pico's protestation that he follows no previous exegete, that clear links can be established between the Heptaplus theory of allegory and ideas in other texts Pico read and wrote.

In the Glossa ordinaria all senses of a passage coexist on the page without hierarchy, and Nicholas of Lyra, adding prologues to the Glossa, condemned the exaggerated division of literal and non-literal senses and wished to realign the two sides, not dispose of one.

Black holds that the Reformers' attack on the non-literal senses, of which Zwingli's reading of Genesis 1 is an example, was essentially polemical, and that the central pre-Reformation exegetes did not, as a rule, envisage different audiences for different senses.
The tradition of commentary on the two factors of the intellect reached no consensus on whether the active intellect is God, a transcendent entity between God and man, or an aspect of the human soul.
q: no consensus was reached on whether the potential intellect was mortal or immortal, or on whether the active intellect was God himself, or a transcendent entity between God and man, or an aspect of the individual human soul

text: The commentators Black discusses each held a model of intellectual ascent that culminated in the potential intellect becoming united with the active intellect.

Black says a philosopher who wanted felicity to depend on intellectual attainment could adopt an Aristotelian model of conjunction, disagreeing with Thomas Aquinas and his followers, or take the route of Platonism, chosen most prominently by Marsilio Ficino.
Black says Ficino was keen to enlist Pico in his pro-Platonist, anti-scholastic movement, and that the preface to Ficino's Plotinus commentary (1492) demonstrates this.

Ficino's preface, as Black translates it, says almost all the world is held by Alexandrian and Averroist Peripatetics who ruin religion, and that few interpret Aristotle with due piety except Pico, whom Ficino calls his co-Platonist.

Black argues that Pico's own position was more nuanced than Ficino's remark suggests: in the Heptaplus, at least, he made a concerted effort to keep the idea of intellectual ascent without committing himself exclusively to any one camp.

Black reports that the Conclusiones state, according to Averroes, that ultimate felicity is when the active intellect is joined to the potential intellect as its form, and, according to Plotinus, when the particular intellect is fully joined to the first intellect.
Black notes that the Conclusiones also take up Averroes on the unicity of the intellect and Abumaron Babylonius on the identity of the active intellect with God.
Black holds that where Pico himself stood on the intellect conclusions cannot always be determined, since none was censured and none is defended in the Apologia, so his argument for them is unknown.

Black's translation of the Oration has Pico say that if a man cultivates intellectual seeds he will be an angel and a son of God, and that if he withdraws into the centre of his unity he will stand before all things.
Black says Pico takes the Cherubim as the exemplar for human life, and reads their Dionysian threefold process (cleansed, illuminated, perfected) as a method of intellectual ascent.
q: Pico urges his audience to approach the Cherubim ﬁrst, since they will provide the path to the others. They are the “exem- plar” on which human life should be formed.

text: Black reads the stages of the Oration's ascent (moral science and dialectic, then natural philosophy, then divine things) as a hierarchical progression from morality through knowledge to religion, repeated in several analogies.

Black holds that in the Commento Pico posits above the rational soul a higher intellectual and angelic part through which man is linked to angels, contradicting the common scholastic view that the rational soul is the highest part.

Black says Pico gives man two modes of thinking: a rational one dependent on sense data and liable to error, and an intellectual one that receives true intellectual forms directly through illumination.

Black says Pico reads Benivieni's last stanzas as a six-stage ascent from sense to conjunction with the first mind, and that Pico disagrees with the many Aristotelians who hold the universal concept to be the highest knowledge attainable while joined to the body.

Black holds that the soul's rise from contemplation of itself to conjunction with the first mind (stages 5 and 6) corresponds, in the poem, to the light 'suspended near that sun', the sun representing God.

In Black's translation of the Commento, Pico says that when the soul reaches the sixth grade its path is complete and it may not go further to the seventh grade, the sabbath of celestial love, but must rest beside the first Father.
loc: commento | Canzone stanza VIII, sixth grade

text: Black reports that Pico's commentary on Psalm 10 sketches a roughly parallel model of seven levels of intellectual ascent linked to seven degrees of the blessed.

Black says the Commento's higher intellectual part reappears in the Heptaplus, in the fourth exposition, as intelligentia, signified by the supercelestial waters, but without the Commento's explicit refutation of scholastic psychology.

In Black's translation, Pico says the human intellect is illuminated by a greater divine intellect, either God or a mind nearer and cognate to man, as almost all Greeks and many Arabs and Jews hold; Jewish philosophers and Al-Farabi called it Spirit of the Lord.
Black concludes that although Pico does not refute those who identify the higher intellect with God, his sympathies seem to lie with the view that it is nearer to and cognate with man.
Black notes that Pico rejects the view that the illuminating action of the greater intellect occurs only when the human intellect is joined to the body.

Black states that he has not found the direct source of Pico's attribution to Maimonides, Ibn Bajja and others of the view that the greater intellect acts only with the body, though the idea seems to have been commonplace.

Black says the correlation of the transcendent active intellect with the Holy Spirit is in Al-Farabi but not in direct Latin transmission; a composite text attributed to Averroes carried it, and it is at least possible that Pico used it.
Black reads Heptaplus 6.6 as reaffirming that the human intellect can be joined with the first mind, described as the fullness of all knowledge, using the image of drops of water reaching the ocean.

Black argues that in the Heptaplus Pico contrasts the everyday discursive mode of thinking (night, moon) with a direct mode turned to divine things (day, sun), and that he leaves open the use of the direct mode in the present life.

Black holds that both the Commento and the Heptaplus distinguish two levels of felicity, and that the second, the sabbath of celestial love, is treated in depth in the proem to the seventh exposition.
Black reports that Pico distinguishes natural felicity, which philosophers debate and man can pursue actively, from supernatural felicity, the gift of Christ which can only be passively accepted.

In Black's translation of the seventh proem, Pico says the philosophers Avicenna, Averroes, Abubacher, Alexander and the Platonists seemed to offer something more, strengthening reason in the active intellect or in something higher but joined to us, and that he neither rejects nor despises their views provided they concern only natural felicity.

Black argues that instead of designating one of the intellect-and-conjunction models as correct, Pico says they all have some validity provided they are taken to concern natural, not supernatural, felicity.

In Black's translation of the seventh proem, Pico ends by affirming the mutual dependence of religion and philosophy and says that having philosophised with Moses about nature for six days, the seventh day is for divine things and supernatural felicity.

Black takes the proem to the seventh exposition as a comment on the structure of the Heptaplus: the first six expositions concern natural felicity (philosophy) and the seventh concerns supernatural felicity (religion), sacred history from the Fall to redemption.
q: In so doing, he provides another comment on the structure of the Heptaplus. The ﬁrst six expositions are concerned with natural felicitas, that is, philosophy

text: Black notes that Pico leaves the higher level of felicity unexplored in the Commento but devotes an exposition to it in the Heptaplus.

Black argues that in the Heptaplus Pico redirects his overt polemic from Christian scholastic philosophers towards well-known heterodox positions, including the Averroist unicity of the potential intellect.
Black holds that in the Oration Pico envisages a union in which all souls come together in one mind above every mind, and that this first mind is not, according to most philosophers, God.

Black identifies natural felicity with intellectual union with the first mind, and identifies the higher ineffable union with the supernatural felicity of the Heptaplus and the sabbath of celestial love of the Commento.

Black maps the Oration's seeds onto the ascent: cultivating rational seeds gives a heavenly animal, cultivating intellectual seeds gives an angel and a son of God, and withdrawing into the centre of unity gives one spirit with God, which Pico later calls supernatural felicity.

Black says Pico is clear that the higher felicity transcends intellectual achievement, which is why it is not the subject of the Commento or the first six expositions of the Heptaplus, though natural felicity is a necessary preliminary step to it.

Black argues that Pico's division of felicity into two was his own contribution to the debate; it did not settle the controversy or align him with a faction but robbed it of force, since if all accept the higher felicity, disputes about the natural kind matter less.
Black describes this approach as characteristic of Pico's syncretism, and places Pico's limit on intellectual achievement tighter than Avicenna, Maimonides and Averroes but looser than Aquinas.
Black observes that for many commentators the state of direct cognition was equated with prophecy, but that Pico never mentions this except in the case of Moses himself.

Black argues that the theme of intellectual ascent connects the Commento, the Conclusiones, the Oration and Apologia, and the Heptaplus, in three modes: an allegorical reading of a poem, a justification of treating differing philosophies, and a biblical commentary.
Black reports that Gersonides's commentary on the Song of Songs was translated for Pico by Mithridates and survives in a manuscript with copious marks and marginal comments in Pico's hand.

Black reports that Gersonides holds Scripture to contain, beyond moral commands, a concealed speculative knowledge that the masses do not know, and that the Song of Songs is a guide only for the intellectual elite.

Black says Gersonides interprets the kiss as the death of the kiss, signifying conjunction with God, and that Pico too used the death of the kiss to signify the attainment of felicity, in the Commento.

Black lists six themes of the Heptaplus that he finds also in Gersonides's commentary: the masses and the elect, literal and non-literal reading, felicity through comprehending intelligibles, progress from moral to speculative knowledge, union with God as the goal, and Scripture as the ideal guide.

Black argues that Pico goes a step beyond Gersonides: for Pico the Genesis narrative does not merely instruct the reader to achieve knowledge but contains that knowledge hidden within it, namely the emanation of things from God and the grade, number and order of the parts of the worlds.

Black holds that the first six expositions of the Heptaplus set out the orders of things from God, that is the three worlds, man and their inter-relation, and so give the knowledge needed for the ascent to natural felicity.
Black argues that the concealment of knowledge in Genesis is made possible by the union and difference of created things, that is by the hierarchy of being and its principle of mutual containment.

Black reads the ancient fathers' double knowledge, their own and inspiration by the Holy Spirit, as reflecting two cognitive levels: discursive rational thought and the higher level of inspiration or direct illumination, characteristic of angels and prophets.
Black says Pico contrasts the human mind's need for many forms with the angelic mind's need for only a few, connects forms with words, and uses this to express the uniqueness of Moses's text.

Black holds that Moses applied the principle of mutual containment to his words, so that a single term such as terra can do the work of many, and that this allowed the knowledge of man, the three worlds and their connections to be encoded in a short text.

Black says the aim of the Heptaplus is to decode this body of knowledge from Moses's simple words, and that at the very end Pico argues for a yet more extreme encoding, the plan of the whole narrative concealed in one single word.
Black holds that the main body of the Heptaplus is complete, fulfilling its seven-by-seven structure, and that the last chapter is a new beginning rather than a continuation.
