text: Black says that for the first word of the Bible Pico chose a different approach and another method: instead of allegory on the plane of the word, he investigates the letters from which the words of the law are made up.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black argues that the correct interpretation of the word bereshit reveals, in schematic form, the knowledge that is necessary for man's intellectual ascent.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black holds that the single sentence Pico derives from the letters of bereshit summarizes the Heptaplus as a whole, with the macrocosm, the three worlds (head, fire, foundation) and their inter-relationship, the pact, which is good because it unites them with God.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black says that Pico strayed once beyond the letters he was allowed to use and excused himself with a reference to Hebrew grammar that is not entirely accurate.
Black reports that seven of the eleven remaining derived words appear in a passage of the Liber combinationum, a Hebrew work on letter combinations translated for Pico by Mithridates.
Black reports Wirszubski's view that the author of the Liber combinationum was a disciple or latter-day follower of Abulafia, unless he was Abulafia himself.

Black notes that the derivation might seem banal, but that Pico gives the impression he is not simply jumbling letters but obeying undisclosed rules, so any textual authority for the derived words is of interest.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black says the derivation of shabbat, sabbath, from bereshit occurs in Recanati's commentary on the Pentateuch, a source previously identified as influential in Pico's kabbalistic studies.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black summarises the Recanati passage: bereshit is an utterance containing all the rest of the utterances, and it points to the second highest sefirah, Hokhmah, not to the topmost, Keter, though some think a part of the written letter points to Keter.
Black notes that once the three letters that signify the three highest sefirot are discounted, the remainder of bereshit spells shabbat, sabbath, in the Recanati passage.

Black argues that Pico ignores the sefirotic structure in the Heptaplus and also ignores the interpretive possibilities the structure offers, using only the parts of the Recanati passage about bereshit containing everything and the sabbath.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black states that the manuscript in which Pico read Recanati is no longer extant, so the exact form in which he read the text cannot be known.

Black suggests that if Mithridates translated ma'amar as verbum throughout the corpus, as he does in the Bahir, Pico would have read that sentence as a word containing other words, losing the sefirotic and numerical sense.
Black says that the reason Pico abandoned the sefirotic framework he had used effectively in the Conclusiones must remain a matter for speculation.
Black holds that what underlies the last chapter of the Heptaplus is the idea that bereshit contains everything, not the combinatory technique, which is easily learned.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black argues that Pico's radical exegetical method is more than a display of ingenuity: it is the most likely interpretation available to him of the opening of Recanati's Genesis commentary, which he is known to have read carefully.
loc: heptaplus | exposition of the first word

text: Black notes that Recanati quotes the Zohar, in which the sabbath is identified as the foundation of the world, and asks what the sabbath means in the Heptaplus.

Black describes the second proem's first explanation of the seven expositions: one exposition for each of the three worlds, one for man, two on the links between man and the three worlds, and a final exposition corresponding to the sabbath.
q: There is one exposition for each of the worlds; one exposition for man, who is “a fourth world, in which are also found all the things that are in the other worlds”

text: In Black's translation of the second proem, Pico calls the seventh exposition a sabbatical narration on the felicity of created beings and their return to God, unlocking what Moses openly hid about the advent of Christ and the Church.

In Black's translation, Pico's second explanation for the seven-fold division is that everything corresponds to the seven days, and that each exposition's seventh chapter turns towards Christ, the end of the law and our sabbath, rest and felicity.
q: since the expositions are distributed into seven books, and each book is divided into seven chapters, everything corresponds to the seven days of creation.

text: Black argues that the sabbath is the crucial element common to both of Pico's explanations of the structure, and that the first explanation appears to depend on the idea of the sabbath rather than on the material itself.

Black holds that the justification of the fifth and sixth expositions is less fully argued, that Pico relies on the numerical structure, and that the requirement of the sevenfold form appears to be the formative element.

Black finds Pico's alternative explanation, imitation of Basil and Augustine, somewhat unsatisfactory, since neither Basil's hexaemeron nor Augustine's Genesis commentaries are divided into seven sections.
Black analyses the Heptaplus as an allegory with a constant subject, the six days of creation, and a changing object, the philosophical framework of each exposition.
Black argues that the sabbath is the object, not the subject, of the allegory: the biblical text Pico expounds stops at the sixth day, and he never comments directly on the seventh.
Black holds that the title-page, a sevenfold hexaemeron, shows a tension that runs through the work, in which the question of form is persistently presented and equated with the sabbath.

Black says the sabbath in the Heptaplus represents rest and felicity and the return of created things to God, is the antithesis of the Fall, and is linked to prophecies of Christ, the Church and the conversion of the Gentiles.

Black argues that the Heptaplus does not discuss the literal creation events, such as creatio ex nihilo, but projects them into a static picture of the cosmos and into man's final destiny, so that the sabbath signifies redemption and man's rest after completing his journey.

In Black's translation, the proem to the seventh exposition calls that treatise the sabbath of the commentary and says it will treat the sabbath of the world and the repose, that is the felicity, of created things, listening to Moses as a true prophet of things to come.
Black says the literal sabbath is a microcosm of the allegorical sabbath, a microcosmic approach also seen in each exposition's seventh chapter, which discusses Christ.

Black holds that the Heptaplus's cluster of ideas around the sabbath (macrocosm, ultimate goal of man, redemption and rest) has strong links with the Jewish tradition in its esoteric form as made available to Pico by Mithridates, and through them to the ideas of knowledge and hermeneutics.
Black says the jubilee is a macrocosm of the sabbath: as the sabbath signifies temporary rest, so the jubilee comes to signify ultimate rest, or redemption.
Black reports that Pico's Conclusiones say that whoever knows in kabbalah the mystery of the gates of understanding will know the mystery of the great jubilee.
loc: conclusiones | Conc. cabalisticae secundum secretam doctrinam sapientum Hebraeorum Cabalistarum, 13

text: Black states that the Conclusiones's remark on the jubilee has sources in the manuscript corpus, citing the Expositio decem numerationum, which equates the great sabbath and great jubilee and gives its numeratio fifty gates of understanding, and Gikatilla's Portae iustitiae.
Black argues that the jubilee, as Pico understood it, signifies supernatural felicity, the repose of created things.
Black reports that the Babylonian Talmud says fifty gates of understanding were created in the world, forty-nine of them revealed to Moses, because God made him a little lower than the angels.

Black says the Nahmanides extract deepens the doctrine of the gates by identifying them explicitly with a complete taxonomy of creation, from minerals up to the heavens and their hosts, forty-nine categories of which Moses acquired knowledge.

Black holds that whether Pico read Nahmanides is a problematic question: the Heptaplus's citation of him has an intermediate source in Recanati, no Latin translation is known to have been available, and yet Pico owned the text and might have received its ideas orally.
Black argues that the forty-nine gates revealed to Moses comprised the knowledge of all created things, the same knowledge Pico argued is to be found in the Genesis account.
Black reports an Abulafia passage he says Pico can be more confidently said to have read, in which Moses received the law in two ways, literal and with its secrets and hidden things.

Black argues that the non-literal way of knowing is how the contents of Moses's prophetic vision, the forty-nine gates, were incorporated into the Pentateuch, and that this is the key to a crucial statement in the second proem about Moses's experience.

In Black's translation, Pico says that Moses, speaking sufficiently of the world, discussed all four worlds, and that his writing has truly portrayed an image of the world, as he was commanded to make everything according to the exemplar he saw on the mountain.

Black concludes that the exemplar Moses saw on the mountain is the forty-nine gates, the knowledge of the taxonomy of created things needed for natural and supernatural felicity, and that the Heptaplus reflects the gates in content and in structure, through its seven expositions of seven chapters.
loc: heptaplus | second proem; seven by seven

text: Black states that the core of his argument is that Pico's theory of allegory derives from the connection between epistemology and ontology found in Proclus and Pseudo-Dionysius, so that emanation from God down a hierarchy is matched by reversion up it by knowledge, culminating in union with God.

Black argues that knowledge of the simple conceptions at the top of the hierarchy is extremely hard for humans to attain because of their dependence on sense and matter, and is the type of knowledge associated with angels.

Black says the commentators on Aristotle argued that if the human intellect rises to comprehend immaterial separate substances it becomes equivalent to the angelic intellect and, in some accounts, is gifted with prophecy.

Black holds that in the Jewish tradition Moses was considered to have ascended from knowledge of manifold material substances to the highest level of angels, separate intelligences and pure intelligibles, and that Pico's project was to find how this knowledge is encoded in Moses's text.

Black argues that Moses's text expresses the same concepts with very few forms, that is words, and so represents the simplicity of forms by which angels, and by extension prophets, understand things normally beyond human reach.
q: Pico’s project was to ﬁnd and interpret the ways in which this knowledge was encoded in Moses’s text.

text: Black concludes that Pico's exegesis in the Heptaplus is anagogical in the Dionysian sense, leading the exegete upwards along the hierarchy of being, and that the absence of the fourfold scheme and humanist philology shows it to be a fundamentally different type of work.

Black holds that the Heptaplus is separated from the literal sense: its subject is cosmology, not cosmogony, and it comments on the words in principio only in the last chapter, and then outside their literal temporal frame.

Black holds that the Heptaplus's hermeneutic stance owes more to Neoplatonism and Judaism than to Christian scholastic and monastic traditions, and that its esotericism appears anachronistic given the late medieval trend toward aligning the literal and non-literal senses.

Black argues that the Heptaplus does not support the modern commonplace that Pico symbolises the transition from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance: its only nod to humanism is its Latin style, and as biblical commentary it was outdated before it was written.

Black summarises Pico's conception as a soul with two intellectual faculties, a rational one for discursive reasoning and intelligentia for direct comprehension of intelligibles; the latter leads to natural felicity, union with the first mind, above which is an inexpressible union with God.
Black suggests that Gersonides's commentary on the Song of Songs is a precedent Pico knew for reformulating the ascent theme as biblical interpretation, which Pico applied to Genesis.

Black concludes that Pico deliberately gave the Heptaplus a numerical structure based on seven, reflecting the sabbath, and that his concept of the sabbath was influenced by kabbalistic texts which give it a polyvalent significance as microcosm and macrocosm.

Black summarises the doctrine that Moses passed through forty-nine of the fifty gates of understanding on Sinai, that is, acquired knowledge of all created entities, and proposes that the Heptaplus is a guide to how that knowledge was concealed in Genesis, reflecting the gates in content and structure.

Black suggests that the Heptaplus's more discreet handling of the intellect controversy, compared with the Commento's attack on scholastics, may be due to the recent memory of the affair of 1487 and the papal condemnation still hanging over Pico, though it may equally reflect a wish to find common ground.

Black argues that Pico did not try to arbitrate the internal disputes about the intellect among Christian Peripatetics or between them and Muslim and Jewish philosophers, but sought to defuse them by focusing on the higher supernatural felicity that transcends philosophies, a strategy he calls syncretist.

Black argues that the links between the Heptaplus and the earlier works cast doubt on Gianfrancesco Pico's claim that his uncle underwent a conversion, and shows continuity before and after Pico's imprisonment.

Black concedes that a reader may feel the allegorical readings arise from the Genesis text and its philosophical contexts without needing Pico's framework, but holds that Pico's allegorical theory stands at the centre of his ideas about man, the cosmos, the intellect and the ascent to felicity.

Black reports that Thomas held that in this life we cannot know immaterial substances in their own mode through either the potential or the active intellect, and that ultimate felicity does not consist in knowledge of separate substances.

Black reports that Pico was in Padua between 1480 and 1482 and met exponents of Averroism, including Elijah Delmedigo and Nicoletto Vernia, and that Delmedigo wrote two works on Averroes's ideas of intellect and conjunction specifically for Pico.
Black notes that on 4 May 1489, as Pico was writing the Heptaplus, the Bishop of Padua published a decree forbidding all discussion of the unicity of the potential intellect.

Black reports that Alemanno extrapolated from the idea of hierarchical progression through philosophical disciplines an entire curriculum, beginning with the Torah and ending in what he took to be the highest divine science, kabbalah and magic.
Pico says the common arguments for human excellence left him unsatisfied, among them that man is only slightly inferior to the angels.
q: I was unsatisfied by the arguments put forward by many men to explain the excellence of human nature

text: Pico allows that the common reasons for human dignity are not the principal ones, and asks why the angels and the blessed choirs of heaven should not be admired more.
q: These reasons are indeed great, but they are nonetheless not the principal ones

text: Pico says the condition that man received in the universal order is one to be envied by the beasts, by the stars and by the intelligences dwelling beyond this world.
In Pico's account of creation God had already adorned the supercelestial region with intelligences and given the heavenly globes eternal souls before man was made.
q: He had already adorned the supercelestial region with intelligences, enlivened the heavenly globes with eternal souls

text: Pico says that when man was to be made every place in the world was already filled and had been assigned to the highest, the middle and the lowest orders.
q: nor was there among the seats of the world any place for this contemplator of the universe

text: Pico says the highest spirits, which the editors translate as Intelligences, are from the beginning or soon after what they will be for all eternity, whereas man may become what he wills.
Pico says that a man who cultivates his intellectual seeds will be an angel and a son of God, just as cultivating the rational seeds makes him a heavenly being.
q: If he cultivates his rational seeds, he will become a heavenly being. If he cultivates his intellectual seeds, he will be an angel and a son of God

text: Pico says that a man who, dissatisfied with the lot assigned to any other creature, gathers himself into the centre of his own unity becomes a single spirit with God in the solitary darkness of the Father and, having been placed above all things, will become superior to all things.
Pico says the most secret Hebrew theology transforms Enoch into an angel of divinity, named in Hebrew, and at other times reshapes other men into other spirits.
q: even the most secret Hebrew theology at one time transforms holy Enoch into an angel of divinity

text: Pico says that what makes an angel is spiritual intelligence, not separation from the body.
q: not the circular body that makes the heavens, but straightforward reason; not the separation from the body that makes an angel, but its spiritual intelligence

text: Pico ranks the philosopher of right reason as a heavenly creature, and the pure contemplator withdrawn into the mind as neither earthly nor heavenly but a still more eminent spirit in human flesh.

Pico urges his hearers to fly to the otherworldly court near the highest Divinity, where seraphim, cherubim and thrones hold the first places, and to emulate their dignity and glory without accepting second place.
q: let us fly off to the otherworldly court that is near to the most eminent Divinity

text: Pico says that by living the life the highest angels live, which man is able to do, we may not be inferior to them and may equal their lot.
q: If so we wish, we will not be inferior to them at all

text: Pico characterises the three ranks: the seraph burns with the fire of love, the cherub shines with the splendour of intelligence, the throne stands in the steadfastness of judgment.
q: The seraph burns with the fire of love; the cherub shines with the splendour of intelligence; the throne stands in the steadfastness of judgment

text: Pico says that a man devoted to the active life and caring rightly for inferior things will be strengthened by the steadfast solidity of the thrones.
q: if we, being dedicated to an active life, undertake the care of inferior things with proper consideration of their worth, we will be strengthened by the steadfast solidity of the thrones

text: Pico says that a man released from action who meditates on the Creator in creation and on creation in the Creator will shine with cherubic light.
Pico says that a man who burns with charity for the Creator alone will burst into flame in the likeness of the seraphim.
q: If we burn for the Creator alone, with charity, with its all-consuming fire, we shall burst into flame in the likeness of the seraphim

text: Pico says that God flies over the cherub, who is the contemplator, and imbues him with warmth as if brooding over him.
q: Over the cherub, that is, over the contemplator, He flies and, as if brooding over him, imbues him with warmth

text: Pico says that the seraph, who is a lover, is in God and God in him, so that he and God are one.
q: He who is a seraph, that is, a lover, is in God and God is in him; indeed, he and God are one

text: Pico says that the power of the thrones is reached by judging and the height of the seraphim by loving, that neither judging nor loving is possible of things unknown, and gives Moses as the example who loved what he had seen and judged as a contemplator.
q: Great is the power of the thrones that we may reach by judging; supreme is the height of the seraphim that we may reach by loving

text: Pico says the cherub, placed in the middle, prepares us by his light for the seraphic fire and illuminates the judgment of the thrones.
q: the cherub, located in the middle position, uses his light both to prepare us for the seraphic fire and likewise to illuminate for us the judgment of the thrones

text: Pico calls the cherub the bond of the Prime Minds, the order of Pallas and the overseer of contemplative philosophy, and says he is to be emulated first so that we may be raised to love and descend to action.
q: The cherub is the bond of the Prime Minds, the order of Pallas, the overseer of contemplative philosophy. First we must emulate him, thirst after him and to the same degree understand him in order that we may be raised …

text: Pico proposes to ask the apostle Paul, raised up to the third heaven, about the activities of the cherubic hosts, and says Paul will answer, according to the interpretation of Dionysius, that they are cleansed, then illuminated, and afterward perfected.

Pico says that emulating the cherubic life on earth means purging the soul through moral science and dialectics, then bathing it in the light of natural philosophy so that it may be perfected by knowledge of divine things.
q: emulating the cherubic life on Earth, curbing the drive of the emotions through moral science, dispersing the darkness of reason through dialectics

text: Pico says the patriarch Jacob teaches through a figure that a ladder of many rungs stretches from the lowest earth to the highest heavens, with God at its height and the contemplative angels moving up and down it in turns.
q: let us also consult Jacob the patriarch

text: Pico asks who will dare touch the Ladder of God with unclean feet or unwashed hands, since it is unlawful to touch the clean with the unclean, when we try to imitate the angelic life.
q: if we are to carry out these things in our efforts to imitate the angelic life, who, I ask, will dare to touch the Ladder of God, either with unclean feet or with unwashed hands

text: Pico says that the hands and feet, the entire sensual part of the body in which resides the attraction that drags the soul back, must be washed in moral philosophy lest we be held back from the ladder, and that to be companions of the angels who hasten up and down Jacob's ladder we must also be prepared to be promoted from step to step and to wheel away nowhere from the course of the ladder.

Pico says that inspired by the cherubic spirit and philosophizing through the grades of nature, we descend and ascend in turn until we rest in the bosom of the Father, who is at the top of the ladder, and are made perfect in theological bliss.
q: Once we, inspired by the cherubic spirit, have reached this point through the art of speaking or of reasoning

text: Pico proposes to ask Job what God most desires among the tens of hundreds of thousands who assist Him, and says the answer will be peace.
Pico says that the middle order interprets the precepts of the supreme order for the lower ones, and so has Empedocles interpret the words of the theologian Job.
Pico says the peace that God makes in His heavens is the peace the descending angels announced to men of good will, so that men, ascending to heaven, would be transformed by it into angels.
q: that peace which God makes in His heavens, which the angels who came down to earth announced to men of good will so that these men would, ascending to heaven, be transformed by it into angels

text: Pico says Moses is only a little inferior to the fountain of sacrosanct and ineffable intelligence whose nectar inebriates the angels.

Pico says that, raised to the most eminent heights of Theology and roused by ineffable love, we shall be borne outside ourselves like ardent seraphim, filled with the godhead, no longer ourselves but He Himself Who made us.
Pico says the noonday light of theology is the light that squarely enflames the seraphim and equally illuminates the cherubim.
Pico says that, according to the doctrines of the cabalists and the Moors, there is no place for unclean spirits in the region of the noonday light.
Pico proposes that after the fall of our man, we call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician, to free us with moral philosophy and dialectics as healing drugs.
q: let us call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician, to set us free with moral philosophy and dialectics, as if with healing drugs

text: Pico says that once restored to health Gabriel, the strength of God, will lead us through the marvels of nature and deliver us to Michael the high priest, who will bestow the insignia of theological priesthood.
q: Gabriel, the strength of God, will abide in us and, leading us through the marvels of nature and showing us everywhere the merit and the power of God, he will finally deliver us to Michael the high priest, who will …

text: Pico says the Cabalistic books, as Esdras rightly proclaimed, contain a vein of understanding and a font of wisdom that is the exact metaphysics of the intelligible and angelic forms.
Pico says that in the Kabbalistic books he found the fall of the demons and the hierarchy of the angels, the same things read every day in Paul, Dionysius, Jerome and Augustine.
q: of the fall of the demons, of the hierarchy of the angels, of Purgatory, of the punishments in Hell. I saw the same things that we read every day in Paul, Dionysius, Jerome, and Augustine

text: The editors report that Ficino's Platonic Theology places the soul between matter and angelic intelligences, while for Pico man's calling is the dynamism of transcending the world of images and becoming one with the Absolute rather than enjoying this central position.

The editors note that the sequence sense, reason, intellect reappears in the three-stage ascent by the angelic orders, thrones, cherubim, seraphim, and that man is meant to transcend even the angelic orders.
The editors note an order of angels, stars, lower creatures in section 6 and say it is repeated in reverse order in section 11.
The editors gloss the clause or soon thereafter in section 26 as meaning after Lucifer's fall.
The editors adduce the Heptaplus second proem, where man's make-up is said to include the angelic mind and the image of God, as a parallel to the seeds of every kind of life.
The editors report that Bausi traces the passage on man's cultivating his seeds to Iamblichus.
The editors report that Garin points also to medieval sources for the passage, John of Salisbury and Alan of Lille.
The editors report that Tognon proposes John Scotus Eriugena's De divisione naturae as the precise source of this whole section.
The editors report De Lubac's view that the Oration repeats an idea expressed many times before in patristic literature.
The editors cite Ficino's Platonic Theology 14.3, where the soul lives a life of plant, beast, man, hero, demon, angel and God, as a parallel to the passage.
The editors report that Bori and Bausi suggest Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses among several plausible sources for the passage.

The editors report Copenhaver's remark that, apart from one exception, Pico's examples of mutability in this part of the Oration are negative and ambiguous, and that the only clearly positive transformation is angelic.
The editors report that Garin and Tognon refer to the Ethiopic Book of Enoch 40.8 for the Enoch of this passage.
q: Both Garin and Tognon refer to the Ethiopic Book of Enoch 40.8 (first or second century; see Knibb 1978)

text: The editors judge it more likely that Pico draws on a complex apocryphal tradition of Enoch texts than on a single book, and say the reference could include the Third Book of Enoch.
q: Rather than referring to a single text, Pico more likely elaborates on a complex, and apocryphal, textual tradition. His reference could include the so-called Third Book of Enoch

text: The first printed edition leaves a blank where the Hebrew word should stand, and the two Basel editions supply a Hebrew retroversion of the Latin words angelum divinitatis instead.
q: The princeps edition has a blank space where the Hebrew word should be. Both Basel editions (1557 and 1572) have Mal'akh ha-Sekinach, Hebrew retroversion of the Latin angelum divinitatis

text: The editors report that Bausi, following Wirszubski, restores the characters found in an earlier version of the Oration in a Florence manuscript and reads them as Metatron.
q: Following Wirszubski (1989, 232), Bausi (Pico 2003, 171–72) restores in his edition the characters found in the earlier version of the Oration (possibly one of two drafts Pico prepared in fall 1486 while in Umbria before moving to Rome) in …

text: The editors point to the Commento, which says almost in the exact terms of the Oration that Enoch was transformed into Metatron, angel of divinity, and that any other man may be transformed into an angel.
q: A reference to Metatron can be found in Pico's Commento sopra una canzona (written in the same period as the Oration and the Conclusiones, 1486) almost in the exact terms of the Oration, as a synonym of transfiguration

text: The editors direct readers to Conclusiones 1.19.2 and 2.11.10 for the interpretation of the Enoch-Metatron transfiguration.

The editors say it is generally held that the name Metatron has three possible etymologies: the Greek Methathronius, one derived from mat-ara (keeper of the watch), and one derived from metator (guide).

The editors quote Scholem's account that two traditions were combined in the figure of Metatron, one of a heavenly angel created with the world and one that makes him Enoch, who ascended and was changed from a man into an angel.
q: As Scholem writes, “two different traditions have been combined in the figure of Metatron. One relates to the heavenly angel who was created with the creation of the world, or even before, and makes him responsible for performing the most …

text: The editors quote Scholem's view that the tradition associating Metatron with Enoch, absent from the Talmud and the most important Midrashim, is evidently connected with the Talmudists' reluctance to regard Enoch in a favourable light.
The editors say it is perhaps not surprising that the identification discussed in the note holds a prominent place in Pico's Christian Cabala.
q: It is perhaps not surprising that the identification occupies a prominent place in Pico's Christian Cabala

text: The editors report that Bausi takes the passage to show that Pico does not hold metempsychosis and agrees with Ficino on a moral and allegorical reading of the transformations.
The editors give Seneca and Aristotle, echoed by Dante's Convivio, as possible sources for the paragraph on the philosopher and the pure contemplator.

The editors say that the words quoted from Ps. 81, You are gods and sons of the most high, were spoken by God to the angels condemned for their sins and are applied by Pico to men to incite them to rise toward an angelic form.

The editors reject Wallis, Miller and Carmichael's translation of caelestia contemnamus as 'let us struggle toward the heavenly', keeping the classical meaning of contemnare and translating caelestia as 'celestial' rather than 'heavenly'.
The editors say that spurning the celestial is consistent with section 40, where Pico suggests a higher stage of contemplation beyond the earthly and the celestial.
The editors note that the word dignity appears for the first time in the Oration at the passage on emulating the dignity and glory of the seraphim, cherubim and thrones.
The editors say that Pico represents here the three divisions of the highest order of angels according to the scheme of Pseudo-Dionysius, which Thomas and Gregory confirm.
q: In accordance with the scheme set out by Pseudo-Dionysius (see §70 of the Oration) and confirmed by St. Thomas (Summa Theologiae 1.108, art. 6) and St. Gregory (In evang. II hom. 34), Pico represents here the three divisions of the …

text: The editors say that calling the cherubim contemplators does not mean that the seraphim and thrones are not contemplators.
q: The fact that Pico specifically calls the cherubim contemplators does not, of course, mean that the seraphim and thrones are not

text: The editors say that man's task is to emulate the highest angels and that dialectics is the necessary intermediate stage in the mystic process, citing Bori.
The editors report a suggestion, from Farmer, that Pico consciously overlaid the sefirot on the Dionysian hierarchy, so that seraphim correspond to Hesed, thrones to Din and cherubim to Binah.
q: It has been suggested (Farmer 1998, 346–51) that Pico consciously overlaid the cabalistic sefirot on the celestial hierarchy elucidated by Pseudo-Dionysius. In this arrangement, as it applies here, each of these three types of angels is associated with a specific …

text: The editors identify the passages in which Yahweh flies through the heavens mounted on a cherub as the background of God flying over the cherub.

The editors say Pico himself glosses the unusual image of God brooding in the Heptaplus, where the Spirit of the Lord that brooded is the spiritual Olympus, seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warming with its light.
q: This unusual phrase, in which God “broods,” is glossed by Pico himself in Heptaplus 2.2

text: The editors observe that the gloss of Ephrem, to which Pico's Heptaplus appeals for the sense brooded, says the thing that hovered over the waters was a normal wind and not the Spirit of the Lord.
Noting, with Bausi, that most commentators direct the reader to Job 38:7, the editors say a more likely source is actually Ps. 148:4.
The editors say that the seraphim, cherubim and thrones are known as the first hierarchy because they are closest to God.
q: These three classes of angels are known as the “first hierarchy,” as they are closest to God

text: The editors say that the need for the middle level to join the upper and the lower is addressed in the Heptaplus in imagery consonant with this passage.
The editors say the Prime Minds are the angels and the Order of Pallas is a phrase referring to the cherubim, in so far as they preside over the contemplators, citing the 2003 commentary.
q: The “Prime Minds” are the angels; the “Order of Pallas” is a phrase referring to the cherubim, insofar as they preside over the contemplators (Pico 2003, 26–27)

text: The editors cite Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio and Heptaplus 6.6 in the note on the section 66 phrase.
The editors report Bausi's view that the language of the wish to know what life the cherubim lead is drawn directly from Ermolao Barbaro.
The editors say the Dionysius of the Celestial Hierarchy was taken to be the follower of Paul mentioned in Acts.
q: Celestial Hierarchy 165b–c, 205c–209d. This Dionysius was, of course, thought to be the homonymous follower of Paul of Acts 17:34

text: The editors say the mystic three-stage path was often articulated as purgatio, illuminatio, unitio or perfectio.
q: The mystic three-stage path, or triplex via, was often articulated as purgatio-illuminatio-unitio (or perfectio )

text: The editors say that Augustine among others regularly defines the cherub as plenitudo scientiae, the fullness of knowledge.
The editors suggest that Pico may also have been thinking of Richard of St. Victor's De arca mystica, where cherub means fullness of knowledge.
The editors say that Richard of St. Victor's De duodecim patriarchis takes Jacob's twelve sons as the successive stages of the contemplator's quest for mystical enlightenment.
The editors say the topos of Jacob's image engraved in the throne of God comes from the Aggadic tradition.
The editors say that Jacob saw God on earth only in a dream, while in heaven the vision of God is attainable in a waking state.
The editors say that Pico's depiction of the relatively harmonious comings and goings of the angels on the ladder is a rather joyous contradiction of the typical iconography of the ladder.
q: Interestingly, Pico's depiction of the ... relatively harmonious comings and goings of the angels on the ladder is a rather joyous contradiction of the typical iconography of the ladder to God

text: The editors cite Genesis 28:12-13, the Commento, Philo and Iamblichus in the note on the ladder.
The editors identify Plato's Phaedo 67b as the source of the maxim that it is unlawful to touch the clean with the unclean.
The editors suggest that the passage on philosophizing from centre to centre may be inspired principally by al-Batalyawsi, citing Idel.
The editors say the passage could refer to the metaphor of eternal happiness as circular movement, which the Heptaplus proem to book seven expresses.
The editors cite Job 25:2, Dan. 7:10, Gen. 1:2 and Heptaplus 3.6 for the passage on the multitude before God and the peace He makes in the heavens.
The editors cite Pseudo-Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy 209a-b, and Conclusiones 2.5.3 for the middle order interpreting the precepts of the supreme order for the lower.
The editors cite Luke 2:13-14 and Heptaplus 7.4 for the angels who announced peace to men.
The editors say the image of heavenly nectar goes back to Plato's account of the angelic charioteer who refreshes his horses with ambrosia and nectar.

The editors judge it probable that Pico starts from the Platonic notion of nectar in heaven and adds the reference to intoxication through Plotinus's reading of the Symposium, where it means the passing down of knowledge from higher to lower levels.
The editors cite Philo for the cherub as the supercelestial charioteer who guides the soul in an orderly fashion away from discord.
The editors tie the ardent seraphim of section 113 to sections 54 and 57 and to Ficino's De divino furore.
The editors give Gregory the Great's XL Homiliarum in Evangelia 34.9, where Raphael is called the medicine of God, as a possible source of this angelological conclusion.
The editors give the same work of Gregory the Great for the meanings of the names Gabriel, strength of God, and Michael, who is like God.
The editors say that a connection between the names of the angels and the doctrine of the sefirot, for which they cite Yates, might be alluded to through the words the most hidden mysteries.
q: On the names of the angels as connected to the doctrine of the sefirot (a connection which might be alluded to through the words “the most hidden mysteries”), see Yates (1979)

text: The editors say Pico identifies Michael, the high priest, with the sefirah Keter, which he takes as the symbol of the priesthood.
q: See also §141, “sacerdoti summo Michaeli” in reference to the archangel, whose name in Hebrew translates as “Who is like God?”

text: The editors say that the order of Pallas is described as cherubic contemplation that fulfils the link between love, the seraphim, and justice or law, the thrones.
q: See §161 and §§65–66, where “the order of Pallas” is described as that of cherubic contemplation that brings to fruition the link between love (the seraphim) and justice or law (the thrones)

text: The editors say Pallas signifies the intellectual nature which leads to wisdom and that the Orphean Pallas is associated with the cabalists' Metatron in Conclusiones 2.5.14 and 2.11.10.
q: throughout the Oration and Conclusiones, as the personification of Wisdom or Philosophy, Pallas signifies the intellectual nature which leads to wisdom (in Conclusiones 2.5.14 and 2.11.10, the Orphean Pallas is associated with the cabalists' Metatron)

text: The editors say the archangel Uriel appears to Esdras in a vision and that Esdras writes down the angelic revelations in seventy books.
The editors say the three archangels Pico mentions represent dialectics, natural philosophy and theology, and give the section number as 135.
q: The three archangels Pico mentions in §135 represent dialectics, natural philosophy, and theology

text: The editors report Tognon's phrase that at this point in the first redaction of the Oration Pico underwent an intellectual conversion to the Cabala.
The editors say the passage of section 240 recalls the image of Jacob and the ladder and that Moses instructs us to prepare for a heavenly vision through philosophy.
Dionysius is presented as a Platonist in the manner of Proclus.
loc: oration | the seven-step ascent, ending in the Father's darkness

text: The deification that Pico's speech promotes eliminates the human self and any human trait such as dignity, so the Oration liquidates rather than aggrandizes the self.
The only glorious change mentioned in this part of the Oration is Enoch becoming Metatron, the highest angel, stationed behind the throne.
loc: oration | Adam, chameleon and Proteus passage (Oration I)

text: Although Metatron enters the Oration with a hint of a more secret theology, the speech has said nothing yet about Kabbalah and supplies none of the context, so Christian readers could not have grasped the hint.
q: The Oration has said nothing yet about Kabbalah when the orator announces that “with their more secret theology, Hebrews too sometimes

text: Pico's Kabbalistic thesis identifies the figure Kabbalists call Metatron with what Orpheus names Pallas, Zoroaster the Father's Mind, Mercury God's Son, Pythagoras Wisdom, and Parmenides the Intelligible Sphere.

Metatron was also a Jewish name for the Agent Intellect of Muslim mysticism; Abulafia, in a text translated for Pico, says that the Intellect that takes ours from potency to act is Mattatron, Prince of the Faces.

text: A thesis by Pico on Themistius confirms that the Agent Intellect is what Metatron is in Kabbalah.

text: Philosophers are to ascend from plant to animal to human to divinity, and the contemplators who strive to shed their material coverings become angels, as Enoch becomes Metatron.

Since fallen humans must change, the speech urges sinners to turn into angels, but this angelic life is only an aspiration for the wicked; they must climb a ladder of grace that they cannot touch while defiled by sin.
Pico states his purpose: humans must live like angels in heaven, in particular like Cherubs, and being in the flesh they must turn to the ancient Fathers for guidance.
Pico's exhortation to see what life the Seraphim, Cherubim and Thrones live is read as a call to make human destiny equal to that of three choirs of the hypercosmic court.

The three highest of the nine angelic orders oversaw purification, illumination and perfection in the mystical ascent, as the Areopagite explained; Copenhaver pairs the three choirs with Heman, Jeduthun and Asaph.
In the Zohar, Asaph gathers good angels to guard the righteous; Heman leads in the morning, Jeduthun at twilight, and Asaph at midnight, and the angels prepare for Metatron's arrival.
Copenhaver says Pico knew a Kabbalist comment on a Psalm that deflated human arrogance by belittling man's nearness to the angels while recalling his kinship with beasts.

No angels in the Hebrew Bible are called Thrones; Paul lists Thrones in Colossians, and Dionysius the Areopagite was the first to organize nine ranks of angels into three orders of three with Thrones, Cherubim and Seraphim at the top.

Pico arranged the highest three angelic orders in a hierarchy by agency (active, contemplative, unitive), psychology (judgment, contemplation, love) and substance (mass, light, fire), with humans living like Thrones, Cherubs or Seraphs accordingly.

The Areopagite did not connect Thrones with judging but with detachment from the earthly, and Gregory the Great described them as channeling the Creator's activity to creatures; Pico, thinking of a Psalm, read them as judging.

In a Kabbalist text known to Pico, nine hierarchies of angels bear names different from the Dionysian ones and appear in a different order; Copenhaver cites thesis T1K2, which lists Cherubim before Seraphim.
q: The Areopagite’s nine ranks became canonical for Christians, though Jewish tradition often preferred ten groups. In a Kabbalist text known to Pico, the names were those that he used in the Conclusions, while changing the order:

text: The immutable angels are Seraphim and Cherubim; Pico mentioned Cherubim first as a life for humans to emulate, while Thrones, who reach down toward lower changeable things, are the Hasmalim that Pico listed third and are also the Kis'oth.
q: T1K30 No angel with six wings ever changes. The immutable angels were Seraphim and Cherubim, but Pico mentioned Cherubim first, ready for humans to emulate in a “Cherubic life,” whereas Seraphs blazed beyond reach and Thrones reached down toward “lower …

text: Pico's ordering of the ascent, guided by the Areopagite, is to judge like Thrones, then know like Cherubs, and finally love like Seraphs, because judging and loving both require knowledge, which the Cherub supplies.

Because the Kabbalistic thesis identifies what Orpheus names Pallas as Metatron within the Seraphic fire surrounding God, Copenhaver concludes that Pallas Athena, the wise goddess presiding as Wisdom at S2, ties the Cherub's knot.
q: The Cherub is the “knot” that ties these “primary minds” together, said Pico. Pallas, goddess of wisdom and “protector of contemplative philosophy,” governs this angelic order. Since thesis T2K10 identifies “what Orpheus names Pallas” as Metatron—within the Seraphic fire surrounding …

text: Pico, who could see Pallas in a Kabbalist way, also learned mysteries from Proclus, other pagan Platonists and Ficino; Copenhaver says that Proclus replaced Pallas with Hecate in the Chaldean theology.
q: Pico, who could see Pallas in this Kabbalist way, also learned mysteries from Proclus, from other pagan Platonists and from Ficino, their master explicator.

text: Pico had abundant help from Ficino, since much of the ancient theology in Plato's dialogues had already been explicated by Proclus, whose insights Ficino used in his own commentaries.
loc: oration | Oration II, 13 (Pallas) and the Platonist puzzles

text: Copenhaver holds that when Ficino first met Pico, around ten years before the Plotinus edition, Pico was a boy, immature, arrogant and careless even with friends like Marsilio, so that sour notes from earlier times must have tempered the festive music of 1492.
Ficino, though dazzled like Pico by Platonic arcana, preferred explicating to obfuscating, whereas the younger Pico meant to mystify.

Recognizing the wise Pallas as the Cherub shows which angels Pico wanted humans to emulate: the message of the Oration to this point is to form our lives on the Cherubic life, though those who mind the flesh cannot reach even Cherubs and must consult the ancient Fathers.
Pico's thesis says that the Kabbalists' reticent naming of the highest Sefirah ratified the Trinity and Incarnation and agreed not only with Kabbalists but with the theology of Dionysius.
At the top of the angelic hierarchy, as Dionysius describes it, Thrones cleanse sinners, Cherubs enlighten them and Seraphs perfect them.
q: At the top of the angelic hierarchy, as described by Dionysius, were Thrones to cleanse sinners, Cherubs to enlighten them, and Seraphs to perfect them.
loc: oration | Oration III, 16 (Paul's third heaven and the Areopagite)

text: Pico's instructions from the Areopagite directed him to a three-stage climb from cleansing through illumination to perfect completion, in which the initiate passes beyond the Cherubic light into God's nameless shadows.
Dionysius's practical theology, an occult tradition revealed only to initiates, is described as ascetic, ecstatic, esoteric and theurgic, and as otherworldly as the Cherubic life Pico advocated.
In Jacob's dream, angels went up the ladder and down again to examine the person whose face they had seen carved into the Throne; Copenhaver reads Pico's Jacob passage against this rabbinical motif.

Copenhaver suggests that a Book of Imaginary Circles by Ibn al-Sid al-Batalyawsi, known to Jews in Pico's Italy, may have been more useful to Pico for the ladder: angels move down a line between two circles of a cosmic Soul, below the Agent Intellect, bringing divine power to human souls so that sinners can ascend by the same route.
q: More useful to Pico, perhaps, was a Book of Imaginary Circles by Ibn al-Sid al-Batalyawsi, known to Jews in the prince’s Italy. Convinced that higher realities transcend ordinary geometry, Batalyawsi envisioned a straight line or ladder running between two circles …
loc: oration | Oration III, 17-19 (ladder 'from center to center')

text: Angels are everywhere in the Oration, and Pico's first question to Job, what God wanted from his myriads of angels, is answered by the thesis that God wanted peace among angelic warriors, the Southern Water and the Northern Fire with their Commanders.

The peace on high ends warfare between Michael, commanding the Southern Waters of S4, and Gabriel, commander of the Northern Fire of S5, who reconcile at S6; Gersonides saw their harmony as a fixed order of stars.
Pico's thesis T1K28 makes the birds of heaven, on Elihu's saying, angels within the world who appear to humans, not those that appear only in spirit.
Pico took his angel lore in the Job passage from books of Kabbalah, and read Gersonides on Job alongside.

Copenhaver reads the peace that God makes on high between his angelic armies, who descend so that humans ascending might be made into angels, as an angel magic, a theurgy emulating Enoch's transformation into Metatron and a joyous surrender of human personality.
In the summary of Oration III, 20-25, human souls uniting with God in peaceful matrimony is a blessed death for saints, their reward for changing into angels.
According to the Zohar as Copenhaver reports it, three troops of angels chant the Psalm and guard the evening hours, and the angels on watch decide which souls may go up.

Pico's thesis T2K11 says that rational souls are sacrificed to God by an archangel only through the soul's parting from the body, and only secondarily, in the death of the kiss, through the body's parting from the soul.

Copenhaver characterizes the mysticism of the Oration as Dionysian, Kabbalist and Neoplatonic, and says its project fixed the role of the self in Pico's Cherubic program: a person's happiest end is to be consumed in the Godhead.
loc: oration | Oration III, 26-32 (conclusion of the section)

text: Pico's description of the climax of initiation, transported beyond ourselves like burning Seraphs, is offered as the point at which the soul is no longer itself but becomes the One who made it.

The seventh exposition of the Cherubic life starts with Zoroaster, and its path to happiness ends with angels, who already have the wings that humans need; a healed soul moves through Nature with Gabriel toward Michael's theology, having been healed by Raphael.
Copenhaver says the four rivers that flow from the garden are also angels: Gabriel, Michael, Raphael and Uriel, in a passage on the Zohar's nut garden.

Augustine is reported to have interpreted the Psalmist's morning, noon and evening prayer as angelic knowledge that penetrates time's barriers, the mid-day light being the nondiscursive cognition of bodiless spirits that shines on the Seraphim and lights up the Cherubim.
loc: oration | Oration III, 34 (midday light of theology)

text: Raphael, God's healing, dispenses at S10 the medicines of ethics and dialectic; Gabriel at S5 teaches natural philosophy; and Michael's theology at S4 surpasses Gabriel's science.

The first of Pico's Kabbalist theses introduces Michael, stationed below the higher angelic choirs but a high priest nonetheless, whose priesthood is that saints be sacrificed by a good death of the kiss; his place is S4, just beneath the supreme triad.
q: The very first of Pico’s Kabbalist theses (T1K1) introduces Michael, stationed below these loftier spirits but a high priest nonetheless. The purpose of his priesthood is for saints to be sacrificed by a good death of the kiss.

text: Michael, the archangel who vanquished his fallen brethren and will preside on the final Day of Judgment, is the patriarch's partner at S4 and a messenger of death whose death is benign; the priesthood of theology is what he will bestow on us after service in philosophy.

Copenhaver says Ficino, Poliziano and others will have known more or less what their friend was up to without making much sense of it, whereas those best able to understand his project were Flavius and other Jews who helped him with Kabbalah.
loc: conclusiones | the 1486-87 project, before the Rome condemnation

text: Copenhaver asks whether Pico wanted to advertise natural magic while keeping quiet about angel-magic, and says his theses on magic suggest so; he notes that a plea to Saint Michael was a short step from a liturgy for Metatron, a secret but arguably lawful magic invoking an angel.
loc: conclusiones | Magical theses (T2M); Oration V on magic

text: Pico's speech conjures with the names Gabriel, Metatron, Michael and Raphael as monitors of the Cherubic life; Abulafia is quoted as giving Cherub, Enoch and Metatron as different names for the Agent Intellect, who rules over the hierarchy of angels.
loc: oration | Oration V-VI; the four named angels

text: Pico did not invoke angels when he defended magic in the Oration, nor did he turn, as Ficino did, to the occult qualities of scholastic metaphysics; Kabbalah was on hand to solve the problem of two types of magic.
The hymn that magic forces us to sing ('full are the heavens') is angelic, Seraphic in fact, better than Cherubic, and hopes for the bliss of nothingness to come.
loc: oration | Oration V, 60-62 (the hymn 'full are the heavens')

text: Abulafia urged followers to turn into separate angels by attaining prophecy, and identified Metatron, the angel prince, with the Agent Intellect; union with the Intellect or Metatron eradicates the self, and the initiate becomes an angelic savior.
q: He wanted them to “turn into separate angels” by attaining the state of prophecy and to be “saved by this from natural death on the day of their . . . death and live forever.”

text: Shekinah, Shaddai and Holy Spirit were other names for Metatron, and addressing Metatron as Shaddai, a name of God, rested on the numerical value 314 of both names; Copenhaver says Pico would thereby have had evidence for more than one Trinity among the Sefirot.
loc: oration | Oration VI (Metatron and the Trinities among the Sefirot)

text: Speculations about Metatron not only justified fearing demons and ratified confidence in angel magic, but also reached into places that good Christians like Pico should have approached only with rites sanctioned by the Church.
Copenhaver says Pico could have asked Metatron, the mightiest angel of all, to protect him against evil spirits like Azazel and Samael.

Copenhaver reads the speech's phrase about a finished metaphysics of angelic forms in Ezra's books as perhaps a complete formal metaphysics that a Kabbalist theurgy, an angel magic, might make practical, but concedes Pico's terse clues are hard to follow.
loc: oration | Oration VI, 66 (Ezra's books; the spring of wisdom)

text: Pico's list of Christian doctrines that books of Kabbalah confirm includes the orders of angels and the fall of the demons.

text: Copenhaver says Pico listed atonement, orders of angels and a heavenly Jerusalem among topics connecting the two faiths of Abraham, on which he expected to defeat Jews in debate.

No authority gets more theses in the first part of the Conclusions than Proclus's 55, and his metaphysics of divine triads was crucial for Pico's most daring innovation, deriving the Trinity from Kabbalah, though the Oration names him only once.
Only nine theses are listed for Iamblichus, mainly on the Mysteries of Egypt, which Ficino owned but had not yet published in translation; the prince once asked to borrow Marsilio's Iamblichus.

Angelology was one link between Pico and Giles of Rome: both were curious about angels, demons and their roles in magic, and three of Pico's eleven theses on Giles discuss angels, including evil angels; but all scholastics dealt with angels, so there was nothing special about Giles in this regard.
Copenhaver suggests, with a hedge, that Pico might have known Abu Ma'shar had identified the Koranic Idris with the biblical Enoch and also with Hermes.

text: Copenhaver suggests that Flavius's earlier alienation of Cardinal Cibò, later Innocent VIII, may have led that pontiff to question Pico's judgment when Pico hired Flavius to translate.

Because the speech relied on coded Jewish secrets, its intended audience of Christian dignitaries could never have grasped its main message, that humans must escape the body and turn themselves into angels using magic and Kabbalah.
loc: oration | the Oration as a whole

text: Pico wants humans to become angels and then to be annihilated in God, and the speech is an exhortation to do this angel magic using Kabbalist techniques of ecstatic transformation.

Where the Oration uses dignitas first, it pairs it with gloria as a prize held by angels, not humans; it denotes angelic rank higher than human, and neither use of the word belongs to human persons except aspirationally.
The cherubic life the fallen children of Adam are commanded to live is a disembodied and disgendered existence of the next-to-highest angels; Pico wears their emblem on the Niccolò Fiorentino medal.

Magic and Kabbalah help mortals achieve union with God, with Kabbalah at a higher level helping humans change into angels and merge with God; the Oration shows little about Kabbalah but comparison with the Conclusions reveals that it is abundantly Kabbalist.

text: Copenhaver thinks Pico probably deliberately avoided the Asclepius passages on making gods, in which the souls of demons or angels are called up into idols, to keep his magic natural.
Three verses of Exodus 14, each of exactly 72 letters, read vertically spell 72 three-letter names of angels, and all 216 letters spell a name of God; this is a method that Pico knew.

text: In Pico's Kabbalah the Sefirot and God's names are actors in dramas of theology, cosmology, angelology and anthropology whose themes are exile, death, atonement and redemption, transposed onto the Trinity and Jesus Christ.
According to Garin, as Copenhaver reports, Kabbalah was secondary and merely instrumental in Pico's thought compared to the Hermetic texts, the Neoplatonic writings or the works of pseudo-Dionysius.

Copenhaver quotes Voltaire, in the Essai sur les moeurs, as dismissing the 900 theses as the Summa of Thomas and a digest of Albert, theology mixed with Peripateticism in which an angel is infinite secundum quid.

text: As translated by Copenhaver: In the Oration, spirits above have been from the beginning what they will be for all the eternities, whereas a human whose seeds are intellectual will be an angel and a son of God.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says that Hebrews, with their more secret theology, sometimes transform the blessed Enoch into an angel of divinity, whom they call מטטרון, and that it is spiritual intelligence, not removing the body, that makes an angel.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says that in the hypercosmic court nearest the most exalted divinity, according to the sacred mysteries, Seraphim, Cherubim and Thrones hold the first places, and that we can be their rivals for rank and glory.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says a Seraph burns with the fire of love, a Cherub flashes with the brilliance of intelligence, and a Throne stands steadfast in judgment; God sits above the Throne to judge and hovers over the Cherub.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says the greatest exaltation, attained by loving, belongs to Seraphim and the power of Thrones is attained by judging, but since neither judging nor loving is possible of what is unknown, the Cherub prepares us with its light for Seraphic fire and lights our way toward the judgment of Thrones.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico calls this the knot of primary minds, the order of Pallas, protector of contemplative philosophy, which we must first emulate before ascending to the heights of love and descending to duties of action.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says that Paul, raised to the third heaven, will answer, while Dionysius interprets, that the armies of Cherubim are cleansed, then enlightened, and finally completed.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico speaks of angels of contemplation taking turns moving up and down Jacob's ladder, and hopes to join them if those who aspire to the angelic life keep the ladder clean.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico calls the peace that God makes on high one that angels descending to earth have announced to men of good will so that through it they, ascending to heaven, might be made into angels.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says the midday light, sung of by David and explained by Augustine, shines directly on the Seraphim to set them on fire and, with equal effect, lights up the Cherubim.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says we should call on Raphael, a heavenly physician, to heal with morals and dialectic, then Gabriel, God's strength, will lead us through Nature, finally handing us over to the high priest Michael, who bestows the priesthood of theology.
As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says these books contain a spring of wisdom, a complete metaphysics of intelligible and angelic forms.
As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says he read about, among other things, the fall of the demons and the orders of angels, the same things read every day in Paul and Dionysius, Jerome and Augustine.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico says Dionysius the Areopagite confirms that the founders of our religion transmitted the more secret mysteries from mind to mind, without writing, with only speech mediating.

As translated by Copenhaver: Pico's conclusion 1G5 says angels were not created with grace; 1G6 says an angel is stubborn and unrepentant because certain divine instincts were taken away; and 1G7 says a higher angel illuminates a lower one by comforting and strengthening its intellect, not by showing it a luminous object.
As translated by Copenhaver: Pico's conclusion on Themistius says he believes the Agent Intellect that only illuminates to be in Themistius what Metatron is in Kabbalah.

As translated by Copenhaver: conclusion 1K2 says there are nine hierarchies of angels named Cherubim, Seraphim, Hasmalim, Haiot, Aralim, Tarsisim, Ophanim, Thephsarim and Isim; 1K28 says the flying fowl of the fifth day are angels within the world who appear to humans; 1K30 says no angel with six wings ever changes.

As translated by Copenhaver: conclusion 1K1 says that just as a human being and lower priest sacrifices the souls of nonreasoning animals to God, so Michael, a higher priest, sacrifices the souls of animals that reason; 1K24 says that Job understood the Southern Water, the Northern Fire and their Commanders.

As translated by Copenhaver: conclusion 2K10 says what Kabbalists call מטטרון is beyond doubt what Orpheus names Pallas, Zoroaster the Father's Mind, Mercury God's Son, Pythagoras Wisdom, Parmenides the Intelligible sphere; 2K11 says rational souls are sacrificed to God by an archangel only by the soul's parting from the body.

As translated by Copenhaver: conclusion 2K34 says that the name in three letters he, vav and aleph, most properly applied to God, is most consistent not only with Kabbalists but with the theology of Dionysius the Areopagite.
As translated by Copenhaver: Saying of God that he is an intellect or intelligent is more inappropriate than saying of a rational soul that it is an angel, according to 2UD49.

The Hebrew word in thesis T2K10 is blank in the printed edition of the Conclusions; Ebgi prefers Hokmah (S2), following Zorzi, but Copenhaver holds that Wirszubski's choice of Metatron seems better because the Agent Intellect, explicitly identified with Metatron by another thesis, better matches the other entities named in the thesis.
q: In T2K10, a space to be filled by a Hebrew word is blank in the printed edition of the Conclusions; Ebgi 2014, 215–225, prefers Hokmah, S2, following a commentary by Francesco Zorzi; Wirszubski’s choice of Metatron seems better, however, because …

text: In Copenhaver's glossary, Metatron is the mightiest angel, sometimes the Agent Intellect, and a model for mystical union because he was once a human, Enoch.
The glossary says that at thesis T2K10 Pallas is Metatron and that at Oration 15 Pallas is the knot of primary minds, the highest angels, and the guardian of philosophical contemplation.

In the glossary Cherubim are bodiless spirits of contemplation, with the loving blaze of Seraphim above them and Thrones judging below, who show humans how to shed the body and surpass humanity; Thrones' duty is firm judgment as a foundation for Cherubic contemplation.
The glossary describes pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite as a Christian contemporary of Proclus who wrote around 500 CE in a Neoplatonist way about mystical theology and angelology.
Plotinus taught that love is given in Nature but, unlike his successors, never divided this unitary force into a hierarchy of angels and demons; the love was personalized and subdivided by Porphyry.

Barbaro, whose only peers as Hellenist and expert on the technical language of Greek philosophy were Ficino and Poliziano, wrote to Pico in April 1485 praising his godlike genius, with politics and patronage on his mind.

Pico's reply to Barbaro, in which a resurrected scholastic answers Barbaro's mockery of barbarian philosophers, argued that philosophers may talk as they wish to achieve their own purposes; philosophy wants truth, and the best philosophical style resembles God's speech in scripture.

In the exchange with Barbaro, Pico used his mastery of classical prose and poetry to resist the classicizing of philosophical language; as a writer of philosophical Latin he was more like Scotus than Barbaro, and he refused to stand with humanists.

Innocent VIII launched an investigation of the Conclusions weeks after the book was printed and created a commission in February 1487; sixteen commissioners were appointed, twelve attended the first meeting on Wednesday, March 2, with Bishop Jean Monissart of Tournai presiding, and they included Pedro Garcia, a Thomist who later published a rebuttal of Pico's Apology.

text: Copenhaver holds that the commissioners were not neutral judges but the Pontiff's tools, prosecutors pursuing a guilty verdict, and that the trial's outcome was fixed, as indicated by both chronology and documents: verdicts came in before the third week of March, and every vote was registered as unanimous and unqualified.

Innocent's charge to the commission savaged Pico's theses as confused, deviant, intolerable, irregular, obscure, scandalous and reeking of heresy, and armed the commissioners with the technical phrase ex vi verborum, which they repeated in four of their verdicts.

After the Pope condemned some of the 900 propositions, Pico had to fend off the Pope's agents in a closed and contentious trial, wrote the Apology to recover, and lost again quickly and decisively when Innocent extended his original ban on thirteen theses to the Conclusions as a whole.

Durand concluded that Christ's descent to Hell was not a movement in place in Christ's soul but an effect the soul has on those who need to be saved; Pico protested that he could not understand Durand's position, which he did not hold, yet used the Durand case to complain of unfair treatment.

text: In The essay on Pico's philosophy of religion, De ente et uno is presented as reconciling the Aristotelian identity of the One and Being with the Platonist priority of the One over Being, which matters for Pico's account of God.

The essay reports that Pico distinguishes two senses of being, and that Aristotle, in identifying Being and the One, was using being in the sense of what is outside nothing, so that Aristotle's view is compatible with the Platonist one.
The essay reads Pico's view of God as the plenitude of existence as reproducing the Thomistic position that God is the act of existence itself.
q: Pico’s view here reproduces the Thomistic position that God is ipsum esse, the act of existence of itself.

text: The essay reports Pico's three worlds, the first being the angelic realm for theologians and the intelligible realm for Platonists, and says Pico adds the human person as a fourth.
q: Pico distinguished between the ultramundane, celestial, and sublunary worlds. The last world is the one inhabited by all living things on earth. The first is the angelic realm (as described by theologians) or the intelligible realm (as described by Platonists). …

text: The essay argues that the mutual containment of the worlds is the metaphysical basis of Pico's method of allegorical interpretation, because discourse about one level must refer to others.
q: Pico is explicit that the basis for his method of allegorical interpretation is a metaphysical principle of the mutual containment of all levels of reality

text: The essay argues that Pico keeps the medieval chain of being but departs from it in one respect: the human person's ontological status is not fixed, between the angelic and animal worlds, but open to ascent or descent.
In a note the essay reports that Neoplatonists such as Ficino placed the human soul in the middle of the Great Chain of Being, between angel and body.
The essay argues that for Pico the multiplicity of perspectives derives from the emanation of the One through a succession of intermediaries, and truth is finally one.

The essay says Pico, following the Platonists, sets an intellectual and angelic part of the human soul above the rational soul, unlike the Latin Aristotelians who take the rational part to be the highest.
The essay's note suggests that in placing an angelic part in the soul Pico is implying that angelic cognition, immediate knowing without reasoning, lies within the natural capacity of the human mind.

The essay reports the Thomist view that a human knower in this life has no direct cognition of any spiritual being, so humans can only approximate the angelic mode of knowing in rare moments of immediate intuition.
The essay says the Heptaplus gives a fivefold account of human nature, the fifth part being an intelligence shared with the angels.
The essay says Pico is undecided in the Heptaplus about what the higher intellect illuminating ours is, God or a mind akin to man's, and does not identify it with the agent intellect.
The essay argues that Pico apparently entertained the Averroist unicity of the intellect, against Aquinas and against Ficino.
The essay judges that Pico's promise to reconcile Averroism with personal immortality remains unfulfilled, since a universal intellect cannot be reconciled with a personal soul.

The essay's note says Pico reads the birth of Love from Plenty and Poverty in the Symposium as the growth of the Platonic Ideas in the Angelic Mind from an inchoate state to a perfected one through love.

text: The essay reads Pico's Oration as setting contemplation, associated with the cherubim, between the active life of the thrones and the unitive love of the seraphim, the highest order.

The essay says the Dionysian triad of purification, illumination and perfection frames both the cherubic life Pico urges and the philosophical curriculum, and that the cherubim correspond most directly to illumination between the lower and higher orders.
The essay reads Jacob's ladder in the Oration as a figure of nature, with descent and ascent standing for the analysis of the one into the many and the gathering of the many into one.

The essay reads the midday light that inflames the Seraphim and illuminates the Cherubim as showing that natural philosophy does not suffice and that the highest illumination needs an infusion from beyond the soul.
q: This is that midday light, which, perpendicular, inflames the Seraphim, and at the same time illuminates the Cherubim.”

text: The essay observes that in On Being and the One Pico calls even angelic intellectual knowledge imperfect, in contrast to the Oration's emphasis on ascent, and it suggests the later works are perhaps more sober.

The essay argues that despite differences of context, the Oration and On Being and the One agree in doctrine that all knowledge remains imperfect until illuminated and united to its object, and that the seraphim too must undergo illumination.
The essay says the Oration reminds the reader that love is ultimately higher than knowledge, since the seraphim are closer to God than the cherubim.
The essay notes that Pico announces in the Oration and in the first of the theses according to his own opinion the theme that Aristotle and Plato agree in meaning and substance.

The essay reports that the papal commission's list of thirteen theses included the thesis that it is more improper to say God is intellect than that the rational soul is an angel, and qualified it as wrong and open to a heretical twist.

The essay hypothesizes that the members of the commission were those who had lobbied against Pico or that the pope wanted to chastise him, perhaps because of a tense political relationship with the Medici.

The essay says Pico's cosmology has three worlds, the transworldly (angelic or intellectual), the heavenly and the sublunary, which contain one another, so that the sun as fire in heaven is seraphic intellect in the transworld realm.
