Edelheit says historians have not stressed enough the differences between Ficino and Pico, whom they sometimes treat as two equal and similar representatives of Florentine humanism or philosophy.

Edelheit contrasts the two: Ficino, in On the Christian Religion, offers a historical picture of religion and of Christianity's place in it built on newly arrived Neoplatonic texts and ignores the doctrines of the Doctors, whereas Pico's Apology is concerned with purifying religious opinions and beliefs.

Edelheit says Pico's mastery of scholastic philosophy, in which he was far more expert than Ficino, allowed him to show theologians in their own terms how fragile some scholastic dogmas were, and that he appealed not to a dogmatic philosophy such as Platonism but to the doubting method of the skeptical Academy.

Edelheit argues that treating Ficino and Pico alike as continuers of scholasticism, because both use scholastic terms and procedures, disregards the difference in their scholastic education and their aim in using such terms.

Edelheit argues that Pico uses scholastic literature and argument in the Apology only in answering the papal commission, to show his technical competence, while his own account of theology and religion uses a different Latin style and arguments linking the ancient Academy's skepticism with faith.
Edelheit says Pico, when he wrote his Apology, put Scripture and revelation as the true foundation of Christianity, and did so more explicitly than Ficino.

Edelheit says Ficino and Pico, Ficino in practice and Pico more explicitly and methodically, tried to redraw the line between dogmas with divine sanction and later disputable opinions, and relied on the earliest Fathers such as Augustine and Origen in doing so.

Edelheit connects Pico, Ficino and Savonarola through the subordination of church rulings to revelation: Pico, in the Origen discussion, makes the decrees of councils subordinate to revelation, Ficino builds his theology on revelation such as prophecies and miracles, and Savonarola claimed direct divine inspiration and that even the pope could err.

Edelheit says Pico, who wrote the famous speech later titled De hominis dignitate, was regarded by Poliziano and Barbaro as a member of their intellectual milieu, so that on Kristeller's approach he would be excluded from humanism for being too involved in philosophy and scholasticism.

Edelheit reports Schmitt's view that Pico, by proposing the harmony of Plato and Aristotle among other theses, went beyond Ficino's notion of two unbroken traditions of truth, so that truth for Pico resides in many traditions.

Edelheit reports Trexler's model that both Lorenzo de' Medici, as patron of culture and humanism, and Savonarola tried to reform the nature of public rituals, and offers it as an example of connecting culture to religion, though he prefers to focus on the theology of Ficino and Pico.

Edelheit holds that Ficino and Pico share a sense of crisis, reject scholastic approaches to religion, and draw on newly discovered pagan philosophies, but that their attempts at a new theology part ways and give very different results.

Edelheit says Ficino's Platonic Theology contains hidden echoes of Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles, the only scholastic text that contemporary sources expressly say Ficino studied, and takes the lack of express references as evidence of Ficino's attitude.

Edelheit reports Allen's description of Ficino's On the Christian Religion as an explicitly apologetic work written after Ficino's admission to the priesthood that avoids many of his characteristically Platonic ideas, and says he will give a different interpretation.

Edelheit says Ficino was, at the start of Savonarola's reforms, one of Savonarola's supporters, and traces a sense of crisis developing from Caroli through Ficino's early sermons and his friends and pupils, to Ficino himself, to Savonarola.

Edelheit says Pico does not stress the feeling of crisis in so many words, but that his demand to treat all theological opinions later than Scripture and the early councils as mere opinion, to be re-examined for probabilitas, is a humanist answer to a crisis of authority in theology, and its essence differs from Ficino's solution.

Edelheit says Ficino's arguments in his account of religion are metaphysical and mostly taken from Neoplatonism, in whose translation and dissemination Ficino played a key role, and that his concept of the history of religion is richer and more consistent than the mere use of historical examples in sermons.

Edelheit says the Platonic and Neoplatonic writings supplied Ficino with his framework for the history of religion, while for Pico the instrument for a first, philosophical re-examination of religious opinions is the concepts of probabile and verisimile, which he learned by his own admission from the skeptical Academy's writings in Latin.

Edelheit says that in the Apologia Pico uses two styles: scholastic Latin and argument when refuting the papal commission's scholastic points, and humanist Latin and historically contextual arguments when presenting his own approach to religion.

Edelheit says Ficino, and some other humanists, borrowed the concept of ancient theology, prisca theologia, from the Neoplatonic tradition to designate pre-Christian pagan theology culminating in Plato.
Edelheit says that through the influence of Gemistos Plethon Pico planned a work interpreting ancient poetry on a Neoplatonic allegorical basis but did not live to write it.

Edelheit says that although Plotinus and Proclus figure largely in Pico's 900 theses, Pico is in no way a Platonist like Ficino, and appears to offer their opinions as further opinions to be examined.
q: Although Plotinus and Proclus figure largely in the theses, Pico is in no way a Platonist like Ficino, and it seems that he offers their opinions as yet more opinions to be examined.

text: Edelheit says the Apologia is Pico's theoretical exposition of the reason for publishing the 900 theses without comment, and suggests it was his contribution to the public debate the theses invited, which never took place.

Edelheit says Pico uses the Academy's procedures only at the lower, philosophical level of judging opinions by probability, and remains a Christian who accepts Scripture, the Creed and the first councils as binding and of divine origin.
Edelheit says both Ficino and Pico use new and different philosophical approaches to reconstitute Christian theology, and that the new theology each produces is still clearly Christian and Catholic.

Edelheit's footnote reports Garin's remark that Caroli, though he admired Giovanni Pico's very elegant style, did not accept Pico's conclusions and discussed them with his friend Pietro Negro, and notes that Giovanni di Napoli discussed Caroli's critique of Pico's Theses.

Edelheit suggests that a passage in Ficino's early sermons on the distinction between animal instinct and human self-directed action may be an important source for the famous words at the beginning of Pico's oration, composed a few years later.
Edelheit says that in Ficino's sermon on Christ's temptation the three hierarchies of angels are equated to the three levels of evangelical truth, a use of angelic orders as an exegetical scheme.

Edelheit says Ficino's sermon on Paul's rapture draws on Hebrew philosophers, Dionysius the Areopagite and Thomas Aquinas, and that Thomas and Augustine are the only late Christian sources Ficino employs in the sermons, probably because of their unique status.

Edelheit says that Ficino's sermon on Paul's suffering attributes incredulity to demons rather than to the humours and says angels strengthen faith, and that Ficino's theology cannot be separated from his philosophy, cosmology and medicine.

Edelheit observes that in Ficino's sermons the human soul is a third nature inclined both up and down, temporal through the senses and eternal through the intellect, set between the mortal nature of animals and the eternal nature of angels, and calls this a Neoplatonic framework with Christian influences rather than Aristotelian physics.
Edelheit says Ficino's prisca theologia was intended to replace the Aristotelian metaphysics that had played a dominant role in scholastic theology.

Edelheit says Ficino calls for replacing the Aristotelian foundation of scholastic theology with an ancient Neoplatonic theology serving as a preamble of faith, on the model of Augustine, and regards this as what Ficino means by legitimate wisdom.

Edelheit suspects that Ficino's discussions of prisca theologia may be aimed at professional theologians such as Caroli, indicating to them that Platonism is more relevant to understanding Christianity than the traditional Aristotelianism of the scholastics.

Edelheit says the ancient theologians are in harmony with one another for Ficino and are all represented in Plato, who is interpreted by Neoplatonists who adopted the mysteries of Christianity, so that Christianity is the climax of the histories of both religion and philosophy.

Edelheit says Ficino claims to have found that the chief mysteries of Numenius, Philo, Plotinus, Iamblichus and Proclus were taken from John, Paul, Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite, and that whatever they said about the divine mind and the angels was taken from those figures.

Edelheit says Basil and Augustine confirm only that the Platonists used the mysteries of John the Evangelist, so that Ficino, who names Basil and Augustine, is placing this idea in his own cultural programme after centuries in which the Greek authors had hardly been known in the Latin West.

Edelheit reports Allen's view that Ficino's programme differed from Augustine's and was more radical: to champion Platonism not as a stepping stone but as an integral, complementary theology given to the gentiles like a gentile Old Testament, with Plotinus, the arch interpreter, taking centre stage or sharing it with Plato.

Edelheit cites Ficino's letter to Pico in which Ficino writes that Pico tells him he daily persuades many, and has persuaded some, to leave Epicurean impiety or an Averroist opinion and to follow Plato's view of the soul and God, as a kind of middle way toward Christian piety.

Edelheit reports that a Dominican, Vincenzo Bandello da Castelnuovo, refuted Ficino's theory of will and intellect at length and politely, which Kristeller took to show that Ficino was taken seriously by his scholastic contemporaries.

Edelheit identifies the studies full of causes and reasons that Ficino says harm the religion of the young as scholastic Aristotelianism, and says the Pythagorean school seems to Ficino more sympathetic to religion than other ancient sects.
Edelheit says that in Ficino's humanist theology the pagan ancient theology replaces Aristotelianism and gives Christianity historical and philosophical profundity, without validating it.

Edelheit says Ficino locates one factor in the decline of Christianity in scholastic theology, whose Aristotelian philosophical foundation separated Christianity from the ancient wisdom of the ancient theologians and so from its historical profundity.

Edelheit says Ficino's solution to the crisis of his time is a renovation of Christianity from its past, and that it is therefore unsurprising that Ficino supported Savonarola when Savonarola became powerful, since the priest-king ideal Ficino announced in On the Christian Religion seemed about to be put into practice.

Edelheit says Savonarola does not represent all aspects of the new humanist theology: he represents the supernatural aspect of Christianity that Ficino missed in his Iron Age, but was not a philosopher and had only a partial humanist education.

Edelheit says that what Ficino does in practice, Pico makes explicit in many of his arguments, especially the problem of divinely inspired authoritative texts as against the mere opinions of theologians, and he attributes the difference to the character of the two works and the personalities of the two authors.

Edelheit says Ficino's De Christiana religione is a positive work for the widest Christian readership, and that it is part of Ficino's character to spread his views positively rather than by dispute, whereas Pico, a wealthy aristocrat and not a priest, dependent on no patrons, shows an argumentative strain in his writings and social behaviour.

Edelheit says that because the problem of authority is central, Pico does not offer in the Apologia a completely new system of religion and theology, and that nine hundred theses or a discussion of one central philosophical problem as in De ente et uno are a far cry from Ficino's De Christiana religione, Theologia platonica and project of translating Plato, Plotinus and later Platonists.

Edelheit reports Granada's argument that Ficino's notion of ancient theology can be seen as a Christian apologetic, a part of rational theology preparing men for Christianity, and disagrees, holding that for Ficino religion has such status that an apologetic point of view is not relevant.

Edelheit says Ficino does not state explicitly the boundary between divine truth and human opinion, but his references to mixing the human with the divine, and the absence of most Fathers and all Doctors, make it fairly clear.

Edelheit summarises the sequence: in 1486 Pico planned a council in Rome to dispute nine hundred theses, including Neoplatonic and Kabbalistic material; some theologians had him suspected of heresy; a papal commission found thirteen theses heretical or of dubious orthodoxy; and the Apologia of 1487 answered the condemnation of those thirteen.

Edelheit says that on the issue of authority in philosophy and theology the positions of Ficino and Pico are not all that different: what Ficino does by selecting and omitting sources, Pico does explicitly by critical discussion of Doctors and Fathers and by rejecting the authoritative status of their opinions.

Edelheit says both Ficino and Pico represent a new humanist theology which rejects most of the medieval tradition, returns to Scripture and early Christianity, and introduces materials from newly discovered texts, especially of Plato and the Neoplatonists, and that Pico introduces Hebrew and Arabic sources as well in his nine hundred theses.

Edelheit says the Apologia matters to his study in two ways: it discusses openly and in detail the medieval tradition that Ficino silently rejected, and it uses concepts and techniques from the skeptical Academy to examine theological opinions.

Edelheit remarks that the most technical theological work in his study was written by a layman, Pico, who nevertheless officially demanded a reformulation of Catholic theology, unlike the friar Caroli or the ordained priest Ficino.

Edelheit reports that De Pace, on his understanding, sets a Pico scepticus in place of the Pico platonicus, aristotelicus or averroeticus of earlier scholarship, and offers a different point of view of his own.
Edelheit says the distinction between the Creed, the dogmatic formulations and the opinions of Fathers and Doctors is the key to the humanist theology that Pico developed.

Edelheit says that Pico's move is therefore to be placed somewhere between the Thomists and the Scotists, the two main schools of scholastic theology in this period, and that Pico's humanist theology can be understood as an endeavour to establish a new relationship between opinio and fides in response to both.
q: Pico’s move is therefore to be placed somewhere between the Thomists and the Scotists—the two main schools of scholastic theology in this period.

text: Edelheit cites Pico's Apologia where Pico says those who have addicted themselves to a school, favouring Thomas or Scotus, can test their doctrine on a few questions, whereas he has trained himself to be sworn to no one's words and to consult all masters of philosophy.

Edelheit reports the papal denunciation of the theses: theologians and legal experts reported that many conclusions were heretical or smacked of heresy, scandalous, restored the errors of the pagan philosophers, or favoured the faithlessness of the Jews or disciplines hostile to the faith under the guise of natural philosophy.

Edelheit gives the chronology of the affair: the commission's denunciation of thirteen theses on March 13, 1487, three of them heretical; publication of the Apologia on May 31, 1487; Pico's oath on July 31, 1487 to accept the pope's future decision; and the pope's denunciation of the theses on August 4, 1487.

Edelheit says the theologians of the commission mostly did not read Greek, and that the twenty-four-year-old Pico, though not a professional theologian, showed familiarity with the Latin and Greek Church Fathers, scholastic theology and Greek philosophy from Plato and Aristotle to the Neoplatonists including Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus and Dionysius the Areopagite.
Edelheit reports Alison Brown's publication of a letter showing that the condemnation process started earlier than previously thought and was connected with the condemnation of Jean Laillier.

Edelheit says Pico is often represented as the humanist with the best scholastic training, but that the Apologia, in which he fully expressed his scholastic competence, has been discussed less than his other works and lacks a detailed analysis.

Edelheit's view of the purpose of the nine hundred theses is that Pico was putting forward a deliberate critique of scholastic theology, confronting the Church and demanding a decision on a vast range of opinions in order to produce a historical-critical perspective.

Edelheit says Pico offered concordia as the criterion for judging opinions, reached by systematic critical analysis of all human knowledge with reason, experience, authority of authors, and historical and philological analysis, and then a higher concordia between the tested opinions and scriptural faith.

Edelheit says the principle of concordia, achieved in two stages of examining theological and philosophical opinions, was Pico's original contribution to the crisis of ultimate authority in matters of faith.

Edelheit reports the thirteen condemned theses of the Apologia, of which six were condemned and seven declared suspect, among them 'An Deus intelligat', 'De abdita animae intelligentia', 'De Magia naturali et Cabala Hebraeorum' and 'De Salute Origenis'.
Edelheit reports that the commission had sixteen members, including Pietro Garsia, Pico's main opponent, and Giovanni Cordier of the Sorbonne, who supported Pico.
Edelheit argues that the affair shows a general authority crisis in contemporary theology rather than Pico's personal crisis, so that both Pico and his opponents represent the true tenor of the age.

Edelheit reports Di Napoli's view that Garsia's Determinationes magistrales of 1489, his response to Pico's Apologia, show confusion between theological opinion and truth of faith, and that Garsia wrongly identified faith with a thesis merely inferred from an article of faith.
Edelheit reports Di Napoli's suggestion, in a note, that Lorenzo de' Medici was not a theologian but saw well that the theologians near the pope were not serious scholars.

Edelheit says that Pico's statement that he is sworn to no master's words and learned from all schools is important, since his alleged philosophical path from Aristotelian scholasticism to Platonism seemed clear to his contemporaries, and that Pico cannot commit himself to any opinion because he intends to examine the status of opinion itself.
Edelheit cites Barbaro's letter to Pico, printed in Pico's Opera omnia, calling Pico a philosopher who had been first Aristotelian and was now become Platonic.

Edelheit cites Di Napoli's claim that Pico was consciously proud to be the first to bring Plato and the Platonists into a public disputation, resting only on Pico's own words that the doctrine of the Platonists was brought by him into public disputation for the first time in many centuries, as far as he knew; Edelheit notes Di Napoli offers no other evidence and does not treat the point as important.

Edelheit says Pico's summary of his conclusion is that because only Christ's soul descended, and souls are separated and not 'compatible' with space, it seems he did not descend by local movement but only through his operation: without physical presence, his soul was present in hell and produced the effects.
q: After a short summary of his conclusion, where he points out that because only Christ’s soul descended into hell, and souls are separated from any substance, and are therefore not ‘compatible’ with space, it seems that he did not descend …
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says the first explanation, resting largely on Gregory of Nyssa, identifies presence with operation for incorporeal substances such as angels or separated souls, so that Christ's soul was neither inside nor outside hell but truly nowhere, and was said to be in hell because it operated there.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says that Pico, after presenting the first explanation, states that although many Doctors hold it he does not hold it and did not follow it, and gives no reasons or refutation, since what matters to him is that many Doctors accept the explanation.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says the second explanation, that of Scotus and the Scotists which Pico prefers, holds that an incorporeal substance may be truly in a place definitively and locally, but that its reason for being in a place is its operation passing outward, not its substance.
q: With these words Pico begins the presentation of the second explanation of his opinion, the explanation of Scotus and the Scotists, which he prefers.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says Pico is not interested in determining which opinion is truer, and quotes Pico as saying that he does not decide whether the Scotists' opinion or the one he follows on the way separated substances are in a place is truer, only that his opinion was held by so many celebrated Catholic Doctors that those who condemn it as heretical are more rash than he.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says Pico argues that Parisian article 218, that an intelligence, angel or separated soul is nowhere, supports his position no less than article 204, on separated substances being somewhere by operation, opposes it, so that the articles contradict each other.
q: And indeed, Pico is trying to prove that article 218 supports his position no less than does article 204 oppose it. It is clear, then, that they also contradict each other.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says Pico argues that the Parisian articles oblige believers only insofar as they rest on Scripture or decisions of the universal Church, and jokes that they do not cross the Alps, as the English say they do not cross the sea.
q: These articles do not oblige all believers, says Pico, and we do not have to believe in them, unless they rely on the Scriptures, or on the decisions of the universal Church.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says Pico argues that Thomas did not hold the same opinion on how separated things exist in a place in different texts (in some it seems Christ descended per effectum, in others things that might suggest per essentiam), and that Pico points out such inconsistencies to show that all such opinions are only probable.
q: Pico argues that Thomas did not hold the same opinion on this question in different texts, but instead held opposite opinions in different places.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit reports Pico saying that when he advanced the conclusion he believed this was Thomas's opinion, that this is shown by his having advanced the conclusion that Thomas and Scotus do not differ on the angels' mode of being in a place, and that to err about Thomas's opinion is not to err in faith.
q: It is enough, and it seems very clear, that when I advanced the conclusion, I believed that this was Thomas’ opinion
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit notes that in this passage Pico's own position is described as something he believes in a probable way, an echo of the Academic probabile, and that theological opinion is set distinct from faith.
loc: apologia | first condemned conclusion, Christ's descent into hell

text: Edelheit says Pico regarded the Apologia as a substitute for the public disputation on the nine hundred theses that never took place, the theses being like musical notes without performance instructions, which the Apologia supplies.
Edelheit says that Pico combines new humanist methods of philology and history with scholastic critical observation in his discussions of the authority of patristic and scholastic theology.
Edelheit says that in De ente et uno (1491) Pico prefers the skeptical to the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's Parmenides and describes the dialogue as nothing other than a dialectical exercise.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Pico's affinity with skeptical positions is shown also in one of his famous controversies with Ficino over the interpretation of Plato's Parmenides in De ente et uno of 1491.
q: Pico’s affinity with skeptical philosophical positions could be demonstrated (as we have already seen in n. 164) also from one of his famous controversies with Ficino, regarding the interpretation of Plato’s Parmenides, shown in De ente et uno of 1491.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says that in De ente et uno Pico wished to show concord between Plato and Aristotle, arguing that in Aristotle unum, ens, verum and bonum are used interchangeably and with equal range, while the Academia prefers to put unum before ens as more simple and universal.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Academia in this context almost certainly means Plato's immediate successors, especially Speusippus and Xenocrates, and that the notion of a dogmatic ancient Academy distinct from Plato was unusual in Pico's day and contrasts, as Pico himself contrasts it, with Ficino's Neoplatonic interpretations.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Pico probably found this type of interpretation in late ancient sources and combined the evidence of some of them, and that how far Pico knew the sources needs checking, though he must have known Proclus's Platonic Theology, where opponents describe the Parmenides as a logical gymnastic.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Pico's skeptical reading of the Parmenides does not commit him to wholesale skepticism, since the context is a comparison of a Platonic dialogue with the dogmatic Aristotle, and that Pico never consistently follows any school but picks and chooses.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit reports Allen's view, in his account of the second Ficino-Pico controversy, that Ficino emerges as a good deal more original than Pico in the interpretation of the Parmenides, contrary to Klibansky, and notes Allen relates Pico's non-dogmatic interpretation to Albinus without giving references.
q: Allen relates Pico’s non-dogmatic interpretation to Albinus (‘The Second Ficino-Pico Controversy…’ p. 427) but he does not give any reference to Albinus’ texts
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Pico does not mention Ficino at all in De ente et uno and criticised the extra-dogmatic Neoplatonic interpretation associated with the Syrianici, from whom Ficino, as Allen shows, tries to separate himself, while Ficino took a middle path in which the dialogue contains both eristic and theological aspects.
q: Pico, who does not mention Ficino at all in his composition, criticized the extra-dogmatic Neoplatonic interpretation which can be related to the Syrianici—those who succeeded Syrianus and those from whom Ficino, as Allen shows, tries to separate himself (p. 443). …
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Allen is so intent on a sharp contrast between Pico and Ficino, and on who was more original, that he does not see some similarity between their positions, and that Allen's evidence shows the originality of both.
q: Furthermore, Allen is so intent on representing a sharp contrast between Pico and Ficino, and on the issue of who was more original, that he does not see that there is some similarity between the two positions.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit cites Allen for a point on which Ficino and Pico agree, that it would normally be indecorous for Plato to have Parmenides treat dialectic alone, while they differ on why Parmenides continued: Pico says because the company was small, Ficino because he was going to deal with the highest matters of theology.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit notes that Jill Kraye's article 'Ficino in the Firing Line' treats Ficino's Neoplatonic interpretations of the dialogues and their critics.

Edelheit says that in the Apologia Pico describes the disputation of the theses as a scholastic exercise in the manner of the Academies among a few learned men, that the theses include impious dogmas of ancient philosophers such as Averroes and Alexander which he had always declared foreign to true philosophy and to the faith, and that they were proposed as opinions held by others.

Edelheit says Pico clearly separates angelic, divine and human cognition, quoting Pico that angelic knowledge, which appropriates the name of intellectual knowledge, is further from God's infinite knowledge that knows all things through essence than from the rational knowledge proper to the rational soul or man.

Edelheit cites Pico's letter of 11 February 1490 to Aldus Manutius saying that no philosophy should keep us from the truth of the mysteries, and that philosophy seeks the truth, theology finds it and religion possesses it, and reads it as making philosophy an instrument of search, with one and the same truth sought, found and possessed.

Edelheit says Pico told Ermolao Barbaro in a letter of December 6, 1484, that he had recently turned from Aristotle to the Academia not as a deserter but as an explorer, and adds that Plato and Aristotle agree in substance and disagree only in words.

Edelheit says Pico's statement about Plato and Aristotle agreeing in things and differing in words is not the position of the skeptical Academy, which regarded Plato as a skeptic and Aristotle as a dogmatic, but suggests Pico may have recalled Cicero's phrasing of a controversy in Cicero and saw some connection in his thought.

Edelheit says that in a letter to Lorenzo de' Medici of July 1484 Pico compares the poetry of Dante, Petrarch and Lorenzo himself, praises Lorenzo's poetry, and introduces his critical attitude to oratorical ornament and his preference for examining what lies beneath words.

Edelheit reports Schmitt's remark that both Ficino and Pico, like most Renaissance Platonists, paid little attention to Academic scepticism, moving almost to a man toward syncretism, and says he will present a more complex picture of Pico, for whom syncretism is not always an accurate term.

Edelheit says Pico's Apologia shows Pico attempting harmony (concordia) between probable philosophical and theological opinions and between them and faith, and that in the realm of probable opinion even the concordia reached is only between probabilia, but that this attempt at certainty in probable opinions transcends the skeptical Academy.

Edelheit says Pico argues in De ente et uno that the Parmenides contains no dogmas about the superiority of the One over being and that the whole dialogue is an exercise in dialectic, and that Pico suggests, from a reading of the dialogue's sequence, an interpretation of his own.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit says Pico, in the Parmenides argument, disregards the doctrines of Speusippus and Xenocrates and adopts an interpretation explicitly based on the skeptical Academy's view of Plato's dialogues, and that a clear echo of Cicero's Academicus Primus leaves little room for doubt.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | on the Parmenides and the Academia

text: Edelheit notes that Pico's opening speech for the planned Roman assembly contrasts discord with peace, which is related to God, so that Empedocles becomes relevant as an interpreter of Job, and that Pico stresses concord, citing Augustine's Contra Academicos to show the concord of Plato and Aristotle.

Edelheit reports that Pico's speech says the concord of Plato and Aristotle was believed by many but proved by none, that Boethius and Simplicius promised but did not deliver it, and that Pico adds many places where he asserts that the views of Scoti and Thomae, and of Averrois and Avicennae, agree.
loc: oration | concord of Plato and Aristotle

text: Edelheit says the technical use of concordia as a criterion in Pico's theological method is related to the ancient notion of philosophic concord, which is common to both Ficino and Pico as well as to other Renaissance thinkers.

Edelheit says Pico explains that when he calls magia and cabala sciences he means natural knowledge that rests on nothing revealed, not revealed theology, and that they can help human knowledge of Christ's divinity without comprehending it.
loc: apologia | conclusion on magia naturalis and cabala

text: Edelheit says Pico is very proud to be the first person to introduce Cabala to Latin readers and argues that in the books of Cabala many or nearly all things is consonant with the Christian faith.

Edelheit says that Pico's frequent use of the terms probabile and possibile in every chapter of the Apologia combines scholastic terminology about what is only possible with the Academic terminology of what is only probable, delaying final judgment.

Edelheit reports Cerretani's account that Marsilio Ficino, Girolamo Benivieni and Ihoanni de la Mirandola, described as very learned were among those who attended Savonarola's sermons on Genesis and listened with admiration to him affirm that he was sent by God.

Edelheit says that Savonarola's dictum that an old woman knows more of the faith than Plato is well known, but that Savonarola rejects Plato in the context of Christian faith while elsewhere using Plato's authority against astrology, and that he later criticised the Platonists in two later sermons, the first of February 25, 1497.

Edelheit suggests that because Plato and the Neoplatonists were popular among Florentine humanists, and Ficino was both a Platonist and an astrologer, that intellectual context could have threatened the popularity and authority of the preaching prophet Savonarola.

Edelheit says that there is no such contrast between Savonarola and Ficino as Allen describes, since Savonarola, though not a Platonist, used Plato's authority for his own purposes and so played a part in humanist theology.

Edelheit reports Allen's account that Ficino's pagan perspective raised the ire of Savonarola, who demanded its repudiation, and that Pico, still in his twenties, was swept away by the Dominican's zeal while the older, more circumspect Ficino remained committed to a very different vision of Christianity than Savonarola's fideism.

Edelheit asks why Ficino wrote his 1498 Apologia against Savonarola, in which he confesses that a hypocrite from Ferrara deceived so many gifted Florentines for almost five years, if Ficino was always contrasted to Savonarola as Allen argues, and prefers Weinstein's reading of Ficino's attack as that of a disillusioned believer.

Edelheit says that Ficino's letter of December 12, 1494 to Giovanni Cavalcanti treats Savonarola positively as divinely elected, showing prophecies as part of the relation between the human and the divine, and takes Savonarola as a realization of Ficino's own vision of revelation.

Edelheit says Gianfrancesco Pico relates Savonarola to the skeptical tradition, and that Edelheit would not go as far as Granada in saying Savonarola's skeptical apologetic aimed to destroy Ficino's apologetic and its foundation.

Edelheit cites Crinito's description of a philosophical dispute between Pico and Savonarola in the Marciana academy of San Marco on the relation between ancient pagan theology and Christianity, and a manuscript of Sextus with annotations by Poliziano, Pico and probably Ficino that passed to San Marco.

Edelheit reports Garin's observation that the themes of the dignity of man and peace among doctrines are dominant in a programme of spiritual reconstruction, which explains Pico's decided approach to Savonarola though his horizon is wider and his speculative problems deeper.

Edelheit says Savonarola was related to Pico, Nesi and the Benivieni brothers, his most critical opponent was Caroli, and it is impossible to measure his impact on the humanists but also impossible to argue there was none.

Edelheit says Savonarola's Compendium presents angels as mediators between God and men, enlightening the prophet's imagination, and that this mixture of Christian and Neoplatonic notions reconciles the need for mediators between the human and divine, and between the one and the many in Neoplatonic doctrine, through angels.
Edelheit says Savonarola compares the duties of the preacher to those of the angels, citing the three hierarchical operations of the angelic hierarchies to purge, illuminate and perfect.

Edelheit says Pico's Apologia, like Savonarola's approach, examines the theological tradition and Church decisions from a historical perspective, and that a humanist theology sharpened the boundary between the human and the divine to save religion from probability.

Edelheit concludes that Neoplatonic metaphysics was central to Ficino's theological perspective as Academic skepticism was to Pico's, and that the pagan Greek corpus was considered by some Florentine writers more relevant to theology than scholastic Aristotelian philosophy.

Edelheit says that in Ficino's De Christiana religione the pre-Christian ancient theology and the post-Christian Neoplatonic philosophy play the role of praeambula fidei, just as Aristotelian philosophy had in scholastic theology.

Edelheit quotes Vasoli that Nesi, tied to a devout interpretation of Ficinian Platonism, adhered enthusiastically to Savonarola's preaching, with continuity between the two experiences and a fusion of the Platonic golden age with the prophecy of renovation.

Cittadini's critical exchange with Pico took the form of three objections and three responses between 1490 and 1496, with a fourth objection Pico never answered; the reconstruction of the dates is Bacchelli's.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Cittadini's objections and Pico's responses

text: Gianfrancesco Pico, in his Vita of his uncle, mentions Cittadini as the only critic named there, calls him an excellent philosopher, and answered the fourth objection after his uncle's death; Edelheit gives lost interest or untimely death as the probable reasons his uncle did not answer it.
q: We possess an interesting account of Cittadini’s reaction to Pico’s De ente et uno in the Vita of his uncle by Pico’s nephew and biographer, Gianfrancesco Pico

text: The proem of De ente et uno, on Edelheit's reading, implicitly faults Lorenzo's reliance on the Platonists against Aristotle over being and the one, and anticipates an implicit criticism of Ficino developed chiefly in the second chapter.
q: What is suggested by Pico already in the proem, in an implicit manner (an anticipation of his implicit criticism of Ficino, mainly in the second chapter of this text), is that Lorenzo’s reliance (“innixus”) on the Platonists for his arguments …

text: The occasion of De ente et uno, according to Edelheit, was a discussion between Lorenzo, arguing against Aristotle from the Platonists, and Poliziano, presumably defending him, after which Pico was called on to show the concord of Plato and Aristotle.
q: the rationale provided by Pico in these words from the beginning of the proem refers to a discussion between Lorenzo and Poliziano (to whom Pico dedicated his text), where Lorenzo argued against Aristotle, relying on the ‘Platonists’, while Poliziano – …

text: Pico's stance is a critical perspective unusual among Renaissance Platonists: he separates the Platonists from Plato and Aristotle, and locates the main disagreement between Aristotle, who equates one, being, truth and goodness, and the later followers of Plato who put the one before being.
Edelheit says Pico reads the Parmenides as nothing but an exercise in dialectic or logic, whereas the 'Academics' regard it as a dogmatic dialogue containing Plato's doctrine of the one and being.

Pico argues that Parmenides, speaking as a Pythagorean, meant God by 'the one' that is what exists, and elsewhere in his poem allowed division and plurality; this detaches Parmenides from the doctrine that the one is above being.
Pico attributes the doctrine that the one is superior to being to the Platonists alone, and notes that even among them Julian and Gemistus do not accept it and treat one, God and being as equal.

For Pico the divine names 'being', 'one', 'good' and 'true' each denote only a particular perfection, whereas God unites all in one perfection and is the principle and cause of plurality; the Peripatetics, followed by the Parisian theologians, allow all these names in God, while Dionysius and then the Platonists deny life, intellect and wisdom of God.
Pico argues that multitude does not oppose the one; prime matter, with Plato, is more being than one, and Iamblichus takes it to be the first duality and root of all multitudes.
Pico's final move in De ente et uno reorders the four names when God is considered as cause: one first, then good, true and being, following final, exemplary and efficient causes.

Cittadini's first objection is that the treatise does not match its title, because it treats only the mutual conversion of being and the one and that only in Plato's usage, not the nature and properties of each.

Cittadini holds it false that the Platonists say God is not being, citing Themistius for the view that the idea, which is the principle of things, is properly being and one, and that many Platonists identified the idea with God; Edelheit notes he used Barbaro's 1481 translation of Themistius.
The critic argues that no divine attribute, including the one and being, fully reflects God, so that to say God is one but not being is senseless.

Cittadini finds it more astonishing that Pico imposes on Aristotle the view that God is not being, since being divides into substance and accident and God, beyond every genus, is neither, and in Aristotle's tradition some place God in a category of His own.

Cittadini contends that what is divided stands to the one in contradiction, not negation, and that good and evil are contraries according to Aristotle in the Categories and a late-antique commentator, against Pico.

In his first response Pico thanks Cittadini, holds that criticism is always useful and praise useless, and says the title and the proem together fix the treatise's focus, which concedes implicitly that it treats the conversion of being and the one.
q: Pico opens his response to the first objections by thanking Cittadini for his criticism and praising in principle such practices through which we become more learned and better.

text: Pico replies that the Platonic denial that God is properly being is well known to readers of the Platonists, and cites Syrianus, Proclus and Plotinus, who place God above beings and above the ideas.

Pico agrees with Cittadini that no concrete name, whether 'the one' or 'being', can be attributed to God, but holds that the division of being into substance and accident shows that God is beyond being, an opinion he finds in Thomas.

Pico says that many Peripatetics hold that Aristotle placed God among the causes of being and not among beings, and that Cittadini errs in siding with those who put God under a genus and in ascribing that to Boethius.

Pico holds that the natures of the oppositions divided-one, false-true and good-evil are a disputed matter among great authors, that his brief treatment was meant as a starting point, and that Cittadini's arguments do not move him from negation.

Cittadini, dissatisfied with the reply, argues in his second objections that if Themistius shows that the idea, foundation of everything, is properly being, then the claim that Platonists following Plato deny God is properly being is untrue, since the idea is God.
Cittadini argues that if 'the one' is a concrete name that may belong to God's substance, then so is 'being', so that Pico's preference of the one over being has no foundation.

Cittadini objects that Pico misuses Thomas: Thomas's division of being into substance and accident concerns created being only, not uncreated being, so Thomas cannot show that the philosopher denied that God is properly being.

The critic says he affirmed by his own will, not from necessity, that God per se is placed in a category on the authority of Boethius and Augustine, because Thomas's authority alone does not suffice to show that Aristotle or the Aristotelians denied it.

Cittadini declares his regular reading of the logicians he names and admires their subtlety though not always their truth, which for Edelheit shows the limits of Pico's openness and his poor acquaintance with the Mertonians.
loc: oration | open inclusiveness towards all schools

text: Cittadini argues that if a thing is one because it is consonant with itself and undivided, then 'the one' would be both one and true, which is impossible; this attacks Pico's identification of the true with the one.

Cittadini, following Boethius against Albert and Thomas, holds good and evil to be contraries in the way of pairs like healthy and sick, and this grounds a substantial reality of evil, which is part of a wider critique by followers of John Duns Scotus and of the modern schools of Thomas on evil.

Cittadini asks Pico to treat his objections with the zeal with which Pico defended Poliziano's argument against Lorenzo, and Edelheit suggests this reflects Cittadini's sense that Pico was losing interest in the debate.

Pico's second response admits the first was too short or obscure, and promises detail, but adds that since Cittadini cannot read Greek he will lead him through the Latin authors, especially Thomas, to explain the Platonists' ideas.

Pico reminds Cittadini of the Thomist distinction between essence and existence: everything around God that is actual is a composite of the two, God alone being pure existence from which all created existence derives.
On the Thomist distinction Pico concludes that God is existence but not essence, so God is not properly called being; we know only that God is, and nothing of what God is.

Pico maintains that if God as idea is called being it does not follow that God considered absolutely takes the name being; God is beyond being as a mark of eminence, and the Platonists call God beyond being, not non-being.

Pico rejects the critic's classing of Themistius as a Platonist, since all ancient authors call him a Peripatetic, and holds that even if he were a Platonist Platonists distinguish God as God from God as idea.
For Pico's Platonist, to call God one states how God is, not what God is, and to ask what God is is an illegitimate question, since God is beyond every essence and everything intelligible.

Edelheit observes that Pico here uses Platonicus and Academicus as synonyms, both meaning the Neoplatonists, although Cicero and Augustine distinguish the Academic Skeptics from the Middle- and Neoplatonists.

Pico's Platonists say God is most similar to unity, as unity is the foundation of numbers though neither even nor uneven, so God, by His indivisible infinity, confines and holds together everything; calling God one thus says how He is what He is.

Pico argues that God falls under no genus because genera are essences and God neither is nor has an essence, and that 'being' as the Peripatetics use it in the sense of the ten categories does not include God.

Pico holds that there is no absolute evil, since evil things always retain some goodness or an admixture of it, so good and evil cannot be really contrary; Edelheit notes that Cittadini rejects both Thomas and Simplicius here and goes a step beyond Thomas in calling them contraries.

Cittadini's third objections and Pico's second and third responses echo a real debate, probably held in Ferrara on 10 and 20 June 1491 during Pico's and Poliziano's tour of manuscripts, and Pico's third response survives as marginal notes to Cittadini's third objections.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Tertiae obiectiones cum responsione in margine

text: Bacchelli finds that Poliziano's presence at the Ferrara debate is evident from a remark in Pico's second response, where Poliziano is said to have answered the critic's question what God is by saying he did not know, following Simonides.

Cittadini's third objections begin with four conclusions debated in Ferrara (God exists, God is one, God is not God, and the contradiction in the first being not existing while gold does), and complain that Pico had not responded for four months.

Pico, on the statement that God exists, appeals to Dionysius: God is greater than any name, even than the name God; Cittadini finds hard to maintain the distinction between 'what is it' and 'whether it is' since the same word occurs in both.

Pico answers Cittadini's demand to show where Thomas denies that God has an essence by saying that for the Platonists there is no distinction between essence and existence in God, so existence takes in God the place of essence in other things.

Cittadini charges that Pico's stance is inconsistent: De ente et uno said God is not being for the Platonists because God's existence is not other than His essence, yet the responses, following the Platonists, deny that God is essence.

Pico cites Thomas's Summa theologiae 1, q. 48, a. 2 to show that 'being' as answer to 'does it exist?' does not signify essence, so that God's being called ens in that sense does not make ens the essence of things; Cittadini replies that if God is being as idea, He is more so as God, since that part is absolute.
Edelheit reads the quarrel over Simplicius as a clash of methods: Pico insists on exact reference in a humanist manner, Cittadini cares for the argument and is content with Simplicius through Thomas.
q: This point exposes two very different methods and approaches: Pico is here following a humanist approach by aiming at maximum precision in any reference, citation or interpretation, an approach which has been adapted in modern scholarship. Thus, attributing to Simplicius …

text: Cittadini prefers 'unity' to 'one' as the proper attribute of God and criticizes the Platonists for using 'similis' rather than 'similitudo'; Pico replies that the Platonists' Greek 'one' is a substantive, not a denominative, and alludes again to Cittadini's Greek.
Cittadini's fourth objections summarize the debate with added sharpness, and Edelheit doubts he expected another reply from Pico, since his final remark suggests he probably did not.

Cittadini's fourth objections argue that to say God is not being because existence is not other than essence differs from saying it because existence in God is taken for essence, and by the latter reasoning a stone, whose existence is its essence, would also be neither being nor good.

Cittadini argues that if existence and essence are really distinct, as Pico's reading holds for things, and the essence of the idea is God, then the existence of the idea would differ from God, giving a real composition in God.
Cittadini and Gianfrancesco Pico corresponded with mutual respect and cordial relations; Gianfrancesco says that Cittadini and Pico were bound before the disputation as compatres by a spiritual bond.
q: This chapter cannot be completed without a short account of the correspondence between Cittadini and Gianfrancesco Pico, in the light of the latter’s response to the fourth objections. The two letters show mutual respect and cordial relations.

text: Gianfrancesco's response draws on a wider range of mainly scholastic authorities than the debate between Pico and Cittadini, naming Scotus, Giles of Rome, Capreolus, Baconthorpe, Gregory of Rimini, Burley, Holcot, Albert and Anselm, and refutes the scholastic Cittadini with authors of his own school.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Defensio de uno et ente

text: Gianfrancesco holds that to reach his point about knowing privations without knowing their essence one must leave Thomas behind and turn to Giles of Rome, and he argues that the idea, as exemplar of created composites, is composed of essence and existence while God in the recess of His divinity is not.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Defensio de uno et ente

text: Gianfrancesco, appealing to Pseudo-Dionysius, argues that outright evil would destroy outright goodness, so only complete privations can be assumed; he distinguishes absolute evil, which is nothing for lack of a subject, from particular evil as privation of some good.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Defensio de uno et ente

text: Gianfrancesco, citing Pseudo-Dionysius, stresses the gap between divine reality and human terms such as 'spirit', and holds that a confused, faith-based grasp suffices to love God.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | Defensio de uno et ente

text: Edelheit concludes that the real contrariety of good and evil demands a substantial concept of evil and a rejection of the essence-existence distinction, which Cittadini follows beyond his authorities in line with Scotists and modern schools, while Pico follows a Neoplatonic path on which evil is only accidental.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | the debate as a whole

text: Edelheit says Christian Neoplatonists such as Pseudo-Dionysius or Augustine began to develop a substantial and 'strong' concept of evil, unlike the pagan Neoplatonists' accidental and 'weak' concept.

Edelheit stresses the importance for the debate of the rediscovery of the Greek Neoplatonists and ancient commentators, Simplicius and Themistius, and that Cittadini's use of them in translation shows an open scholastic, against Pico's insistence on reading them in Greek.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | the debate as a whole

text: Pico used Thomas's commentary on the Sentences excessively as a source for his 45 theses on Thomas, and Edelheit holds that the theses show Pico's familiarity with the context of each discussion they summarize concisely.
loc: conclusiones | the 45 theses according to Thomas Aquinas

text: Pico's thesis on the more blessed angel and aevum is found by Edelheit in Thomas's Sentences commentary (2, d. 2, q. 1, a. 2), where time as participation in eternity is measured by degree of participation and a blessed angel is prior to the fallen one; Pico's wording is his own interpretation of Thomas.

In Quodlibet 5, q. 4, Thomas, following Pseudo-Dionysius closely, stresses the hierarchy between hierarchies and orders of angels and even among angels in the same order, which Edelheit suggests might be the origin of Pico's angelus beatior.
q: A similar line of argumentation can be found in Thomas’s Quaestiones quodlibetales, 5, q. 4, where Thomas, following closely Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, emphasizes the hierarchical structure between different hierarchies and orders of angels – which might just be the origin …

text: Pico's thesis that sin in the will requires defect in reason is, Edelheit shows, the opposite of Thomas's answer in an early commentary, where it appears only as an argument Thomas refutes; Pico had to seek a positive account in a later work, and may have preferred Thomas's later conclusion.

Pico's thesis that there is no plurification of angels within one species corresponds to Thomas's Sentences commentary (2, d. 3, q. 1, a. 4): immaterial simple forms multiply only through matter, so two incorporeal angels cannot share a species.

Edelheit suggests the rare word plurificatio in Pico's thesis on angels comes from Thomas's De ente et essentia 4, where separated substances, with simple essences unreceived in matter, admit as many species as individuals and only a thing whose quiddity is its existence cannot be plurified.

Edelheit says Pico's thesis 22 is discussed in Thomas's commentary on the Sentences (4, d. 49, q. 2, a. 1), though Thomas asks the broader question whether the human intellect can attain to seeing God through essence; siding with the theologians against the philosophers, Thomas holds that it can.

Edelheit finds most components of Pico's thesis 22 in Thomas, but the contrast between visible appearance and intelligible species and the emphasis on in patria are not found there; Thomas's focus is broader and Pico's shows a standard Neoplatonic emphasis on the move from sensible to intelligible.

Thomas teaches, following Augustine, that in this life we know God most perfectly by knowing Him beyond all that our intellect conceives, joined to Him as unknown, whereas in the fatherland we shall see God through the form that is His essence.

Pico's thesis 23 that 'one' adds to 'being' only the privation of division anticipates De ente et uno; Edelheit finds its source in a Thomist quodlibetal question (10, q. 1, a. 1), where 'one' adds only a negation of division and is indivisible being.
Thomas in a quodlibetal question rejects Avicenna's view that 'one' adds a genus of measure to 'being', on the ground that it would fall into infinite regress.

Pico's thesis 30, that being immediately implies ten concepts united not as of one thing but as referring to one thing, corresponds to Thomas's account in his commentary on the Aristotelian treatise on being of being contracted to the categories by modes of predication, though the wording (conceptus interuniti) is Pico's own.

Edelheit says Pico's thesis 31, that essence and existence in any created being are in fact distinguished, concerns a distinction discussed in Thomas's De ente et essentia, where in God essence and existence are identical while in created intellectual substances existence differs from essence and is limited by the receiving nature.
Edelheit says that in this and other theses Pico uses a refined terminology of his own that reflects his understanding, emphasis and interpretation of Thomas's views.

Edelheit relates Pico's thesis 40, that difficulty in understanding may arise partly from the intellect and partly from the object, to Thomas's Summa contra gentiles 3, 45, where separated substances cannot be understood by our intellect in this life; Pico seems to treat it as a more general epistemological question, without committing to separated substances only.

Thomas, following Aristotle's Metaphysics II, argues that the difficulty lies in us, and that since separated substances cannot be understood through material things, our possible intellect can in no way understand separated substances in this life.
Pico's thesis 44, that no idea of prime matter should be placed in God, is less decisive in Thomas, who allows that in a broad sense of idea as similitude prime matter may have an idea in God.

Edelheit concludes that Pico is accurate in reading Thomas but has interests of his own, shown in vocabulary not found in Thomas, and that in some cases Pico seems to push Thomas beyond the context in order to refute William Ockham, a point that deserves further research.
loc: conclusiones | the 45 theses according to Thomas

text: Pico's thesis that demons and sinful souls suffer from fire in the same kind of suffering as bodies is drawn from Henry's Quodlibet VIII, q. 34, where the only solution is that God supernaturally imprints on the nature of angelic and human spirits a common faculty to suffer from corporeal fire.

Pico's thesis that the operations of angels are measured by discrete time is traced by Edelheit through Henry's Quodlibet II, q. 9, IV, q. 17 and XII, q. 8 to the combination found in Quodlibet XIII, q. 7, where the time of the angel and its actions are discrete.

Pico's thesis that angels understand through a scientific habit connatural to them comes from Henry's Quodlibet V, q. 14, where a separated intellect has no proper natural operation but understanding of natural intelligibles, and an angelic intellect informed by intelligible species cannot fail to understand.

Pico's thesis that angels were not created in grace is derived from an early commentary by Giles (2, d. 4, q. 1), where angels can be called blessed in innocence before sin, created with a natural pure love, but not in grace.

text: In Giles's Reportatio (2, q. 31 and q. 34) the good angels reach beatitude through grace with which they were created, which Edelheit says is opposed to Pico's thesis; Pico's thesis derives from the Sentences commentary while the Reportatio gives a more complicated view.
loc: conclusiones | secundum Aegidium Romanum, thesis 5 (angels not created in grace)

text: Edelheit suggests Pico's thesis 6, that an angel is obstinate and impenitent because divine special impulses were taken from it, might be Pico's own conclusion drawn from thesis 5, an instance of concatenatio between theses; the phrase divini impetus speciales is unique to Pico, though the idea is in the scholastic source.

Giles's Reportatio (2, q. 24), citing Pseudo-Dionysius and Isaiah 6:3, says an inferior angel can be illuminated by a superior one within the same order; but the reason and manner of illumination in Pico's thesis is not yet given there.

Pico's thesis 7, that a superior angel illuminates an inferior not by presenting a luminous object or dividing what is united but by strengthening the inferior's intellect, is found by Edelheit closest in Giles's Sentences commentary (2, d. 9, q. 4), where angels mediate between us and God through intellect and illumination; the rejected alternatives in the thesis are not found there, and the thesis may be Pico's own interpretation.

Giles in the Reportatio (2, q. 41) teaches that the angelic intellect is superior to ours because it understands through more universal species, so that a superior angel has fewer species and understands through one what an inferior needs many for.

text: Caroli, a leading Dominican theologian in Florence and opponent of Savonarola in the 1490s, wrote in 1498 a treatise against some of Pico's theses; Edelheit says Caroli's criticism clarifies Pico's intentions and their reception by contemporary theologians.

text: Edelheit, citing Conti, reports that Caroli's starting point, like Garsia's, is the Apology and not directly the 900 Theses, and that the text against Pico was part of his campaign against Savonarola and several followers including Domenico Benivieni and Giovanni Nesi.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Caroli criticizes Pico for using too much philosophy and speculation in theology, obscuring the superiority of the articles of faith; he says Pico talks like a magpie.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: The critic lists as the theses he attacks those on Christ's descent into hell, on the adoration of the cross and images, three on the Eucharist, on magic and Kabbalah certifying Christ's divinity, and on free will and belief; Edelheit identifies several as theses condemned by the papal commission.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Edelheit says Caroli argues that the article should be held simply and not doubted, stressing Christ's will to descend and not the manner, and that Pico's account is too complicated because it focuses on the modus descensus; Pico's relating of locality to operation and not substance seems to Edelheit very far from Caroli's idea of simplicity.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Caroli argues that Christ's descent, like His ascent, was in real presence, and that Christ, though moving as spiritual substances do (through effect), is never a cause separated from its effect, so He cannot simply be treated as a separated soul or incorporeal substance.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Edelheit cautions that Caroli's opposition to Pico must not be reduced to fear, since Caroli's campaign against Savonarola and his followers, among them Pico, makes the relations between these figures in the 1490s complicated.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Caroli's closing appeal on the cross calls on Pico to abandon his cavillations and dialectical, sophistic or philosophical subtleties, and hopes he now perceives the truth after leaving this mortality; Edelheit reads the terms as placing Pico among the modern way and the Mertonians, and Caroli as repeating the papal commission's charge.
loc: apologia | questions 1 and 5, as attacked in Caroli's Super quibusdam conclusionibus

text: Caroli rejects Pico's explanation that the science of magic and Kabbalah in his thesis is human natural science and not revealed theology, saying only divinely revealed science can certify Christ's divinity and human wisdom is folly before God.
loc: apologia | question 5, magic and Kabbalah and the divinity of Christ

text: Caroli attacks the Kabbalah's claimed ancient oral origin from God to Moses, allowing only natural revelation or revelation in figure, and argues that Ambrose, Jerome and other early Christian authors, who should have known it, never mention it.
loc: apologia | question 5, Kabbalah and the Sinai tradition (Apology pp. 176-178)

text: Garsia cites Thomas that if the purpose of the Assumption is liberation from sin only human nature can be assumed congruently, since sin is absent in irrational nature and incurable in angelic nature but curable in human nature.
loc: apologia | question 4, whether a non-rational nature can be assumed by God

text: Garsia devotes 71 pages to magic and Kabbalah against 16 in Pico's Apology, denies Pico's assumption that magic is part of natural philosophy, following William of Auvergne, and rejects the divine authority and antiquity of the Kabbalah, noting the Talmud's hostility to Christianity and that Pico's argument partly rests on the apocryphal 3 Esdras.

Garsia insists on the distinction between the divine and revealed and the natural and acquired: magic and Kabbalah cannot certify Christ's divinity more than theology, and Pico's thesis, implying they can replace faith, is false and heretical; Edelheit sees in the theme antecedents of the Savonarola dispute over true and false prophecy in 1490s Florence.

Edelheit notes Garsia was relatively informed on Judaism and Kabbalah with rather traditional sources (Jerome, Augustine, Josephus, Nicholas of Lyra), and that Pico's accusation of the commission's ignorance of the Kabbalah is probably exaggerated and rhetorical.
Torni, a Florentine philosopher-doctor and Mertonist, took part in the 1489 debate on the origin of evil at Lorenzo de' Medici's palace, where Pico, Ficino and Poliziano were also present.

Edelheit says Torni presents what is called the Merton theorem of uniform acceleration to show that two bodies can be in one place, and since no contradiction is found, that God could move a stone from place a to place b while at the same time it is in place b.
loc: conclusiones | secundum Thomam, thesis 20 (same body in different places)

text: Edelheit could not find Pico's thesis with difficultas intelligendi in Thomas, thinks Pico probably used another source ascribing it to Thomas, and notes Thomas's rejection in Summa contra gentiles 3, 45 of understanding separated substances in this life.

On Albert, Edelheit finds that Pico's thesis on the separate soul understanding through species created with it by an external immaterial substance corresponds in part to Albert's teaching that the rational soul is produced by an external agent, resembles the separate substance that produced it and has its intellect separated from the body; the second part of the thesis he could not find in Albert.
loc: conclusiones | secundum Albertum Magnum, separate soul and species

text: In Albert's commentary on the natural-philosophy treatise, 'being' and 'substance' precede 'body' and 'magnitude' in the natural order and are found before them in the intelligences and separate substances, and dealing with them belongs to first philosophy; Edelheit says this is the substance of Pico's thesis.
loc: conclusiones | secundum Albertum Magnum, thesis on first philosophy

text: Edelheit reports that Garin refuted the assumptions that Pico was from an early stage a disciple and follower of Ficino, or that he became a Thomist after an encounter with Savonarola in Ferrara.

Edelheit says Poliziano's model of philosophy was exclusive, differing from both Ficino's and Pico's inclusive models, and that Pico's model of the historian of philosophy differs from those of Poliziano, Barbaro and even Ficino.
