text: Edelheit thinks the parodies of Pythagoras in Poliziano's Lamia reflect Poliziano's exclusive approach and not a direct critique of his friends Ficino and Pico, who held two different inclusive approaches.
Edelheit says Delmedigo's relation with Pico, begun at Padua, shaped Pico's basic understanding of Averroes and helped develop a critical approach to Averroes's Latin commentators.

In his closing chapter Edelheit sums up that Pico's reading of the Latin scholastics is thorough, competent and creative, that he uses his own terminology for Thomas and takes the Sentences commentary as the source for Thomas's views, and that this engagement is a component of his claim to originality.

Edelheit sums up that Garsia criticizes what he regards as Pico's Nominalist views, which he associates with Scotus and his followers, and that the dispute over the 'common way' shows disagreement about its definition, Garsia's understanding being flexible and issue-dependent.
q: Moving to theology, Chapters 14 and 15 contained discussions of the attacks of Pedro Garsia and Giovanni Caroli on Pico’s Apology, on some theses and on his approach to theology in general. Garsia criticizes what he regards as Pico’s Nominalist …

text: On Being and the One was addressed to a named humanist as part of a continuing quarrel between Aristotelians and Platonists.
It seems likely to Howlett that De ente was part of Pico's planned concord of Aristotle and Plato.
De ente was also a response to Ficino's writing on Being and the One.
q: It was also a response to Ficino’s writing on Being and the One.

text: Pico's polemic in De ente was contested from the Platonic side by Ficino and from the Aristotelian side by Cittadini, and in letters to Cittadini Pico says he is attempting something new that leaves neither side content.
q: But Pico’s ‘polemic’ was disputed not only by Ficino (from the Platonic perspective) but also by his friend, the Aristotelian, Antonio de Cittadini. Over a series of letters with Cittadini, Pico argues that he is genuinely attempting to do some-thing …

text: Howlett reads the commentary on a canzone as taking a Platonism based more on Plotinus than Ficino's was at that time.
Howlett reads the commentary as Pico's opening move against Ficino, presenting himself as a rival expert on Platonism with a truer understanding drawn from Plotinus.
Pico's commentary names 'our Marsilio' and says he made mistakes in every part of his treatise on the Banquet.
Howlett states that Pico's main disagreement with Ficino in the commentary concerns Ficino's view of physical love and beauty.
Howlett describes Heptaplus as Pico's first cosmological work, an alternative or addendum, according to viewpoint, to Ficino's cosmology in the Philebus commentary.
Howlett says Pico's universe joins the Latin emphasis on positive theology with the negative theology prominent in Byzantine Orthodoxy, at a time of renewed interest in Pseudo-Dionysius.
Howlett holds that in Pico's ladder the positive attributes of God structure the ascent, while what God is not lies beyond the ladder and beyond the universe.
Howlett describes the mystical tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius as the living spirit that binds together the Platonic, Aristotelian and Kabbalistic parts of Pico's world.
Howlett notes that Platonism and Christianity are already combined in Pseudo-Dionysius' account of henosis and suggests that Pico was largely unaware of such prior connections.

Howlett says that because Ficino's Platonism was still evolving, Pico could assert a Platonism in contradiction to Ficino's and claim a purer reading through Plotinus, and that contradicting Ficino is arguably axiomatic to his work.
Howlett points out that Ficino's Platonism was not pure either, being influenced by his antecedents such as Aquinas and combined with Christianity.
Howlett says Pico's Enneads use in 1486 preceded Ficino's published translation, so his Platonism belonged to a revival still in progress.
Howlett argues that Pico challenges Ficino not because he is an Aristotelian but because he believes himself closer to the real Plato, and also to assert his own abilities.
Pico reportedly told Ficino his purpose was to compare Plato with Aristotle, and Aristotle with Plato, in alternate studies.
Howlett reports that Pico's aim moved from alternating study of Plato and Aristotle to showing their compatibility, a desire that persisted until 1490.
Howlett says that Pico learned Platonism in large part from Ficino and had conversations on Kabbalism from an Aristotelian Jew, preferring Kabbalistic commentaries influenced by Maimonides.
Howlett says Aquinas in the thirteenth century tried to marry Aristotelianism with Christianity, and that Ficino built his union of faith and reason on Platonism and Christianity following Augustine.
q: Various solutions were proposed, for instance in the thirteenth century, Aquinas attempted to marry Aristotelianism with Christianity20;

text: Howlett says Pico attempted something more ambitious, maintaining parts of scholasticism as well as Plato and other ancient wisdom in one grand concordance between philosophy and Christianity.
Howlett says Pico tended toward Aquinas and the via antiqua, whose realism made Aristotle the philosopher, while remaining sympathetic to the Paris conversations of the via moderna.
Howlett says Ficino and Pico began as teacher and student in the early 1480s and that their relationship was complex both in life and after Pico's death.

Howlett argues that Ficino encouraged a story of intellectual proximity, casting Pico as heir-apparent of a Platonic Academy and crafting after Pico's death a narrative aligning Pico's birth and arrival in Florence with Ficino's Platonic work.

Howlett says the reading of Ficino and Pico as members of one group makes Pico essentially a Platonist and Pico's deviations from Ficino very confusing, while works on Pico alone tend to sideline Ficino almost completely.

Howlett says that Ficino's letters show Pico involved in more than a fifth of Ficino's correspondence between 1484 and 1488, and that Ficino responds to Pico's demands with praise, attempting to gloss over their disagreements.
Howlett holds that the debates between Ficino and Pico are the points of rupture, where they specifically and publicly engage each other.
Howlett says Pico sent a draft of his Commentary to Ficino and that Lorenzo asked Ficino to invite Pico to live in Florence on his return to Italy, showing a close relationship.
Howlett notes that Ficino's collected letters include no letters about, and no mention of, Pico's De ente.

Howlett says a curious silence falls in the correspondence in 1493-94 and that the relationship was complicated by Pico's constant written disagreement with Ficino and perhaps more by the ascendance of Savonarola.

Howlett writes that up until 1493 it is as if Pico and Ficino are in a decade-long argument, expressed as a series of debates on the position of Beauty and finally on the influence of the stars, though Ficino remained always close to Pico.

Howlett says Pico's request to Benivieni to change his poem let him give a reading of Plotinus truer to the original than Ficino's Platonism of the time, and that Ficino claimed after Pico's death that Pico renounced the work.

Howlett characterises the Commentary episode as essentially a cover-up permitted in large part because Pico did not publish the Commentary or live long enough to complete a self-fashioning of his career.
Howlett summarises De ente as arguing that God is both singular (the One) and Being, and that Plato and Aristotle agree on this.
Howlett reports that Plato is normally understood to posit that the One is above Being, particularly in the Parmenides, differing from Aristotle who places the two together.
q: Plato is normally understood to posit that the One is above Being, particularly in his dialogue Parmenides; differing from Aristotle who places the two together.

text: Howlett says De ente was Pico's last completed manuscript and may have been meant as part of his Concordance of Plato and Aristotle, as he seems to indicate.

Howlett argues that to reach concord in De ente Pico had to remove obstacles in Plato, particularly the Parmenides, which he treats as merely a rhetorical exercise, so that Plato should not be taken at his word.
q: To achieve concord in this case, he needed to remove several obstacles in Plato, particularly Parmenides. Pico argues that the dialogue is simply a rhetorical exercise, meaning that we should not take Plato at his word.

text: Howlett says Ficino translated the Parmenides around 1469 but had probably not yet written a commentary when Pico wrote De ente, and that his commentary was published in 1496.
q: In 1496, a few years after Pico’s death, Ficino published his Commentary on Plato’s ‘Parmenides’. Ficino had translated Parmenides around 1469 but had probably not yet written a commentary when Pico wrote On Being and the One.

text: Howlett argues that a commentary produced between 1492 and 1494, while Pico was still living, follows a sequence that takes on Pico's arguments section by section to refute him.
q: Between 1492 and 1494, while Pico was still living, he produced the commentary. It follows a sequence that specifically takes on Pico’s arguments section by section to refute him.

text: Howlett says Ficino held to the Platonic orthodoxy, deriving from Plotinus and often filtered through Proclus, that Plato argues the One is above Being.
q: Ficino himself holds with Platonic orthodoxy, deriving from Plotinus, often filtered through Proclus, that Plato argues the One is above Being.

text: Howlett argues that De ente was already partly an attack on Ficino, who had written on Being and the One even before his commentary and consistently held the orthodox Platonic view placing the two separately.
q: Ficino is providing a contemporaneous direct reply and counter to Pico. But On Being was already partly an attack on Ficino. Even before his commentary, Ficino had written about Being and the One and was consistently of the ‘orthodox’ Platonic …

text: Howlett notes that this controversy has often been discussed and that Salas has taken apart some inconsistencies in Pico's argumentation.
q: This particular conflict has been discussed often, for instance by Van Haelen (2009), Allen (1995, for example), and Salas (2014) who has taken apart some of the inconsistencies in Pico’s argumentation.

text: Howlett summarises the three major polemical moments as Ficino's Symposium commentary answered by Pico's Commentary, Ficino's traditional view of God as the One above Being answered by De ente, and Ficino's Parmenides commentary in reply.

Howlett says Ficino wished to correct Pico or smooth over the cracks, and that the pattern of confrontation indicates a larger disagreement of purpose or mission between two philosophers whose sources are not so different.

Howlett says the question of mission has become clearer for Ficino in the past twenty years of scholarship through the concept of renovatio, using a Platonized Christianity to aim at a new Golden World through the return to God, but that such a mission has not been so defined in Pico's case.

Howlett argues both Ficino and Pico use Aristotle, Ficino drawing on Aquinas and the peripatetics for analogia entis, act and potency and his theory of Being, so that there is an effort at concord between Aristotle and Plato in Ficino too.
Howlett says Ficino and Pico both use Proclus, Pico using him in 100 of the 900 conclusions, and that Ficino draws on Proclus' Platonic Theology when discussing God as Unity.
Howlett states in a note that Ficino emphasizes one God rather than the Proclan universe of henads, whereas Pico's Kabbalism lets him explore Proclus in all his complexity.
q: Where they deviate is Ficino emphasizes one God rather than the Proclan baroque universe of henads, see Dillon (2011, 14–15), whereas Pico’s Kabbalism allows him to explore Proclus in all this complexity.

text: Howlett argues Pico is remarkable in going back to Plotinus, the point of origin of Neoplatonism, emphasizing him more than Ficino did at the time.

Howlett says Plotinus' emphasis on the One, easily equated with God, allowed Neoplatonism to develop into an increasingly elaborate theological philosophy, and that it is unsurprising that Proclus' key work was the Platonic Theology, from which Ficino took the title of his own summa.

Howlett argues that Pico's use of Plato and Aristotle in De ente is awkward because he attempts a change in the Platonic universe in an effort, he claims, to return to an original understanding of Plato, sidelining the Parmenides as a rhetorical exercise.

Howlett says Pico asserts he is more militantly originalist than Ficino: in the Commentary he criticises Ficino for using intermediaries on Plotinus, and in De ente he says he is going back to the real Plato rather than seeing him through Proclus.
Howlett states in a note that Farmer suggests Ficino's use of Proclus came after Pico's Conclusions.

Howlett argues Ficino tied the ancient theologians together through Platonism into a Platonic-Christian hybrid, while Pico tied them within a Platonic structure using Aristotelian argument and Kabbalism.
Howlett quotes Kristeller that there can be no doubt as to Pico's dependence on Ficino, and says much of Pico's work would not have been possible without Ficino's translations and commentaries.
Howlett says both Ficino and Pico agreed on connecting metaphysics with theology, bringing faith and reason together, which distinguishes them from the scholastics.

Howlett notes that Pico's Disputations indirectly attacks Ficino's astrological magic in the third book of De vita, and that this dispute is unconnected to questions of Platonism against Aristotelianism.
Howlett says it is unclear whether Pico is inconsistent on astrology, making a point about science or political prediction, or whether Disputations is a patchwork of Pico and Gianfrancesco's editing.
Howlett notes there are other, less well explored conflicts between Pico and Ficino such as Pico's discussion of human nature in the Heptaplus and Oration.

Howlett says that without the Academy framework Pico is no longer Ficino's closest protege and that the Academy perspective required arguing that Pico was mistaken in De ente and Ficino gently correcting him.

Howlett notes that concord first appears as a linguistic matter and quotes Pico's thesis that Aristotle and Plato agree in meaning and substance in every natural or divine question, though in their words they seem to disagree.
Howlett cites Pico as finding, on examining the two, that in the words nothing is more opposed and in the substance nothing is more concordant.
loc: letter to Barbaro | words and things

text: Howlett says Pico's Aristotelianism supplies his mode of argument, including insistence on dividing causal from participatory being, while his universe is predominantly a Platonic one inflected by Aristotle.
Howlett says Pico's aim is to show that philosophy leads to theology and then to religious faith, echoing Pseudo-Dionysius.
Howlett argues Pico's concordance hierarchizes the process, so resolution can lean toward one side, which perhaps explains why his Aristotelianism and Platonism seem to alternate.
Howlett says Pico and Ficino both believed that the earlier the knowledge, the truer it is likely to be.
Howlett states that Cardinal Bessarion espoused concordism between Aristotle and Plato.
Howlett quotes a note that Pico did not hold that all philosophers defended the same position in different words, and that he privileged the claims of Christianity.
Howlett reports Schmitt's view that Aquinas was primarily Aristotelian in form but Platonic in his metaphysics, though distinguishing the two was difficult at the time.
q: Schmitt (1983, 29) and also argues that Aquinas was primarily in form Aristotelian, but in his metaphysics, Platonic, though distinguishing was difficult at the time (1983, 93).

text: Howlett reports from Garin that Del Medigo was with Pico in Perugia, where they spent much time talking about being, essence and unity.
Howlett says Ficino uses the prisca theologia to lead a renovatio, whereas Pico seeks the esoteric primarily for private revelation, and that Kabbalism did not have such a distinctive role in Ficino.
Howlett reports Hankins's series of essays contesting the twentieth-century norm of a Platonic Academy in Florence led by Ficino and including Pico.
Howlett reports in a note that in reply to Ficino's invitation to live in Florence Pico addressed Ficino as father of the Platonic family and master of his learning.
loc: letter to Ficino | reply to invitation

text: Howlett reports Farmer's argument that Pico's new philosophy lay in a traditional though exaggerated Neoplatonic framework tied to the highly syncretic Platonic systems of late antiquity.

Howlett says the Conclusions show Pico's three pillars: in section one the largest cohort is medieval philosophy led by Aquinas, then Platonists led by Proclus, and the largest individual sections belong to Proclus, then Kabbalism, then Aquinas, then Averroes.

Howlett says that in Plotinian terms the Kabbalistic Tree can be taken as the many and the God beyond it, the Ein-Sof, as the One, a hidden, unknowable God of whom one can say only what it is not, as in Christian apophatic theology such as Pseudo-Dionysius.

Howlett says the Ein-Sof is also called Being, possibly through Aristotelian influences, though indeterminate being, and that in the philosophical setting of Aristotelians versus Platonists it becomes part of the argument around Being and the One.
Howlett reports that Isaac's circle emphasized the hidden God with the new term Ein-Sof, beyond the Tree of Life and above divine thought, as cause of Thought beyond being or thought.
Howlett argues Pico embraces the Ein-Sof as the unity beyond the sefirot, thereby combining Kabbalah with the Plotinian One through a Platonic version of Kabbalism espoused by the Girona School.
Howlett says Pico calls the Ein-Sof one, in a passage describing God as infinite, as one and as existing through himself, closed in himself and concealed in the abyss of his darkness.
Howlett argues that Keter, given the number one, represents the Ein-Sof within the created universe, so that the Plotinian One raises the question of two Ones, one outside creation and one within.
Howlett reports a passage of Pico comparing Aristotle's concealing of the more divine philosophy with the way Rabbi Moses the Egyptian's Guide for the Perplexed enfolds the mysteries of the Cabala.
Howlett argues the Aristotelian First Cause can be argued as Keter, and the first three sefirot together as the First Cause, each triad mirroring an Aristotelian triad of intellection.
Howlett says the connection between Hokmah and the Active Intellect, made by Maimonides and taken up by Abulafia, is present.
Howlett says Maimonides argued that the ultimate aim of ascent was the Active Intellect, expressed as Hokmah but also as Enoch, Metatron and the Cherubic realm, the higher Active Intellect.
Howlett says Pico links the Metatron with aspects of Orpheus' Pallas, Zoroaster's paternal mind, Hermes' son of God, Pythagoras' wisdom and Parmenides' intelligible sphere.
Howlett says that in Pico's Kabbalistic scheme the guardians of Orphism are powers in Pseudo-Dionysius and the sefira Din in Kabbalah.
Howlett states that Pseudo-Dionysius is probably the closest Christian forebear to Pico's mysticism.

Howlett says the author of the corpus areopagaticum wrote in the fifth and early sixth century, became influential in Latin Europe in the twelfth century and influenced Aquinas and Eckhart, and became even more popular through Traversari's 1436 translation.
q: Pseudo-Dionyisus was writing in the fifth and early sixth century with a body of works (corpus areopagaticum) attributed to him, such as the Divine Names, Mystical Theology, and Celestial Hierarchy. In Latin Europe, he became influential in the twelfth century …

text: Howlett says Pico used Dionysius in the Heptaplus in his description of angelic and celestial worlds and throughout the Oration.

Howlett states that Pseudo-Dionysius thought of henosis, the final stage, as seeing God (epopteia), and that in the ascent she describes we have moved beyond the Aristotelian Active Intellect, beyond Being itself, to Platonic henosis.
Howlett says that in combining Pseudo-Dionysius, Platonism, Aristotelianism and Jewish thought it is unclear what henosis would be in Kabbalism and what the roles of Keter and the Ein-Sof are.
Howlett states that Pico changes Pseudo-Dionysius' hierarchy of angels from nine to ten, the number of the sefirot.
q: Elsewhere, where Pseudo-Dionysius and Kabbalism do not coincide, Pico tries hard to relate Pseudo-Dionysius to Kabbalism. For instance, Pico changes Pseudo-Dionysius’ hierarchy of angels from nine to ten, the number of the sefirot.174

text: Howlett notes that in the Kabbalistic tree of attributes those attributes nearest the point of origin are most like the divine, which in Platonism is the world of Ideas and in Ficino's Christian Platonism the Angelic Mind.
Howlett says Enoch is synonymous with the Metatron, a high angelic power, and that by the middle of the thirteenth century the Metatron had been divided into a higher, Great Metatron and a lower.

Howlett describes Proclus' scheme as triads of henads related to the worlds of the Platonic universe, with orders of angels, demons, heroes and souls below the gods, the triads repeating within an ever more crowded universe.

Howlett states that Pico drew connections between the Plotinian One as God and the sefirot, the Trinity, angels and demons in a Platonic-gnostic structure, finding in Kabbalism the Platonic universe of Proclus he already knew.
Howlett says Maimonides' Jewish Aristotelianism eventually impacted Kabbalism but only later, and that the school in question left only a small place for Maimonides.

Howlett says Recanati could have been the most significant source of Pico's Kabbalistic statements in section one of the Conclusions, with about 25 of 47 and possibly a further 12 deriving from his work, while section two draws more on Abulafia.
Howlett says Pico's sources strongly suggest that the ecstatic theurgical Kabbalism of Abulafia is primary, with Recanati also important.

Howlett says Flavius did not translate the Zohar or Sefer Yesirah, but Pico knew of them through commentaries, and Pico was reading missing works such as the Zohar through commentaries with a preferred perspective.

Howlett says Ficino references the Bahir through Paul of Burgos while Pico is the first to use the text directly, and that Ficino also knew other Kabbalistic material such as Samuel Sarsa's Sefer meqor hayyim.
q: Ficino references the work in his On the Christian Religion but through Paul of Burgos. Pico is the first to use the text directly165 (Ficino does know and use Kabbalah beyond Bahir. For instance, Samu’el Sarsa’s Sefer meqor hayyim from …

text: Howlett says Alemanno, a product of the Paduan Aristotelian circle who gravitated toward Maimonides, worked with Pico, though whether before or after the Rome venture is unclear.

Howlett says Pico's universe is primarily Christian Platonic with attempted concordance with Aristotelianism and Kabbalism, so that Pico's difference from Ficino shows his own contribution, resting in part on a strong preference for Proclus.
Howlett says Pico's God emerges as single but somehow twofold: a God of apophatic theology and an active creator from whom emanation or creation occurs who can be at least partially described.
Howlett says that in Pico's concordance Hokmah is also the Aristotelian active intellect and Christ, another potential end and the Ficinian home of being.
q: For in Pico’s concordance, Hokmah is also the Aristotelian active intellect and Christ (another potential end and the Ficinian home of ‘being’).

text: Howlett describes Ficino's first level as the angelic mind or intellectual, supracelestial world, combining the Christian sphere of the angels with the Plotinian intellect.

Howlett states that Pico uses the basic Ficinian structure while emphasizing Proclus and the sacred geometry of the universe (her own statement); she then quotes Pico's Heptaplus, which reports God presiding over nine orders of angels in the first world.
Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the three worlds are one world because whatever is in any of them is contained in each.
Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that although the natures are mutually contained they are allotted separate seats and peculiar rights.

Howlett says the Plotinian One is an atemporal unity while Pico's creator is located in a temporal framework, that the God of Kabbalism is the Ein-Sof, and that the Aristotelian First Cause is an unmoved mover involving action commensurate with a creator God.

Howlett argues that Pico's syncretic God is twofold and that Kabbalism allows this, positing both the Ein-Sof and the first sefira Keter, which partly shares the Ein-Sof's apophatic qualities yet begins the emanatory chain, so that the problem is knowing which he is referring to.
Howlett says Pico's phrase the solitary darkness of the Father may sound like a description of the Ein-Sof but suggests rather the partially active principle of God as Keter.

Howlett states that Pico's description of God in the Conclusions recalls the Ein-Sof and the God of Christian apophatic theology, and that Pico is taking us from Ficinian Platonism to the darkness of Pseudo-Dionysius.
Howlett quotes Pico's De ente that in the ascent God is being itself, the one itself, the good itself, yet we are still in light, that God is above being, true, one and good, and dwells in darkness.
q: …God is being itself, the one itself, the good itself, and likewise truth itself. We have now advanced two steps, ascending to the darkness which God inhabits, purging from the divine names all blemish that is from the imperfection of …

text: Howlett quotes Pico's De ente as placing God most eminently above unity, goodness, truth and existence, unintelligibly and ineffably above everything most perfect.

Howlett distinguishes the God who is existence, truth and unity itself, still in light, from the unintelligible Pseudo-Dionysian God above even unity in darkness, and reads the former as comparable to the pleroma.

Howlett posits that the coordinated unity Pico names is Keter, a plenitude of attributes in one, while the abstract and uncommunicated unity is the Ein-Sof, and says Keter is God revealed in the universe.
Howlett says there is one God who can be talked about in two different ways, apophatically or, as a philosopher must before mystical ascent, by explaining what God is.
Howlett says it is hard to know which God Pico refers to, taking a Heptaplus passage on God as being itself and derived from nothing as an example.
Howlett notes that early Kabbalism was unsure whether Keter should be counted part of the Ein-Sof rather than a sefira.
Howlett notes that prayer and ascent of a community of believers is also core to Pseudo-Dionysius, hence familiar to Pico, and that Pseudo-Dionysius borrows from Platonic gnostic traditions.
Howlett asks where the Plotinian One is, noting that Pico says God is being itself, potentially an Aristotelian argument, whereas Plotinus and Ficino consider the Plotinian One above being.
q: But where then is the Plotinian One? Is it Keter or the Ein-Sof? And what of the First Cause? Pico has told us that God is ‘being itself,’ potentially an Aristotelian argument, whereas the Plotinian One is considered, by Plotinus …

text: Howlett says that in De ente Pico outlines an apparently Aristotelian view that being and the One are the same, equating the One with the First Cause, and argues this is also Plato's original perspective, later misinterpreted by his followers.

Howlett quotes De ente's report of the received Platonic view that the One is prior to being because the one is more simple and more universal, so that God, whose is the highest simplicity, is one but not being.

Howlett states the problem as how the One can be more than one thing, and suggests, more persuasively as she puts it, that this may be another instance of the Ein-Sof/Keter separation: a Plotinian One above being as abstract unity, and a One containing being as creative principle.

Howlett states that Plato's Parmenides and Sophist both state that being and the One are not the same, but Pico argues that nothing in the Parmenides is positively asserted and that it is nothing but a dialectical exercise.
Howlett judges Pico's treatment of the Parmenides a weak parrying of an inconvenient text and says he sees it as a red herring followed by later Platonists but not Plato's own view.
Howlett says Pico's thesis is that Plato and Aristotle agree that the One contains being, making his One a plenitude rather than the solitary, hidden nought.

Howlett reports Pico's first argument in De ente that since nothing is outside all things but nothing itself, being includes all things, and the one cannot include more than being, nor fewer, so being and the one are equals.

Howlett says Pico's second argument apparently contradicts his first, reasoning that God is not being but is above being and is the one above being, which Howlett identifies as the Ein-Sof also as the Plotinian One.
q: His second argument apparently contradicts his first

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Conclusion that the grades of the universe can be divided in five ways, from that-above-being to truly-not-being, and places it in the group on Plato.

Howlett argues that the Ein-Sof/Keter division partially solves the inconsistency between a God above being (the atemporal Plotinian One) and a One that contains being, the coordinated unity allowing the One to contain the many.

Howlett argues the distinction Pico consistently makes between formal being and causal being makes the riddle simpler: causal being, suggesting Aristotle's First Cause though he refers also to Plotinus, is the cause of the abstract concept being, as opposed to formal being.
q: Further, if we consider also the distinction he consistently makes between formal being and causal being in his work,40 then the riddle becomes even simpler. Causal being, suggesting Aristotle’s First Cause (though he refers also to Plotinus), is the cause …

text: Howlett reports Lohr's argument that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas' distinction between different types of being.
q: Lohr (1988, 583) argues that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas’ distinction between these different types of being.

text: Howlett says Pico argues in the Commentary that Platonists view God as the cause of everything, not a thing but the cause of all things and not intellect but the source of all intellect.

Howlett argues that the causal-formal-participatory distinction is at odds with Ficino's understanding of Platonism, quoting Pico's remark that these statements give great trouble to modern Platonists and that a distinguished Platonist was astonished at Plotinus saying God understands nothing.
q: This differentiation between the causal and the formal (and participatory, forming of course a triad) is at odds with Ficino’s understanding of Platonism: Pico says ‘These statements give great trouble to modern Platonists…. I remember that a distinguished Platonist once …

text: Howlett says Pico's Platonism binds Aristotelianism and Platonism by rereading Aristotle through the lens of later Platonism, moving between kataphatic and apophatic theology.

Howlett argues that Pico's God as Ein-Sof is so far above us that only apophatic theology can apply, whereas the revealed divine within the void, carrying the kinetic energy of God, the emanated universe or Tree of Life, is part of kataphatic theology.
Howlett says Pico's universe is both emanated (Platonic) and created (Judaeo-Christian), and that the result is confusing.
Howlett reports Craven's argument that in the Heptaplus the worlds are not emanated but direct acts of creation starting with the lower world.
Howlett lists Pico's quasi-dualisms: a hidden God and the One of plenitude; Ein-Sof and Keter; prime matter of privation and of potentiality; and an emanatory and a created universe.

Howlett argues that with Aristotelian causality God as First Cause may only participate in the first hypostasis, and lays out a triad of causal being in the One, formal being in the angelic mind and participatory being in the rational soul.

Howlett notes that both Ficino and Pico hold that all created beings desire beauty, but that in the Commentary Pico argues that God has no desire because he lacks nothing, so that the love of beauty is alien to Him.
Howlett says Pico's doctrine that beauty is a subcategory of the good differs from Ficino, who, as Pico argues, places beauty below the good in the first emanation.

Howlett reports Pico's commentary saying that love is not in God as Marsilio believes, since that would be an imperfection, but is the love of creatures for Him, and cites Allen on how strange this is.

Howlett says that in his Platonism Pico disagrees with Ficino on love, beauty and the good, adopting alternative Platonic viewpoints based on Plotinus and Proclus, and that divine beauty must lie in the first world of the emanated universe, Ficino's angelic mind.

Howlett states that the first hypostasis is the supracelestial or intellectual world, called the angelic mind in Ficino's Christian Platonic universe, and that in Kabbalism it consists of the triad Keter, Hokmah and Binah, which is also for Pico the Trinity.
q: This first ‘hypostasis’ is the supracelestial or intellectual world, also known in Ficino’s Christian Platonic universe as the angelic mind. In Kabbalism, this world consists of a triad of sefirot: Keter, the crown or throne of God; Hokmah, the incomprehensible …

text: Howlett says the first triad of Keter, Hokmah and Binah is the Platonic Christian angelic mind, the realm of seraphim, cherubim and thrones, the top of Jacob's ladder, the place of the Metatron, the world of forms and of formal being.
q: This first triad of Keter, Hokmah, and Binah is also the Platonic Christian angelic mind and as such is the realm of the seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. It is the top of Jacob’s ladder and the level we try to …

text: Howlett states that Keter is the one plus nine, the primal unity presiding over the nine orders, and that Keter or Hokmah, most persuasively Hokmah, is Aristotle's Active Intellect.

Howlett quotes Pico's conclusion that when Plato says Love was born from the union of Poverty and Plenty on the birthday of Venus, he means that the first love, the desire of beauty, was born in the angelic mind when the splendour of ideas began to shine.

Howlett quotes Pico's Commentary that the Angelic Mind did not have its perfect natural being until Love was born and turned it to God, and that the ideas descend from God into the Angelic Mind, becoming imperfect through distance from God.
Howlett quotes Pico that the Platonic forms are in their essence in the angelic mind, where they are first produced by God, and are in the rational soul by participation.

Howlett argues that in Ficino's Christian Platonic universe the angelic mind is the home of being, whereas Pico distinguishes formal being in the angelic mind from the locations of causal and participatory being.
Howlett says Pico reorganizes Ficino's hierarchy of forms or understands them differently, for instance making beauty a subspecies of the good.

Howlett says that in Ficino's Christian Platonism the epistemological and ontological are linked, the world of forms combined with the mind of God, which can then also be Aristotle's agent or active intellect.

Howlett says Alexander of Aphrodisias argued that the active intellect was the agency of divine intelligence and was universal, and that Augustine connected the world of forms with the angelic sphere.
Howlett says Averroes held both intellects universal and unified, Padua followed Averroes, and Aquinas disagreed, arguing that the active intellect is part of the individual mind.

Howlett argues that in Pico's universe the angelic mind is the world of forms with an active intellect, and that the Ein-Sof places much of the dynamism of the One into the angelic mind, perhaps supporting Ficino's attempt to bring act and dynamism from intellect to the One.
q: In Pico’s universe, the angelic mind is the world of forms, so there are universals. There is also an active intellect and it must be in the angelic mind too especially as Pico’s use of the Ein-Sof, places much of …

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that ideas are the exemplary forms of natures and that things in the first level have causal being in the divinity and formal being in the angelic nature.

Howlett says the angelic mind is home to angels with Christ present above them, that it can be called the son of God, and that in Kabbalism it is the home of the Metatron, the transfigured Enoch, who can prefigure Christ.

Howlett states that Abulafia's commentary on the Guide uses Maimonides to describe the Metatron as the agent intellect actualizing our intellect, an intellect detached from matter, the prince of the world and the angel of the Face.

Howlett argues that the Metatron can also be the ascended Enoch, the apotheosis of the seeker, implying that the mystic becomes a son by actualized intellect, a double intellectual sonship, and that the note finds this transformative understanding of intellectual activity also in Pico's Oration where the intellectual man can be an angel and son of God.

Howlett says that below the Metatron there are three ranks of three groups of angels making nine layers, thrones, cherubim and seraphim in the angelic mind, and principalities, archangels and angels in the celestial realm.

Howlett says angels are partly imperfect, at one remove from perfection, and quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the angel's double imperfection is that it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and not intelligence itself but only happens to understand.
q: But angels are at least partly imperfect in that they are at one remove from perfection, and so adulterated by matter. Pico speaks of a ‘double imperfection’: ‘the one, that it is not being itself but only an essence to …

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the angels understand God only so far as His nature is manifest in their own substance.

Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that true and perfect felicity carries us back to union with the beginning, that the angels can be raised to it but cannot ascend to it, and that man cannot go to that level but can be drawn.
Howlett says that in the Heptaplus Pico refers to Isaac, who relates the sefirot to the ten layers of the celestial world, the empyrean being the tenth sphere.

Howlett says only nine realms of the celestial world are active, reflecting the nine-plus-one variant of the Tree and the nine levels of angels, and that the planets form triads in which Uranus is God, Saturn the first mind and Jupiter the world-soul, just as in Ficino.
q: But only nine realms are active within this world reflecting the nine plus One variant of the Tree of Life. This nine obviously uses again the Platonic and gnostic triads just as they reflect the nine levels of angels. The …

text: Howlett states that in the Heptaplus and the Oration Pico describes the celestial world as needing the divine mover, in that heavenly bodies are adapted to circular motion but unable to perform it without being turned.

Howlett says that Pico's inconsistencies may be due to a change of views, problems of argument, an incomplete project or missed points, but more persuasively arise from attempting to combine what is partly similar and partly very different.

Howlett poses the questions raised by Pico's metaphysics: how a hidden God can act, whether the One belongs to apophatic or kataphatic theology, whether the divine presence resides only in the angelic mind, and how emanation and creation co-exist.

Howlett reports that Pico told Barbaro he had turned from Aristotle to the Academy not as a deserter but as a scout, going to Ficino while suggesting that he was viewing Platonism as an Aristotelian, though Platonism became a key part of his outlook.

Howlett describes the relationship between Ficino and Pico as perplexing, inspiring and often antagonistic, Ficino portraying a deep friendship at least in retrospect and Pico seeing Ficino as his philosophical archnemesis.

Howlett says Pico's first extended philosophical piece directly challenged Ficino's work on the Symposium, and that in doing so he became immersed in Plotinus, an author Ficino had only recently started to explore.
Howlett cites Pico telling Ficino that Plotinus had not left his thoughts and that he had Plotinus's works at hand and felt obliged to study him.
Howlett states that in May Lorenzo sent word through Ficino that the returning Pico should live in Florence, lending him a villa at Querceto near Fiesole.
Howlett reports a disputation at Lorenzo's house in 1489 between a Franciscan theologian and a Dominican, with Pico, Ficino and Lorenzo apparently siding with the Franciscan.

Howlett says that, following Pico's threefold division of the soul, the highest part, intelligence, is shared with the angels, and that the intellect is illuminated by a greater, even divine, intellect which she glosses as the divine active intellect, the spirit of the lord or the Kabbalistic Metatron.

Howlett says the intelligence is connected to the angelic mind of the universe, quoting Pico that intellects are eyes and that the power of the soul in which we are like the angels is called sight by all the Platonists.

Howlett argues that Pico seems to suggest our intelligence is active, functioning in the Aristotelian manner, while also arguing that God's grace impels us, suggesting it is partly passive and needs a universal active intellect, and offers a third way in which the particular mind's upper level becomes an active intellect opened to the divine one.

Howlett argues that if Pico's intellect is the Aristotelian active intellect it has a far stronger role than Ficino's, which tends to reflect the divine somewhat passively, and that epistemological concerns become more central in Pico as he amalgamates Aristotelianism with other traditions.

Howlett says Ficino insists on the immortality of the soul, that Aristotle was ambiguous, and that Alexander of Aphrodisias, reading De anima III, held the active intellect to be outside the individual soul, while Averroes removed all that could be considered immortal in our souls.

Howlett cites a note that Ficino's defence of the soul's immortality is a conscious reaction against later medieval thought, a fight in the name of Plato and Augustine against Aristotle or his commentators, and says Pico is left needing to bridge Averroism with immortality, an argument left unmade.

Howlett quotes Pico's commentary on which parts of the soul various ancient thinkers held immortal: Proclus and Porphyry the rational part only, Xenocrates and Speusippus also the sensitive, Numenius and Plotinus every soul.

Howlett says Pico's Oration sends the ascending soul to the court of the cherubim, seraphim and thrones, the angelic mind, and quotes that the seraph burns with love, the cherub shines with intelligence, and the throne stands in judgement.
Howlett states that henosis requires God's grace, the illumination of the Active Intellect activating our will, and that only we and the angels, of all created beings, can be drawn in this manner.
Howlett says the God who is felicity is the Plotinian One but also the best of what can be thought of, meaning Keter rather than the Ein-Sof.
Howlett states that the two ascents, through love and mystical ascent, come together in Kabbalism and Christian thought, especially Pseudo-Dionysius.
Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that love arouses a memory of the intellectual part and leads the purged soul to be most happily transmuted into angelic form.

Howlett says the resting-place at the end of the ascent is not a unio mystica, in the sense of union with the One itself, and supports this by quoting Pico's commentary that the soul ends its journey at the sixth step, is not allowed to move on to the seventh, and rests at the side of the First Father.

Howlett states that Ficino's and Pico's ladders are not the same: Pico moves immediately away from earthly love, replaces Ficino's Platonic reminder of innate beauty with an Aristotelian abstraction while keeping a Platonic Idea at the end, and changes the poem so that we cannot ascend as far as God.
Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that desire is sensitive, rational or intellectual, that is bestial, human or angelic, an intellectual and angelic will.
Howlett says Ficino argues that heavenly beauty descending into a human body imprints itself, somewhat equivalent to Pico's grace, though Pico says our souls form our bodies when we descend.
Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that the soul which follows heavenly love is completely united with the Intellect and from a man becomes an angel.
Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that love makes men equal to angels, and says this was Enoch's fate, an intellectual rapture, transformed from man to angel.
Howlett says that in the Heptaplus Christ opened a seventh or sabbatical exposition, and that our first aim is to become cherubim and our final apparent aim to be seraphim next to God.

Howlett says Pico's henosis is similar to Ficino's with more emphasis on Plotinus, that in the body the soul reaches the edge of the celestial world and probably no further, and that Pico could be playing with triads, cherubim representing the celestial world and seraphim the angelic mind.
Howlett says Pico follows the threefold path of Pseudo-Dionysius from purification to contemplation to illumination.
Howlett says Ficino's focus is on return after a temporary sight of the angelic mind and renovatio, whereas Pico's focus is on the movement up.

Howlett says Pico brings together philosophy, theology and religious experience as necessary for ascent, much as in Pseudo-Dionysius, Iamblichus and Proclus, and quotes Copenhaver that the Oration is a mystic's manifesto for ascent to self-annihilating union with God.

Howlett says Pseudo-Dionysius' three-stage path from the Celestial Hierarchy is purgatio, illuminatio and unitio or perfectio, and Iamblichus' curriculum is moral philosophy, dialectics, natural philosophy and theology, both matching steps in Pico's three pillars.

Howlett quotes Pico's Commentary that the descent of what is higher is not a real movement downward but its drawing us to itself, a compulsion to ascend, and concludes that this suggests no return once the soul has left the body for the angelic mind.

Howlett says that in the Oration Pico appears at times to agree that the divine presence couples with Binah, so that we do not ascend to the Active Intellect or Hokmah but are infused when we reach understanding, and that the mystic literally becomes the Agent Intellect, henosis as noesis.

Howlett reports Idel's argument that both Pico and Alemanno believe the soul can cleave to the Ein-Sof, and says she sees no evidence of this in Pico, whose language suggests the soul cleaves to Keter.

Howlett states that the obvious candidate for the Active Intellect among the sefirot is Hokmah, and that if the Active Intellect is our end point it is a form of noesis, with a more permanent noesis or even a form of henosis possible for those who die.

Howlett states that Pico uses the Kabbalistic mors osculi or binsica for the ineffable union of the soul with God and its emancipation from materiality in the commentary and the Conclusions, and that in the commentary binsica, death from a kiss, is said to occur when the soul unites itself in intellectual rapture to things separate from it.

Howlett says Maimonides may have been Pico's source for the kiss of death in the Conclusions, though the Commentary adds Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, perhaps a triad of sefirot, and that the intellectual ecstasy of the kiss suggests noesis and not henosis.

Howlett says that in the Commentary Pico agrees with Ficino on the kiss in which souls join, but that Pico's kiss is never given to another person and looks only to noesis or henosis without full union.

Howlett argues that unlike Ficino, Pico does not discuss returning to the world with the blueprint from the glimpse of the divine, whereas in Ficino the returner is a divine magician able to change the world.
Howlett says there is remarkable consistency between the commentary and Pico's methodology and views in De ente.
Howlett says Pico's answer to the faith and reason divide differs greatly from Ficino's, who understands Christianity as coherent with Platonic philosophy and so makes Platonism central.
Howlett says that within Platonism Pico favors Plotinus and even more the baroque gnostic structures of Proclus, but owes most to Ficino.

Howlett says Kabbalism can be the hermeneutics for understanding Plato and Aristotle, and that Pico aims to show each tradition consistent with the other, even in strange cases such as his use of the Parmenides in De ente.

Howlett asks how to reconcile the hidden God of apophatic theology and Kabbalism with the unmoved mover and the Plotinian One, and finds it tempting to distinguish the Ein-Sof from the active presence of God in Keter.

Howlett states as one of her re-evaluations that Pico's concord succeeds when it builds on similarities and shared histories but reveals significant difference, so that creation is complicated by emanation and the God of negative theology cannot be the pleroma.

Howlett states that Pico's henosis is a cleaving not with a wholly transcendent One but with its active attributes within our universe, beginning with those of mind and understanding, and that it can be a noetic process in which our minds touch the Aristotelian active intellect.

Howlett describes Ficino as very much part of the collective desire for change and on a mission to renew the world, while Pico's journey was of the self, an ascetic personal journey of the soul with no second step of return and reform.
Howlett quotes Pico's Oration in a note: with Dyonisio as interpreter, souls are first purged, then illuminated, and finally perfected.

Howlett cites Copenhaver that Pico's ascent has moral philosophy for purification, dialectics for clarification, natural philosophy for information, theology for meditation, and religious practice leading to divinization, described in the Oration as being apart in the Father's darkness, a phrase borrowed from Pseudo-Dionysius.

Howlett reports Papio's suggestion that Pseudo-Dionysius has taken aspects of the Greek Eleusinian mysteries, linking the four frenzies to the three stages, and that three archangels represent the stages.

Howlett quotes Pico's conclusion that the Metatron of the Cabalists is without doubt what Orpheus called Pallas, Zoroaster the paternal mind, Hermes the son of God, Pythagoras wisdom and Parmenides the intelligible sphere.

Howlett cites Ogren for a note attributed to Ficino, from late 1479 or early 1480, stating that all Kabaliste hold the world created and souls created together at the start, and which dates the world by a Hebrew reckoning.
Howlett cites Busi that a letter from Ficino to Domenico Benivieni concerns a debate in 1485 at Pico's house between Mondego, Flavius and a Jewish physician.
Howlett cites Scholem that two traditions were combined to create the greater and lesser Metatron: the angel Yahoel, a lesser YHWH, and the Enochian tradition of Enoch as scribe.
Howlett cites a note that Garin, though treating Pico's occultism persuasively, sold Kabbalah short, preferring to foreground Pseudo-Dionysius and Hermeticism.
Howlett says Pico focused on Plotinus and several later Platonists but was always mindful of the positions of his former teacher Ficino, whom she calls his most important scholarly friend and rival.
