text: Whatever is, is undivided from itself and divided from other things, which is what is meant by one and by Plato's words that a thing is the same as itself and other than other things.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: Every being is necessarily true, since to say a thing is not true gold is to say it is not gold, and Augustine's definition of the true as that which is does not make being and true the same in concept but the same in fact.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: The author holds that Olympiodorus is mistaken in arguing that good and being differ because we desire the good without qualification but not being, only well-being, and that he fails to see that the good is multiple just as being is multiple.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: Natural being carries an undivided natural goodness, accidental beings such as wisdom are different goods, and if someone wishes to be only if happy, the conclusion is that happiness is another being, not that good and being differ.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: Each thing is good insofar as it is; in being we can admire God's power, in truth his wisdom, in goodness his liberality, and in unity his simplicity, which united each thing to itself, to others and to himself.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: The false is the same as nothing, and since there is no efficient but only a deficient cause of evil, the author says this refutes those who posited two principles, one of goods and one of evils.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: To divide a thing is to destroy it, since the whole is not its parts but the one thing that emerges from them, so that natural unity cannot be taken away while its being remains.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: The four are not in God in relation to a cause, and can be considered in him as he is absolutely in himself or as cause of other things, a distinction that does not apply to creatures, since God can not be a cause and creatures cannot fail to be from him.
q: Let us examine once more how these are in God. They are not in God in relation to a cause that God does not have; for he, the cause of all things, is from nothing.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 9

text: God, conceived as the plenitude of existence, is one with no opposite, most true and truth itself, and goodness itself; those who imagine many principles or gods err.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 9

text: The good has three conditions, perfect, sufficient and desirable, and God is thereby the fullest being, individual unity, most solid truth and most blessed good.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 9

text: The author suggests that these four names are the quaternity by which Pythagoras swore and which he called the principle of ever-flowing nature.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 9

text: If the four names are assigned to God as cause, the sequence is reversed: he is first one, since understood in himself before as cause, then good, true and finally being, because the end is prior to the exemplar and the exemplar to the efficient cause.
q: If we were to assign these four names to God as he is the cause of things, the sequence must be reversed. First, he would be one, since he is understood in himself before he is understood as cause. Second, …
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 9

text: The chapter turns the argument to the ordering of life: we must not live in a low condition while investigating the highest things, lest we dispute for others rather than for ourselves.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: The mind, to which divine things are accessible, cannot be of mortal race and will be happy only by possessing divine things; it wanders here as a stranger.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: The disputation warns that to be blessed we must imitate God by possessing in ourselves unity, truth and goodness.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: Ambition disturbs the peace of unity, pleasures lose the light of truth, and avarice steals goodness, and it is characteristic of goodness to communicate its goods, so Plato answers that God created the world because he was good.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: The three worldly loves named by John are not of the Father, who is unity, truth and goodness itself, and the reader is urged to flee the world to the Father.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: We are not one unless we bind sense to reason by the union of virtue; otherwise we are a kingdom divided against itself, following God with the law of mind and Baal with the law of the flesh in turns.
q: We are not one if we do not bind, by the union of virtue, sense bent downward with reason which looks at heavenly things. If there are two princes in us, reigning in turns, as it were, we for a …
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: If reason is enslaved by sense we have a false unity, being untrue: we appear to be men but are brutes, and the image does not correspond to its exemplar, since we are the image of God, who is spirit.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: One, true and good follow being by perpetual connection, so when we are not these three we absolutely are not, even if we appear to be, and although we may seem to live we would be ever dying rather than living.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: Miller says the treatise was occasioned by a discussion in which Lorenzo maintained the Platonic view that the one is higher than being, that Lorenzo probably followed the traditional reading of the Parmenides shared by Ficino, and that the treatise was written to show a merely verbal disagreement between Plato and Aristotle.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno proem

text: Miller says Pico follows the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato on which beings depend on an ineffable one beyond the many definite essences, being being a second level of reality derived from the one.

Miller says Pico held that in the Parmenides Plato did not intend to assert positive metaphysical doctrine and that the structure of the eight hypotheses shows a dialectical exercise, a dialogue of method, not content.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 2

text: Miller says the Neoplatonic emphasis on the first hypothesis read it as a negative description of the one as pure identity, gaining authority from Proclus's commentary, which breaks off at the end of the first hypothesis, so that a reader relying on Proclus takes those texts as Plato's last words on the one.
q: Ficino's interpretation had been influenced by the Neoplatonic emphasis on the first hypothesis of the dialogue. This first hypothesis describes the ineffable transcendence of the one, which is above and apart from all being and determination.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 2

text: Miller says Proclus's commentary had greatly influenced the Christian interpretation of Pseudo-Dionysius and was read, in its thirteenth-century Latin translation, by later medieval and Renaissance thinkers.

Miller says Pico's reading of the first hypothesis as no more important than the other seven rests on new attention to the form and method of Plato's dialectic and attempts to free Plato's meaning from the misleading emphasis of a partial commentary.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 2

text: Miller reports that Ficino, in his commentary on the Parmenides begun in the same year as Pico's treatise, replied that Pico's interpretation is against the opinion of all the Platonists.
q: (Ficino, in his commentary on the Parmenides, begun in the same year as Pico's On Being and the One, 1492, replies that Pico's interpretation is "against the opinion of all the Platonists."
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 2

text: Miller reports that for Ficino, following Plotinus and Proclus, the dialectical form of Plato's dialogue is only an outer covering for a profound metaphysical content.
q: For Ficino, following Plotinus and Proclus, Plato's dialectical form is only an outer covering for a profound metaphysical content.)
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 2

text: Miller says Ficino, the first Renaissance thinker to know all of Plato's writings, continued to read Plato within the Neoplatonic tradition, and that though Pico's interpretation differs in some respects from Ficino's, both follow the medieval tradition of the concord of the two Greek philosophers.
q: Marsilio Ficino, the first Renaissance thinker to know all of the original writings of Plato, continued to interpret Plato within the framework of the Neoplatonic tradition, pagan and Christian, which Platonism had acquired during the previous thousand years

text: Miller says that in the passage on being in the second sense Pico is utilizing the metaphysics of Aquinas, the first Christian philosopher to base his metaphysics on the real distinction between that which participates existence and the act of existing itself.
q: Being in the second sense means that which does not lack existence (esse). That which is (ens) means whatever participates existence. Pico is here utilizing the metaphysics of St. Thomas Aquinas, who was the first Christian philosopher to base his …
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller states there can be no doubt that Pico derived his metaphysic of existence from Thomas.
q: There can be no doubt that Pico derived his metaphysic of existence from Thomas.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller reports that Pico's nephew Gian Francesco says that of ten thousand propositions in Thomas, Pico disagreed with only three or four.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller says that of the nine hundred theses Pico proposed for disputation at Rome, forty-five are taken from Thomas, more than from any other philosopher.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller says the apparent disagreement is resolved because the one of Plato, identified with the Biblical God, is above being in the sense of not being another thing that has or shares in being.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller says that on Pico's interpretation Aristotle's God, being under none of the ten categories, is above being, so that Plato and Aristotle agree that God is beyond being.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 4

text: Miller says that historically Plato's metaphysics is altogether different from Aristotle's, since Plato's being derived from the pure relation of identity or the one is incompatible with Aristotle's being as concrete individual substance.

Miller says the two Greek philosophies can be made to coincide only when transformed into a different philosophy in which the highest principle of each is identified with a God who is existence itself, so that Pico's concord is accomplished by transforming both.
q: These two Greek philosophies can be made to coincide only when transformed into an altogether different philosophy: the highest principle in Plato turns out to be the same as the highest principle in Aristotle only because they are both identified …

text: Miller says the created world in Pico has a double aspect: the reality of things is intrinsic, as in Aristotle's metaphysics, and referential, as in Plato's.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: Miller says the philosophy of participation in being itself has consequences for conduct and that Pico adopts the Aristotelian view that the good and being are convertible, differing in thought but not in fact.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 8

text: Miller says the Neoplatonic notion of return to the one is assimilated by Pico to the Christian idea of divine grace, and that Pico doubtless read in Proclus the notion that the end of each thing is to return to its first beginning.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: Miller says Plotinus's announced reunion with the one meant loss of human personality in the one beyond being, whereas Pico's return to God means becoming a perfect image imitating in a human way the unity of God.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 10

text: Miller says that, like his co-Platonist Ficino, Pico understood his materials not strictly historically but in accord with his own constructive purposes and was convinced of the unity of pagan and Christian thought.
The volume's short biography states that On Being and the One was written in 1491 at Fiesole.
The translators state that On Being and the One was translated from Garin's 1942 critical edition and that they are heavily indebted to it for identifications of quotations and references.
The translator's note identifies the dedicatee as Angelo Ambrogini, poet and intimate friend of Ficino and of Pico.
The translator's note identifies the proem's quotation as Manilius, Astronomicon III.39 and cites Aristotle's Metaphysics IV.2 and XI.3 for the convertibility of one and being.
The translator's note records that Pico, in the Parmenides passage he quotes on the exercise in dialectic, used Marsilio Ficino's translation.
The translator's note cites Plato's Sophist 237d and 238a-c for the passages Pico quotes on the one and not-being.
The translator's note identifies the Simplicius reference as In Physicorum and the reference on God as being as Pseudo-Dionysius, De divinis nominibus I.6.
The translator's note cites Plotinus, Enneads V.1.8 alongside Plato, Parmenides 137c-142b for the claim that the first hypothesis treats of the first principle.
The translator's note identifies Thomas's teaching that God is above being as St. Thomas Aquinas, In I Sententiarum, d. 19, q. 4, a. 1, and cites Aristotle, Metaphysics VI.2.
The translator's note identifies Aristotle's Metaphysics XII.10 and Homer, Iliad XVI.204 as the sources of the passage on the one ruler.
The translator's note cites Seneca, Epistles CII and CXX for the remark that we begin to die when we begin to live, and Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos 134 for the removal of particularity.
The translator's note identifies the quotation of Dionysius as De mystica theologia V and cites Plutarch and Varro (De lingua Latina) for the views on God's nature discussed there.
The translator's note identifies the Augustine doctrine as Sermon 340, Plato's idea of the good as Republic VI 509b with Aristotle, Metaphysics XII.7, and Anselm as Proslogium XV.
The translator's note states that the reference for the Psalm verse Pico quotes according to the Hebrew text is uncertain and that Pico interprets the Hebrew text.
loc: de-ente-et-uno | De ente et uno ch. 5

text: The translator's note cites Plato, Timaeus 49a, 51a and 52d for what Pico says of prime matter, and gives no note for the reference to the Platonist called divine.
The translator's note identifies the added terms something and thing as Avicenna, Metaphysics I.4, and compares Helias Cretensis, Quaestio de ente, essentia et uno.
The translator's note identifies Augustine's definition of the true as Soliloquia II.5 and the Neoplatonist criticised on good and being as a sixth-century author of a commentary In Phaedrum.
Pico says he was moved to examine the secrets of the book of Moses by emulation of the studies of Lorenzo dei Medici, and dedicates the work to him.
Pico says the work was written at Fiesole in a retreat provided by the man he addresses, made pleasanter by the constant visits of Angelo Poliziano.
Pico believes that the secrets of all nature are contained in the works of the six days.
Pico argues that the sages of old either did not write on religious subjects or wrote of them under another guise, which is why such subjects are called mysteries.
Pico says Plato himself concealed his doctrines beneath allegory, myth, mathematical images and unintelligible signs.
Pico cites Dionysius the Areopagite, whom he calls Paul's disciple, as witness that the churches kept the more secret doctrines for oral communication to the initiated.

Pico holds that if the book treats anywhere of the whole world, it does so above all where it treats of the emanation of all things from God and of the grade, number and order of the parts of the world.
Pico says he will make no mention of what earlier interpreters wrote in the Chaldean language, and will offer seven interpretations of his own discovery.

Pico names three difficulties: keeping Moses from seeming to speak inadequately, keeping a single coherent line of interpretation, and avoiding making Moses say anything alien to nature or to the truths of the better philosophers.
Pico says he will interpret the whole creation continuously and without confusion in seven senses, and not merely one, in a completely new work.
Pico says antiquity imagined three worlds: the ultramundane, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers the intelligible, the celestial, and the sublunary world we inhabit.
Pico characterises the lower world as one of darkness and the upper as one of light, the heavens compounded of both, and says the Hebrew name for heaven joins fire and water.
q: This is the world of darkness; that the world of light; the heavens are compounded of light and darkness.

text: Pico contrasts the worlds: alternation of life and death below, eternal life and unchanging activity above, and in the heavens stability of life but change of activity and position.
Pico says the highest world is of the divine nature of mind, and that the third world is moved by the second and the second governed by the first.
Pico says Moses diagrammed the three worlds in the three parts of the tabernacle, the Holy of Holies with its winged cherubim being the angelic world.
Pico says that since the fall of Lucifer there is no stain or sin above the moon, and that the angelic world is held far more holy than the celestial.
Pico reads the rending of the temple veil at Christ's death as opening the way to the supercelestial world and communion with the angels.
Pico says the three worlds are one world because whatever is in any of them is contained in each of the others, and says his purpose almost wholly depends on this.
Pico tentatively ascribes the doctrine of mutual containment to Anaxagoras, as expounded by the Pythagoreans and the Platonists.

Pico illustrates containment by heat: the element among us, the sun as fire in the sky, and the seraphic intellect as fire in the ultramundane region, differing in that the elemental fire burns, the celestial gives life and the supercelestial loves.

Pico illustrates containment by water: the element in our world, the moon in the heavens, and the minds of the cherubim above the heavens; moisture quenches the heat of life below, feeds it in the heavens, and the supercelestial understands it.
q: There is water in our world; there is water in the heavens, the mover and mistress of ours, namely, the moon, the vestibule of the heavens

text: Pico says that in the first world God, the primal unity, presides over nine orders of angels and, without moving, moves all toward himself.
Pico says the empyrean heaven presides over nine heavenly spheres and is itself unmoving in imitation of God, and that the elemental world has nine spheres of corruptible forms after prime matter.
Pico says Scripture itself indicates mutual containment, in the Psalm that the heavens were made in understanding and in the text that angels are spirits and his ministers a flame of burning fire.

Pico says the science of all allegorical interpretation flows from the mutual containment of the worlds, and that correct interpretation requires knowledge of the hidden alliances and affinities of nature.
Pico says man is a fourth world containing what is in the rest, and that it is a school commonplace that man, the lesser world, includes reason, the angelic mind and the likeness of God.
Pico says mutual containment yields a fourfold exposition: the text is read first of the angelic and invisible world alone, then the celestial, then the sublunary, then of the nature of man.
Pico says the fifth exposition arises because the natures, though distinct, are linked, and the sixth shows fifteen ways in which one thing may be joined to another.

Pico says the seventh, sabbatical exposition treats the felicity of creatures and their return to God, and that the text hides an explicit prophecy of Christ, the Church and the calling of the gentiles.

Pico says he will not pile up what philosophers and theologians have said about God, angels, matter and the heavens, as Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides did, but will only show what the text means.
q: We shall not, however, imitate those who, having tried sometimes to explain the creation of the world, have heaped together whatever philosophers or theologians have anywhere said about God, the angels, matter, the heavens, and the whole of nature. Among …

text: Pico says the work is not meant to teach those who have not learned these matters elsewhere, but to let readers recognise in the words of the Prophet what they already know.
Pico says the seven expositions are arranged in seven books of seven chapters each, and that the seventh chapter of each is turned to Christ as the Sabbath.
loc: heptaplus | proem to the seven expositions

text: Pico says it is believable that the teaching of Moses about the worlds is arranged as God arranged them, so that the scripture of Moses is the exact image of the world.

Pico says the First Exposition treats the corruptible things below the moon, which the work of the first day includes, and starts from the natural philosophers' principles of matter, privation, efficient cause and form.
Pico says that the divine Platonists remind us natural agents are not primary causes but instruments of a divine art, so that the Platonists propose an instrumental and an ideal cause.
Pico reads heaven and earth in the first verse as the active and material causes, and says the Stoics called heaven the active cause and earth the material.
Pico appeals to the ancient Simeon as testimony that the ancient Hebrews, like Albert and many Peripatetics, held the Hebrew word bou to signify the rudiments of form in matter.

Pico says that in the myth the poets ascribe the unitary rule of Saturn to the union of the intelligible world enfolding all within itself, after which the sensible world was divided among Jove (celestial), Pluto (subterranean) and Neptune (the region between moon and earth).
Pico calls the Platonists ever the imitators of Hebrew learning.
Pico says that as man is the perfection of all lower things, so Christ is the perfection of all men, and that man is the term at which the corruptible world halts.

Pico says a third explanation for Moses' figurative terms is that with them the same words, context and order suit all the worlds, so that the book of Moses excels all others in doctrine and is new and untouched.
Pico says, on the authority of Dionysius and Thomas, that among angelic minds the highest is the one that understands with the fewest concepts what lower minds understand with many.
Pico says a tenth heaven, fixed and at rest, is believed to lie above the nine spheres.
Pico reports that Isaac the philosopher takes the tenth sphere to be what Ezekiel called the sapphire in the likeness of a throne, its immobility being signified by the likeness to a throne.
q: This Isaac takes the tenth sphere to be what Ezekiel designated as the sapphire in the likeness of a throne, since the color of the sapphire signifies the splendor of its light, the likeness to a throne its immobility.

text: Pico argues that the light of the visible heaven comes from the highest heavens, the tenth sphere being the unity of lights, and calls the tenth heaven the empyrean.
Pico says the empyrean governs the nine spheres beneath it as a general his army or a form its matter, and by exhibiting the image of unity completes the group of ten.
Pico reports a doubt whether the empyrean is corporeal and leaves the matter open, insisting only that the treasuries of light are there.

Pico says the nine choirs of angels may be called gods because they participate in divinity, whereas God in the absolute sense is the indivisible Trinity presiding over them, as the empyrean presides over the nine orbits.
Pico reads the Spirit of the Lord that brooded over the waters as the empyrean, the closely adhering spiritual Olympus and seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warming the crystalline sphere with light.

Pico says that up to this point the Prophet has treated the heavens as luminous bodies and has said nothing of their intelligence or motive force, following the order of the Timaeus of body first and soul after.

Pico says that Moses, about to declare the heavens possessed of a rational soul, uses man as an allegory, meaning the rational soul, and that what is said of the soul of man is carried over to the soul of the heavens.
Pico says Scripture often represents all angelic and rational natures by man, as in the prophets for the good angels and for the evil demon, who does not differ from the good angels at all in nature.
Pico says the heavenly souls do at once contemplation and the government of their bodies, and that the ancients, as in the Orphic hymns, named these two powers male and female.

Pico believes a mystery of the ancient wisdom of the Hebrews lies hidden here, the dogma that Jupiter and Mars are included by the sun and Venus and Mercury by the moon, and notes that the Hebrews themselves give no reason for it.
Pico summarises what the Prophet has related of the celestial world: its divine body, the number of its spheres, its nature, properties, function, motive power, rational substance and intelligence.

Pico invokes the Platonic notion that the Divine Artificer compounded our souls in the same mixing bowl and of the same elements as the celestial souls, and says man is a soul, an intelligence that transcends the boundaries of heaven and the passage of time.
Pico cites the Chaldeans against exaggerating the influence of the stars and against seeking goods of body or fortune from the heavens, saying they will not give them.

Pico says that much about the angelic and invisible nature was handed down by the ancient Hebrews and by Dionysius, and that his plan was to expound the words of Moses according to the teaching of both schools.
q: Since much about the angelic and invisible nature has been handed down by the ancient Hebrews and much also by Dionysius, it was my plan to expound the words of Moses according to the teaching of both schools.

text: Pico says he decided to put off the Hebrew teaching because it is unfamiliar to the Latins and would require explaining nearly all the dogmas of the ancient Hebrew learning, which he will publish more fully elsewhere, examining how far they agree with Egyptian tradition, Plato and Catholic truth.

Pico says that where the Hebrews agree with 'us' he will hold them to their fathers' traditions, where they disagree he will attack them, and what is holy and true he will bear off from the synagogue to the legitimate Israelites.
Pico says that in the meantime he will tread in the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather Paul and Hierotheus, whom Dionysius followed, to bring light on the shadows of the law.
Pico says every number is perfected by unity, and proposes to apply these notions to divine things after the Pythagorean custom.
Pico says God alone is wholly simple and is being itself, and that other things are not being itself but exist by means of it.
Pico argues that an angel is not unity itself, since then he would be God, and so is left to be a number, a number in one respect and a multiplicity in another.
Pico says whatever is imperfect in an angel is to be ascribed to its multiplicity, as a creature, and whatever is perfect to its participation in unity, which it has from being associated with God.

Pico finds a double imperfection in an angel: that it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and that it is not intelligence itself but only happens to understand, the second depending on the first.
Pico says God is the unity from which angels draw their being, life and all their perfection, and that their perfection comes by unity from above.
Pico reads the void and empty earth as the crude and unformed angelic essence which God created, and denies that only the formation of essence and not its creation is the work of the Artificer.
Pico says that with the earth God created the heavens, meaning the actuality of that essence and the unity shared in multiplicity, that is, being itself.

Pico says an angel cannot fulfil understanding and contemplation unless surrounded by intelligible forms, and reads the deep as the angel's intellectual capacity, over which is the darkness until illuminated by spiritual concepts.

Pico says the Spirit of the Lord is the spirit of love, that an angel is filled with spiritual light only by turning toward God, and that this turning is the motion of love, which follows understanding.
Pico says light was made in the angel, the light of intelligible forms, and that intelligible species are united to angelic minds by eternal links and an indivisible bond, unlike the human intellect.
q: God said "Be light made," and light was made in the angel, the light of intelligible forms

text: Pico reads the firmament set between the waters as signifying the three angelic hierarchies, the first and last being the waters above and below the heavens and the middle the firmament.
Pico says, following Dionysius, that the highest hierarchy is given only to contemplation and praises God unceasingly, and that the middle rank is assigned to the work of the heavens.
q: All this, if we consider the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, could not be more in accord with the teaching of Dionysius. Since, as he writes, the highest hierarchy has leisure only for contemplation, it is properly symbolized …

text: Pico says the last hierarchy, though above the heavens by nature, has charge of things under them and is divided into principalities, archangels and angels, whose activity concerns only what is under the moon.

Pico says, following Paul, that the angels sent to carry out the duties of this world are all guardian spirits sent to minister to those who receive salvation, gathered into one place to look after the salvation of man alone.
q: What it may be for the waters under the heavens to be gathered together into one place would perhaps be doubtful if it were not explained to us by Paul, in whom we read that the angels sent to carry …

text: Pico says the angels are said to be gathered in one place only as rivers flow to the ocean, since different angels preside over different corporeal and non-human things, as Platonists and Christian philosophers, Augustine, Gregory and Origen hold.

Pico reports the Damascene's opinion that the angel who sinned was one of the most contemptible kind, presiding over the terrestrial order, and says all the angels' care for lower things is subordinated to man's benefit.
Pico says the middle hierarchy administers heavenly matters, and that of the third hierarchy nothing more can be said beyond that it is above all active motion and given only to contemplation.

Pico says Moses' 'sun' and 'moon' are not the visible stars but the angelic powers which govern the sun and moon, and that these invisible angels illuminate an equally invisible earth, the substance of our souls.

Pico says, citing Dionysius, that the three angelic activities of purification, illumination and perfection are distributed so that the lowest order purifies, the middle illuminates and the highest perfects with a fiery and life-giving dew.
q: since, as Dionysius says, there are three angelic activities, purification, illumination, and perfection, they are so distributed that the lowest order purifies, the highest perfects, and the middle one, which we are now discussing, illuminates.

text: Pico says the winged Seraphim of Isaiah and Ezekiel's birds and beasts, which the Hebrews take as spiritual substances, come to his aid, and that the ancient Hebrews all hold Moses here to intend the angelic host.

Pico says the Prophet refutes the philosophers who admitted princely intellectual substances but denied that each is set over a multitude of lower rank, and that the leader of each of nine orders is to be imagined as a great sphere with its host as inhabitants.
q: Prophet refutes the error of the philosophers who believed that there are certain princely intellectual substances but denied that each of them is set over a numerous multitude of lower rank, like the commander of a legion, as the theologians …

text: Pico says Moses mentions man in the angelic world not because man is an angel but because he is its end and terminus, placed between the incorporeal and the elementary, the end of one and the beginning of the other.

Pico raises the objection that man is set over the beasts, birds and fish, which are read as angels, though the philosophers and the Prophet hold man lower than the angels, and answers that Christ as man enlightens and perfects the angels, if we believe Dionysius, and that all of us can be raised above the angels.

Pico says that above reason in man is intelligence, through which we share with the angels as we share through the senses with the brutes, so that we may say with John that our fellowship is with angels.

Pico says a greater, even divine, intellect illuminates the human intellect, which some hold to be God and almost all the Greeks and Arabs and many Hebrews a mind nearer to man's, and that the Jewish philosophers and Alfarabi called this substance the Spirit of the Lord.

Pico says Moses mentioned the bearing of the Spirit over the waters before the formation of man so that we would not think the Spirit present to our intellect only when it is joined to the body, an error he ascribes to Moses the Egyptian and Abubacher the Arab.

Pico says more recent philosophers would take the sun to be the active intellect and the moon the potential, but that since he is in a great controversy with them on this he will expound it otherwise for the time.

Pico says that although the author treats all worlds together everywhere, he assigned individual parts of his work to individual worlds in successive order, beginning with the first world, the angelic.
Pico says the angelic nature is pure intellect and compares minds to eyes, which see by an inner light but need external light, so that the intellect needs forms and ideas as rays of invisible light.

Pico says that from the comparison of intellect to the eye arises the theory of those who consider intellect an unworthy name for God, since God is light itself and needs no step between intellect and the light.

Pico says the common doctrine is that angels are composed of act and potency, that there is a troublesome dispute over what the act and the potency are and how they mingle, and that it is enough for him that the common opinion be somehow accepted.
Pico says Moses divides the substance of the angels on the first day into heaven and earth, the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which God made the angels.
Pico says the Spirit of the Lord borne upon the waters is called the Father of Lights by James, from which the light of intelligible forms rises upon the angelic minds.

Pico says the heavens lie between the waters, meaning angelic and corruptible substances, in respect of their essence, and that there is one earth for the angels and another for the elements since the potency of the two differs.

Pico says that the astrologers draw support for their science of divining by the stars from the statement that the stars were made for signs, and that it has been sharply criticised by Christians such as Basil.
Pico says he puts off deeper questions to a projected work in which, reconciling Aristotle to Plato, he has undertaken to discuss and examine the whole of philosophy.

Pico says he will not discuss whether all life arises from a divine origin, as Plotinus asserted, and remarks that his friend Marsilio Ficino will soon give Plotinus to be read in Latin with ample comments.
Pico says man is not so much a fourth world as the bond and union of the three already described.

Pico says that reason and mind are like God, intelligent, invisible and incorporeal, that man is like God especially in that part of the soul which displays the image of the Trinity, and that the angels, in whom these are stronger and less mixed, have more likeness and affinity with the divine nature.

Pico says the substance of man encompasses by its very essence the substances of all natures, and that not only angels but any intelligent creature includes all things in itself in some degree when, filled with their forms, it knows them.

Pico says God contains all things in himself as their origin and man contains them as their center, so that in God all things are of better stamp than in themselves whereas in man inferior things are of nobler mark and the superior degenerate.
Pico says that man has the sense of the brutes, a soul powerful in heavenly reason and participation in the angelic mind, the simultaneous possession of all these natures being truly divine.
Pico says the heavens labor for man and the angelic minds look after his salvation and beatitude, if what Paul writes is true that all ministering spirits are sent to those destined for salvation.
Pico says there are hangmen and lictors in the commonwealth of God, evil demons sentenced to this basest of professions as punishment for their ancient sins.
Pico says that, because all things are included in man, the gospel saying is that all the angels rejoice in gladness when a sinner repents.

Pico says the unity seen in creatures is of three modes (each thing one to itself, one creature united to another, the whole universe one with its Maker) and that this threefold unity is present in each thing through its own simple unity derived from that One which is both first one and three and one, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Pico says the power of the Father distributes unity to all, the wisdom of the Son sets all in order and unites them, and the love of the Spirit turns everything toward God and attaches the whole work to its Maker.
Pico says that the threefold unity in creatures, as a sign of the Trinity, has so far as he knows not been brought up by anyone before.
Pico says that after running through all the doctrines of the philosophers he found not more than fifteen kinds of affinity between things and that he saw them all pointed out in Moses.

Pico says the Spirit of God is joined to bodies only as art in the mind of an architect is joined to mortar, wood and stone, being a spiritual nature wholly disjoined from traffic with the body, and that in us heaven is the soul and the Spirit of God the intellect.

Pico says the mean is not of the same essence as the extremes but is somehow compounded from them so that it may communicate with both, and that Moses shows this by placing the firmament between the waters.

Pico says that our happiness is that whatever share of intellectual light is in us must be joined some day to the first intellect and the first mind of all, which is the fullness and totality of all understanding.
Pico says the extremes can be joined only through the mean, which must already have united them in itself, and that this mean is Christ, through whom alone the flesh can ascend to the Word.

Pico says the end of all things is the same as their beginning, one God, and that the Pythagoreans called him One and Good, One because he is the beginning as unity is the beginning of numbers, and Good because he is the end and absolute felicity.

Pico says the angelic mind is highest among creatures in natural felicity because of the nobility of its substance and its closeness to its end, and that in this felicity neither plants, animals, men nor angels attain God in himself but only in themselves.

Pico says the philosophers who spoke only of natural felicity ascribe to the angels no knowledge of God beyond that by which the angels know themselves, so that they understand God only as his nature is manifest in their own substance.
q: In fact, even to the angels, whom they call minds and intellects, and whose supreme perfection they acknowledge because the angels understand God, they ascribe no further knowledge of God than that by which angels know themselves, so that the …

text: Pico says that Avicenna, Averroes, Abu Bakr, Alexander and the Platonists seem to allow somewhat more, founding reason on the active intellect or on some greater one related to us, but lead man neither to his beginning nor to his end, and that he neither rejects nor despises their arguments as speaking of natural felicity.

Pico says the angels can be raised to the true felicity, the contemplation of the face of God, but cannot ascend to it, Lucifer having sinned in saying he would ascend, and that men can be drawn but not go, the drawing power being called grace, which makes men and angels pleasing to God.

Pico says that true felicity is to be one spirit with God, possessing God in God and not in ourselves, and that from every imperfection of multiplicity we are brought back to unity by an indissoluble bond with him who is himself the One.

Pico says the two natures capable of the highest felicity are the angelic, called heaven, and the human, called earth, and that Moses says no more of heaven since he is writing the law for men and not for angels.
Pico says the Word of God confirmed the law given to Moses by the angel, and that the gentiles worship the demons dwelling in the murky air.

Pico says his interpretation will furnish weapons against the stony hearts of the Hebrews drawn from their own arsenals, and that it is among the doctrines of ancient Hebrew learning that the six days denote the six thousand years of the world, a view confirmed by Moses of Gerona and mentioned by Jerome.

Pico says that the oracles of Elijah circulate among the Hebrews as well-understood traditions and that he will give the testimony of the Talmudists from the tractate Aboda Zara, which acknowledge that the time predicted by Elijah for the Messiah has passed.
Pico says that, as Jonathan the Chaldean attests, evil demons are often represented in the Holy Scriptures by animals that live in the waters.

Pico says that having completed the sevenfold interpretation he will treat the first phrase last, that he will not discuss the Son as beginning nor prove that the ancient Hebrews thought as he does, which he will do elsewhere, and that he intends through another system of interpretation to give a taste of Mosaic profundity.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says it is the firm opinion of all the ancients that the five books of the Mosaic law contain all knowledge, hidden in the very letters of the phrases, and that by the rules the Hebrews hand down the letters of a passage may be joined into sayings.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says he cannot prove what he claims about the method, having neither tested it nor confidence of being able to, but that he does not deny or despise it, partly because it has mighty supporters.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says that on applying the rules of the ancients to the first phrase he found the whole plan of the creation of the world and of all things in it disclosed in that one phrase.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico gives as the resulting reading that the Father, in the Son and through the Son, the beginning and end or rest, created the head, the fire and the foundation of the great man with a good pact.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says the world is the great man and that Moses represents the intellectual, heavenly and corruptible worlds by the head, the breast and the lower part, the angelic world being the fountain of knowledge because that nature was made for understanding.
q: In the first place, therefore, it should be noticed that the world is what Moses calls "the great man." For if man is a little world, then certainly the world is a great man.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says Moses named the highest part the head, the second fire because many refer to the sky by that name, and the third the foundation, and that the pact is good because it is directed toward God, the good itself, so that the world is one with its Maker.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase

text: Pico says the reading explains the whole plan, relationship and felicity of the four worlds he has discussed.
loc: heptaplus | Exposition of the First Phrase
