text: Wirszubski identifies the likeliest direct source of thesis II (nine angelic hierarchies, with the form Aralim) as Abraham Axelrad's Corona Nominis Boni, found in Cod. Vat. Ebr. 190, on the ground of the unusual number nine and the unusual form Aralim.
q: The unusual number of angelic hierarchies, nine instead of ten, and the unusual form Aralim, for 'Er'elim, ... help to identify the likeliest direct source of this thesis, namely Abraham Axelrad's Corona Nominis Boni, Cod. Vat. Ebr. 190, fol. 177r
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum secretam doctrinam, Conclusio II

text: Wirszubski argues that the tenth grade in the Latin list cannot denote an angelic hierarchy, so the inference from that text is nine hierarchies, whereas ten is the usual number in Jewish sources.
q: What matters is that the tenth grade cannot possibly be taken to denote an angelic hierarchy. Hence the obvious inference from this text is that there are nine hierarchies of angels, whereas the usual number in Jewish sources is ten.

text: Wirszubski adds that that same source accounts for Pico's notion that there are nine angelic hierarchies according to the secret doctrine of the Hebrew Cabalists, just as Dionysius Areopagita has nine celestial hierarchies.
q: the Corona Nominis Boni is the likeliest direct source of Pico's thesis, the different order of the names notwithstanding, because it accounts for Pico's notion that there are nine angelic hierarchies secundum secretam doctrinam sapientum Hebraeorum Cabalistarum (just as there …

text: For thesis I (Michael as the superior priest who sacrifices the souls of rational animals), Wirszubski suggests inspiration from two texts: an anonymous exposition of the ten numerations, and Recanati's commentary, where Michael is the High Priest above because his power is from the sefirah Charity.

Wirszubski says Pico's bipartite division of Kabbala into a science of sefirot and a science of names descends from Abulafia's letter to his disciple, which appears anonymously in Cod. Vat. Ebr. 190 as the Summa Brevis Cabalae, and that Abulafia is almost the only Kabbalist author Pico read who classifies Kabbala.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio i

text: Wirszubski concludes that Pico's 'triplex merchiava' (second thesis of the set secundum opinionem propriam) is a triadic configuration of sefirot, because the fiftieth thesis places the seventh and eighth sefirot in a lower merchiava, and he holds that Abulafia's interpretation of the Merkabah, which omits the sefirot, does not account for it.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio ii (triplex merchiava)

text: Wirszubski notes that many Kabbalists conceived the three triads of sefirot as representing the three stages of being, Intellect, Soul and Nature, citing Azriel's Quaestiones super Decern Numerationibus as the locus classicus.
q: It is, furthermore, noteworthy that many Kabbalists conceived of these three triads of sefirot as representing or embracing the three stages of being, namely Intellect, Soul, and Nature. The locus classicus is Azriel's Quaestiones super Decern Numerationibus, Cod. Vat. Ebr. …

text: Wirszubski reports Frances Yates's conjecture, taken from Scholem, that triplex merchiava with its allusion to the three worlds would correspond to the Path of the Sephiroth, and says his own argument bears the conjecture out.

Wirszubski states that in terms of Kabbala the intelligible and angelic forms of Pico's 4 Ezra formula are the sefirot, and proposes as a working hypothesis that Pico's metaphysica formalis means the same as the metaphysics of intelligible and angelic forms.

Wirszubski infers that the sefirot are somehow involved in Pico's conception of practical Kabbala, a conclusion he admits is at variance with the communis via cabbalistarum and with Pico's own neat division into sefirot and names.

Wirszubski says that in classical Kabbala the sefirot are divine manifestations, potencies, emanations, attributes and other things besides numbers, and that the thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Kabbala to which most of Pico's identifiable sources belong gave the word sefirah a meaning other than its original numerical one.

Wirszubski identifies the unnamed science 'de virtutibus rerum superiorum quae sunt supra lunam' with the doctrine of the ten sefirot, on the ground that the forty-eighth Kabbalistic thesis outlines the correspondence between the ten sefirot and the ten spheres.
loc: apology | Quaestio Quinta, de virtutibus rerum superiorum

text: Wirszubski holds that in the Apology Pico could not state his views clearly, and that the doctrine of the ten sefirot, unlike the art of combining letters, is clearly involved in Pico's Kabbalistic confirmation of Christianity.

Wirszubski quotes Pico's text in which the books he acquired are said to contain a doctrine of the orders of the angels of the same kind as is read in Paul and Dionysius; he does not endorse it, but uses it to show how Pico presented these books as confirming the Christian religion.
loc: oration | the seventy books of Ezra

text: Wirszubski argues that the dividing line between the sefirot of speculative Kabbala and the names of practical Kabbala is not as rigid as Pico's first Kabbalistic thesis suggests, since sefirot and divine names are inseparably linked in the books Pico read and in his theses.
Wirszubski maintains that Pico is the first Christian who considered Kabbala to be simultaneously a witness for Christianity and an ally of natural magic.

Wirszubski notes that none of Pico's Kabbalistic theses from the fifth to the seventy-second presupposes the divisions and definitions of the first four, and allows that the first four were added late, after most of the others had been written.

Wirszubski says the Latin translations of Mithridates, through the intrusion of numbers into the symbolism of the sefirot and of magic into the mysticism of prayer, invite confusion of mysticism and magic in Kabbala.

Wirszubski says the allegorical interpretation of the Death of the Kiss is the link between Plato's Symposium and the Song of Solomon, the divine Solomon and the divine Plato thereby seeing eye to eye, on the assumptions Pico's Commento makes.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. viii, Stanza 4, binsica

text: Wirszubski says the Kabbalists did embrace the allegorical interpretation of the Death of the Kiss as the adherence of the soul to God, but were not its originators: it began with Maimonides and was from the start linked with the allegorical reading of the Song of Solomon.

Wirszubski holds that Maimonides cannot have been Pico's direct source for the Death of the Kiss, since the views differ, and that the clue to Pico's Kabbalistic source is the forty-fourth thesis, which derives verbatim from Recanati's Commentary on the Pentateuch, whose passage is a remarkable discussion of the Death of the Kiss.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. viii, Stanza 4, binsica

text: Wirszubski says Recanati's text accounts for Pico's statements that the Kabbalists hold Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Miriam and others to have died the Death of the Kiss and that it is a state of intellectual ecstasy, but not for what Pico says about the Song of Solomon, which Recanati does not mention.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. viii, Stanza 4, binsica

text: Wirszubski traces Pico's remark that Solomon states in the first verse the whole intention of the Song to the Maimunist commentators, and says Pico certainly read one of them, Levi ben Gershom, whose Latin translation of the commentary on Canticles by Mithridates is annotated throughout in Pico's own hand.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. viii, Stanza 4, binsica

text: Wirszubski says Gersonides places human perfection in the adherence of the human intellect to the Active Intellect, and that the Death of the Kiss in Recanati still shows the outline of Maimonides's theory of prophecy as union of the human intellect with the Active Intellect.

Wirszubski says that Mithridates's Latin of Gersonides's commentary interpolates the word Cabalistarum into the dictum that Moyse, Aarone and Maria died by a kiss, and that the translations Pico read therefore account for his notion that the Death of the Kiss was a Kabbalist allegory, whether or not the lost translation of Recanati was interpolated too.

Wirszubski argues that the distinction between the two deaths, of soul from body and of body from soul, is unknown in Pico's Kabbalistic sources and appears in his eleventh Kabbalistic thesis, where the archangel's sacrifice of rational souls is read in the light of the Platonic distinction.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio xi

text: Wirszubski reads Pico's eleventh Kabbalistic thesis as reinterpreting the aggadah of the archangel Michael's offering of rational souls to God as the ecstatic separation of soul from body, and links it with the mysticism of prayer, since Recanati made clear that sacrifice is prayer.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusio xi (opinionem propriam), Conclusio i (secretam doctrinam)

text: Wirszubski concludes, with a hedge, that although the precise mode of operation of pure Kabbala eludes identification, Pico conceived of operating in Kabbala without admixture of anything foreign as a contemplative activity whose reward is the Death of the Kiss, the indissoluble union of the soul with God.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio xiii

text: Wirszubski judges it likely that the link between puer and intellectus in Pico's thirteenth thesis on the sayings of Zoroaster is the angel Metatron, who is called na'ar (puer) and is sometimes identified with the Active Intellect, and that Pico met Metatron in his Kabbalistic books, without saying Metatron is a specifically Kabbalistic figure.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones secundum Zoroastrem, Conclusio xiii (per puerum ... intellectus)

text: Wirszubski notes that the editio princeps leaves a blank space in the tenth Kabbalistic thesis secundum opinionem propriam, where a Hebrew word or phrase is the key to interpretation, and that Francesco Giorgio assumed the omitted word was Hokmah, Wisdom.
q: The blank space in the text of the editio princeps (indicated by angular brackets) is a reminder that the key to the interpretation of this thesis is a Hebrew word or phrase. Francesco Giorgio, four hundred and fifty years ago, …
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio x (Orpheus Pallas, Zoroaster paterna mens, Mercury Dei filius)

text: Wirszubski argues that Giorgio's reading of the omitted word as Hokmah would make Pico identify the Gentile Ancient Theology's images with Jesus Christ, contradicting Pico's own warning in the Commento against identifying the Hermetic son of God with the Christian Son of God, so that either Pico is inconsistent or Giorgio is out of tune with Pico.
q: If you assume that the omitted word is hokmah, you assume eo ipso that it is hokmah as it is understood in the symbolic language of Kabbala, that is to say Hokmah as the name of the second sefirah. Pico's …

text: Wirszubski says that in the Commento Pico states as plainly as possible that what the Platonists call the son of God ought to be compared with the first and most noble angel created by God.
loc: commento | Book I, chap. iiii, on the first creature and the Son of God

text: Wirszubski asks whether Jewish angelology has an angel that could be called son of God, wisdom, mind and intelligible sphere, answers that there is one, whose best-known name is Metatron, and observes that Metatron is mentioned twice in Pico's writings at about the time of the Conclusiones.
Wirszubski points to the Commento, where Pico says that the cabbalist sages say Enoch is transformed into Matatron, the angel of divinity, as one instance of Pico's mention of Metatron.
loc: commento | Book III, on the death of man transformed into an angel (p. 554 ed. Garin)

text: Wirszubski says the transformation of Enoch into Metatron is mentioned also in Pico's Oration, though the printed editions obscure it, and quotes the reading of the only known manuscript, Cod. Palatinus 885.
q: The transformation of Enoch into Metatron is mentioned also in Pico's Oration. Since this fact is inadvertently obscured by the text of the printed editions, it will be useful to quote the only known manuscript, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence, Cod. …
loc: oration | the Hebrew theology transforming Enoch into an angel of divinity (Oratio, ed. Garin)

text: Wirszubski gives the printed-edition reading and the editio princeps blank for the Oration's Enoch passage, holds that the printed Hebrew phrase may well be a translation of angelus divinitatis, and states that he prefers the manuscript reading because Pico's Commento warrants its authenticity.
q: Asterisks are printed in Garin's edition (see note 44) instead of the name jnoun (Metatron). A blank space was left in the corresponding passage of the Oratio in the editio princeps.
loc: oration | the Hebrew theology transforming Enoch into an angel of divinity (Oratio, ed. Garin)

text: Wirszubski says Metatron is sometimes identified, notably by Abulafia, with the Active Intellect and is also called son, and on that basis suggests that the tenth Kabbalistic thesis should read the Hebrew name of Metatron in the blank, concluding that Pico used Metatron both to show correspondences between Kabbala and the ancient theology of the Gentiles and to draw a dividing line between Christianity and that theology.

Wirszubski says that from the standpoint of Renaissance Platonists the Ancient Theology of the Gentiles was in a sense the pagan counterpart of Kabbala, but that for Pico at any rate the relationship between Christianity and Platonism is not unproblematical, and he takes the Son of God as a case in point.

Wirszubski reads the ninth and tenth Orphic theses, which pair the Curetes of Orpheus with the potestates of Dionysius, as requiring an opus Cabalae related to the Fear of Isaac, which in the language of Kabbala denotes the fifth sefirah, Might or Judgment, so that the Kabbalistic work joined to Orphic magic involves sefirot even though the modus operandi is unknown.
q: Conclusio ix: Idem sunt Curetes apud Orpheum et potestates apud Dionysium. Conclusio x: Qui praecedentis conclusionis opus attentauerit, adhibeat opus Cabalae secundum appropriata timori Isaac.

text: Wirszubski explains mala coordinatio denaria in the tenth thesis of its series as the evil or unholy counterpart of the hierarchy of the ten sefirot, and says it would be risky to draw from this thesis, which is not secundum opinionem propriam, conclusions about Pico's view of evil.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones secundum Mercurium, Conclusio x (decem ultores; mala coordinatio denaria)

text: Wirszubski says Pico's sixty-sixth Kabbalistic thesis maps the parts of the human soul onto the ten sefirot, and that the ten avengers 'within us' of the preceding thesis are its counterpart.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio lxvi

text: Wirszubski says that Pico, by presenting Kabbala as both a mystical theology that confirmed Christianity and an ally of natural magic, set Christian Kabbala on a new course, and that the alliance of Kabbala and magic proved more influential than the superiority of the former over the latter.

Wirszubski says the Liber Redemptionis contains the doctrine of the Active Intellect as the prince of the divine presence, whose name is like that of his master, together with the human intellect's adherence and union with the Active Intellect, and that this Kabbalism combines the rationalistic philosophy of the Guide of the Perplexed with a letter-combinatory method.

Wirszubski argues that the Liber Redemptionis was written in 1273 (the year 5033 from creation) and, given its identical structure with Abulafia's known commentaries, is likeliest by Abulafia himself, despite the name Zerakhia in a Leipzig manuscript.
Wirszubski notes that Abulafia's De Secretis Legis states a world-year corresponding to A.D. 1280.
q: In the De Secretis Legis (fol. 458v), in the course of his discussion on the question whether the world was created or preexistent, Abulafia states, among other things, that "numerus annorum annorum eius [mundi] apud nos hodie sunt quinque milia …

text: Wirszubski says Abulafia was born in 1240, and says the conclusion that he wrote the book in question squares with everything known of his life and work.

Wirszubski quotes a passage of the Latin preface in which the Kabbalistic demonstrations are received from the mouth of the archangel set over the hierarchy of angels called hisim, who is called intellectus agens or Mattatron, and states that some words in it were added: none of the italicized words is warranted by the Hebrew, so the doctrine of the coincidence of opposites was superimposed on Abulafia by interpolation.
loc: 900-conclusions | Kabbalistic set; the Agent Intellect as archangel and prefect of the hisim hierarchy

text: Wirszubski says the phrase 'quodlibet est in quolibet' in a Latin translation argues the translator's acquaintance, not necessarily first hand, with Nicolaus Cusanus' De Docta Ignorantia, whose fifth chapter is titled 'Quodlibet in Quolibet' and begins with Anaxagoras.

Wirszubski prints a Latin passage, a sixth secret on the angel and the intellect, which identifies Mattatron, prince of the face, with the separate intellect that brings our intellect from potency to act, says his proper name is the same as his master's, and reports that the sages call him Henoch, saying Henoch is Mattatron.

Wirszubski says that the closing part of the passage in the Latin text (from 'Antequam autem dicam' on) is improbably by the author, that the purpose of this interpolation is not self-evident, and that the interpolator cannot be assumed to be Mithridates, though he might be.

Wirszubski prints from an anonymous Latin work the statement that the Hebrew word ben, son, is the secret of the Intellectus Agens, who is called son as the principle of the edifice, and reports that a marginal mark, a perpendicular line surmounted by two dots, stands against the last sentences of the second quotation and beside the whole of the first quotation.

Wirszubski says the Liber Combinationum, in Scholem's opinion, is a fourteenth-century popular version of Abulafia's combinational and philosophical Kabbala, and that Pico certainly used it for his first set of theses.

Wirszubski says Pico's fourth Kabbalistic thesis, that Ensoph is not to be counted among the sefirot but is their abstract and uncommunicated unity, aligns Pico with the Geronese school of Kabbala and in particular with Rabbi Azriel of Gerona, on his reading of the evidence.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio iv (Ensoph)

text: Wirszubski says the texts he quotes from Axelrad and from another commentary account for the negative part of Pico's fourth thesis, that 'Eyn-Sof is not to be counted with the sefirot, while the positive part, that it is the unity of the ten sefirot, harks back to Azriel of Gerona, who put the relation in terms of the One and the Many.

Wirszubski says the ten garments God donned at creation are the ten creative logoi, that is the sefirot, so that Pico's thirty-sixth Kabbalistic thesis concerns the mediation of the ten sefirot between the hidden God and the world, a problem discussed in Azriel's treatise, where Wirszubski takes the marginal marks to be Pico's.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusiones xxxv-xxxvi (Deus induit se decem uestimentis)

text: Wirszubski holds that Azriel is the outstanding Jewish representative of the Neoplatonic doctrine that all opposites coincide in God, and that, granted Pico read Azriel's Quaestiones and the preface to Abulafia's De Secretis Legis, it does not seem likely to him that the Kabbalistic strain of the coincidentia oppositorum escaped Pico's notice.
Wirszubski says that in Pico's thesis 'Eyn-Sof is feminine, and that the only other pre-Pico instance of the feminine use he recalls is in the Latin translation of Axelrad's Corona Nominis Boni.

Wirszubski says the Adumbratio Kabbalae Christianae, another Christian Kabbala, is subordinated to the Kabbala of Isaac Luria, who had not yet been born when Pico died, and that its confirmation of Christianity is entirely unrelated to Pico's Conclusiones.

Wirszubski reports that in the autumn of 1486 Pico informed Ficino of certain Chaldean and Arabic books that induced him to study those languages, and that Pico is the only person ever to have claimed to have seen these Chaldean books.

Wirszubski argues that Patrizi misread Ficino's letter to Germain de Ganay: Ficino's 'enarrationes in eloquia sacra' meant commentaries on the Scriptures, not on the Oracles, so the tradition that Ficino said he found Pico's commentary on the Oracles among his papers rests on a misconception.
Wirszubski says the Heptaplus begins and ends with the hierarchical sequence of three worlds, the angelic or intelligible, the celestial and the sublunar, presented differently in each place.
loc: heptaplus | second proem, and the interpretation of the first word of Genesis at the end

text: Wirszubski observes that the analogical likeness of the tabernacle, man and the world occurs in a work of Abulafia in Cod. Chigi, that Pico's familiar markings appear in the margin there, and that it is nevertheless unlikely Pico's elaborate discussion descends from that succinct statement.
loc: heptaplus | second proem (tabernacle) and end (man as microcosm)

text: Wirszubski says the detail in which Pico works out the analogies of tabernacle, man and world is reminiscent of two Kabbalistic books, by Bahya ben Asher and by Isaac of Acre, and that Bahya and Isaac of Acre had a common source in Baruch Togarmi, the teacher of Abulafia.
loc: heptaplus | second proem: the tabernacle in three parts

text: Wirszubski concludes that at the present state of research Pico's direct source for the analogical representation of the three worlds cannot be pinpointed, but that it certainly descends from a Kabbalistic source, whether Bahya ben Asher, Isaac of Acre or even Baruch Togarmi.
q: At the present state of research it is impossible to pinpoint Pico's direct source. But it is certainly true that, directly or indirectly, Pico's analogical representation of the three worlds is descended from a Kabbalistic source, be it Bahya ben …

text: Wirszubski says that what looms behind Pico's monadological conception of the three worlds, that whatever is in all the worlds together is contained in each, is not Kabbala but late Neoplatonism, in particular Proclus's Elements of Theology, proposition 103, and compares Pico's own Conclusiones secundum Proclum 17 on the divine hierarchies.
loc: heptaplus | second proem: the three worlds as one world; 'all in all'

text: Wirszubski quotes the second proem's sentence in which Pico attributes the 'all in all' opinion to Anaxagoras (Quam Anaxagorae credo fuisse opinionem), explicated afterward by the Pythagoricis et Piatonicis, and himself traces the doctrine there to Proclus.

Wirszubski concludes that two motifs stand side by side in Pico's doctrine of the three worlds: the analogical, ultimately from Baruch Togairmi, and the monadological, from Proclus, so that Jewish mysticism and Neoplatonic theology dwell peacefully side by side in the proem of the Heptaplus.

Wirszubski says Kabbala is avoided in the main body of the Heptaplus, which he finds understandable because the Conclusiones were still banned, though the closing interpretation of the first Hebrew word of Genesis is eminently Kabbalistic; in a note he quotes Pico's statement that much about the angelic and invisible nature is handed down by the ancient Hebrews and by Dionysius, and that he decided to put off setting out the Hebrew doctrine.
q: About two years after that letter Pico wrote his Heptaplus. Kabbala is avoided in the main body of the treatise, which is perfectly understandable given that the Conclusiones were still banned at that time. At the end of the seventh …
loc: heptaplus | third exposition: the angelic nature, Hebrew and Dionysian doctrines (ed. Garin p. 246)

text: Wirszubski identifies the Hebrew authors named in the Heptaplus: Simeon antiquus writing in Chaldean as Rabbi Simeon ben Yohay, the reputed author of the Zohar; Neonias as Nehunya ben Ha-Qana, reputed author of the Bahir; the two Moses as Moses ben Maimon and Moses ben Nahman; and Manaem as Menahem Recanati.
loc: heptaplus | proem (ed. Garin pp. 178-180): the Hebrew authors Pico will not cite

text: Wirszubski says the Heptaplus affords the best commentary on the philosophic part of thesis lxvii, and cites the passage in which Pico sets the seraphic fire of the region beyond the world, the fire of the sun in heaven and elemental fire in a threefold gradation, with the cherubic minds above the heaven as waters.
loc: heptaplus | the angelic world as fire and water (ed. Garin pp. 188-190)

text: Wirszubski says the interpretation of heaven (samayim) as fire and water is much older than medieval Kabbalism and that Pico probably found it in the Bahir or in Recanati, which is why the precise source does not matter.
loc: heptaplus | proem: heaven as asciamaim, fire and water

text: Wirszubski argues that the inventory of Pico's library, the authors Pico mentions and even the translations made for him may all mislead, and that the only evidence that can be absolutely trusted for which Kabbalistic texts Pico used is the internal evidence of the theses themselves, by derivation of texts.
q: If we want then to establish with reasonable certainty whether, or to what extent, the four known manuscripts contain the texts that matter for the interpretation of Pico's Kabbala, we must try to pinpoint the direct sources, or at least …

text: Wirszubski says Pico certainly used the Bahir and the Liber de Radicibus, and that some theses secundum opinionem propriam argue his acquaintance with Abulafia's writings, two of which are in the Vaticanus 190 and one in the Chisianus.

Wirszubski says the question whether Pico read the Zohar, which had not been translated by the time he published the Conclusiones and which he could not have read in the original, depends entirely on whether theses that reflect Zohar passages can be derived from quotations of the Zohar in the known translations, notably Recanati; if they can, it would be unreasonable to infer he read it, and if they cannot, the conclusion that he read some of it is inevitable.

Wirszubski says the direct sources of Pico's first set of Kabbalistic theses that can be shown are seven books: Recanati's Commentary on the Pentateuch, Gicatilla's Portae Iustitiae, the Comentum Sepher Iesire, the Expositio Decern Numerationum, the Bahir, the Liber Combinationum and Axelrad's Corona Nominis Boni.

Wirszubski says Recanati is the dominant source of the first set of Kabbalistic theses, with more than half of the theses demonstrably deriving directly from him, and that his position is not likely to be challenged.

Wirszubski says the first set of theses is almost exclusively Kabbala of the sefirot, whereas the second set begins with the distinction between scientia sefirot and scientia semot, which derives from Abulafia, and that the evidence argues strongly, though it does not prove, that Pico fully realised the difference between these two kinds of Kabbala only when he read Abulafia.

Wirszubski says Recanati's Kabbala is mainly concerned with the ten sefirot as divine emanations, using symbolical exegesis of Scripture, whereas Abulafia's is concerned with the name or names of God and uses combinations of letters as a discipline for union with God.
q: Recanati's mystical commentary on the Pentateuch and Abulafia's mystical commentary on Maimonides represent two quite different orientations, and in fact two quite different kinds of Kabbala. Recanati's Kabbala is mainly concerned with the ten sefirot as divine emanations, and its …

text: Wirszubski says all the manuscripts Pico used for his theses were written by Mithridates in his own hand between May and November 1486, that Mithridates worked away from Pico and sent translations in successively, and that Pico probably read them as they came in and wrote his theses as he went along.
Wirszubski says Pico's study of the manuscripts that are the sources of his Kabbalistic theses was brief, having begun only some five or six months before the completion of the theses.

Wirszubski says Pico is the first Christian by birth known to have read a large amount of genuine Jewish Kabbala, that it passed through Latin translation and through the mind of a Christian trained in the schools of philosophy, and that it was transformed in the process while still recognizable in what Pico wrote.

Wirszubski says Mithridates was a competent but arbitrary translator whose own opinions show in his translations, and that he was in a sense Pico's forerunner in the notion that the esoteric tradition of the Jews confirmed Christianity.

Wirszubski says there are significant differences of substance, emphasis and presentation between the extant Latin translations and the Hebrew originals of Pico's Kabbalistic sources, and that some of them bear on the interpretation of individual theses and of Pico's view of Kabbala as a whole.

Wirszubski says Mithridates showed off his skill so as to impress Pico with his usefulness, in order to exploit Pico's interest in Kabbala for his own advantage, and that he considered himself indispensable, though it is uncertain who gave in over the teaching of Chaldean.
Wirszubski says Pico related in November 1486 that Mithridates had refused to teach him Chaldean until he promised on oath not to impart that language to anyone.

Wirszubski says the extant anonymous Latin translation of Recanati's commentary on Genesis used by Egidio da Viterbo cannot be the work of Flavius Mithridates, since its vocabulary and syntax rule that out, against a recent assertion made with confidence but without proof.

Wirszubski dates Mithridates's lost translation of Recanati and his extant translation of the Bahir to roughly May to November 1486, the earlier limit being Pico's love affair at Arezzo in May 1486 to which a parenthesis in the Bahir translation refers and the later limit being Pico's use of Recanati and the Bahir in his theses.

Wirszubski says Pico's nine hundred theses were completed in the autumn of 1486, that on 10 November 1486 Pico was still at La Fratta preparing to leave for Rome, and that Eucharius Silber printed them four weeks later, the colophon giving 7 December 1486.

Wirszubski says that Eucharius Silber left blank spaces in the editio princeps for want of Greek and Hebrew type, and holds that the Vindobonensis and the Erlangensis are descended from the printed text and not, as an editor supposed, its parents.

Wirszubski says that although Nahmanides is explicitly cited by Pico and shares features with Pico's view of Kabbala, the internal evidence of the Conclusiones and the Apology does not bear out the hypothesis that Nahmanides's biblical commentary was an influential direct source, and that no thesis requires Pico's direct acquaintance with it.

Wirszubski says Reuchlin's quotation of Nahmanides conflates a paraphrase with a word-for-word quotation of Pico's thirty-third thesis, which itself quotes Recanati verbatim, so that Recanati and not Nahmanides is Pico's direct source in that case.

Wirszubski argues that there is no conclusive evidence that Pico read Nahmanides before completing his theses: the earliest explicit reference is in the Heptaplus, written about two years after the Conclusiones, after his return from France in 1488.

Wirszubski says Abulafia is never explicitly mentioned by Pico but that Pico certainly read Cod. Vat. Ebr. 190, which includes the De Secretis Legis, before completing his theses, so that the most probable hypothesis is that Abulafia inspired Pico's view of Kabbala as the divinely revealed science explaining the mysteries of the Law.

Wirszubski says Pico read Rabbi Moses ben Nahman's commentary on the Sefer Yesirah, in Latin, by the date of the letter he quotes, since the rabbinic dictum quoted in Pico's letter appears in that commentary only.

Kristeller reports that Wirszubski proves, what had merely been surmised, that the doctrine of the three worlds, angelic, celestial and elementary, in the Heptaplus is of Kabbalistic origin, though it presupposed both the Platonist distinction between the intelligible and the visible and the Aristotelian distinction between celestial and sublunar.
q: Wirszubski proves (what had been merely surmised in the past) that the doctrine of the three worlds, angelic, celestial, and elementary, as advanced in the Heptaplus, is of Kabbalistic origin, although it evidently presupposed both the Platonist distinction between the …
loc: heptaplus | second proem: the three worlds

text: Kristeller says Pico's role was especially important because he used Kabbala to confirm Christian theology and added Kabbalism, and Aristotelianism, to the universal syncretism envisaged by Ficino, associating it with Platonism, Hermeticism and magic.

Kristeller reports that Wirszubski shows it was Pico rather than his Hebrew sources who linked Kabbalistic teachings with the Chaldean Oracles, Orphic hymns, Proclus, Cusanus and Ramon Lull, so that Pico added another dimension to the Platonic syncretism founded by Ficino.
Kristeller states that Pico's main Kabbalistic sources were Abulafia and Menahem of Recanati.
Wirszubski says Pico became interested in Kabbala before he knew Hebrew, and that Pico states in his Commento that he set out to study Hebrew and Chaldean solely for the sake of Kabbala.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. xi, stanza 9

text: Wirszubski reports that on 8 September 1486 Ficino wrote to Pico asking for the return of his Latin Koran, and that Pico's undated reply from La Fratta, not earlier than the middle of October 1486, says he had devoted a month to Hebrew and then given himself entirely to other languages.

Wirszubski argues that by mid-October 1486 Pico could write moderately good Hebrew prose but could not have read an untranslated Kabbalistic book unaided, and that it is quite unlikely that he read any significant quantity of Kabbalistic texts in the original before he wrote his theses, so the range of his acquaintance with Kabbala in 1486 was not determined by his Hebrew.

Wirszubski says Pico learned from Mithridates's translations infinitely more than he could have learned from the Hebrew originals unaided, though the translations kept reminding him that he needed Hebrew to understand what he read.
Wirszubski illustrates what cannot be seen in Latin translation with the isopsephic equivalence of intellectus agens and Israel in Hebrew, both summing to 541.

Wirszubski argues that almost all the manuscripts of Mithridates's translations that Pico demonstrably used date themselves between 10 May 1486, the day of Pico's abduction of Margherita from Arezzo, and Pico's completion of his theses early in November 1486, through allusions inserted in parentheses, and amount to about 3,000 pages in folio.

Wirszubski says it is the likeliest conclusion that Pico began to study Hebrew in the summer of 1486, the summer when the Kabbalistic translations made for him by Mithridates flowed in great profusion.

Wirszubski says Mithridates translated a small Kabbalistic library of some forty books, about 5,500 pages in folio in all, of which the four extant manuscripts preserve nearly 3,500, and that nobody can establish whether it was a chance collection or a selection and by whom.

Wirszubski says it is no longer a matter of opinion that Cod. Vat. Ebr. 189 and 190 are translations made for Pico by Flavius Mithridates, since their subscriptions state it, whereas the subscriptions of Cod. Vat. Ebr. 191 name Mithridates as translator but never mention Pico as recipient.

Wirszubski argues from Mithridates's own notes that Cod. Vat. Ebr. 189, with the twelve books De Anima ascribed to Eleazar of Worms, was written when Pico was already in Rome and after the consequences of the publication of the Conclusiones, so that Pico could not have read it before completing his theses.
q: A remarkable case in point is Cod. Vat. Ebr. 189. Owing mainly to the fact that Gaffarel described a direct descendant of this manuscript in the seventeenth century, the works of Eleazar of Worms rank high in most discussions of …

text: Wirszubski argues that Gaffarel's hypothesis that Pico had the books translated for Sixtus IV translated again by the same translator has no foundation, since none of the extant manuscripts, written for Pico after 10 May 1486, would qualify as any of the three books translated before Sixtus IV's death in 1484.
Wirszubski reports that Mithridates's notes identify 'Malfecta' as Giovanni Battista Cibo, Cardinal of Melfi and Mithridates's former patron, who as Innocent VIII succeeded Sixtus IV.

Wirszubski says Pico did not make his first acquaintance with Kabbala through untranslated texts, that there was little Kabbala in Latin translation before Mithridates's translations of 1486, and that what little was known in translation would scarcely fill a quire of the manuscripts made for Pico.

Wirszubski says that in the thesis that the winged creatures of the fifth day are mundane angels who appear to men the expression 'mundane angels' proves that Pico's direct source was Recanati, quoting the Zohar, whose own text has 'supernal' where Recanati's quotation has 'world'.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum secretam doctrinam, Conclusio XXVIII (angelos mundanos)

text: Wirszubski says the ultimate source of the thesis that no angel having six wings is ever transformed is undoubtedly the Zohar, but that there is no need to look beyond Recanati, who quotes it, for the immediate source.
q: Though the ultimate source of this thesis is undoubtedly the Zohar, part I, fol. 34v, there is no need to look for its immediate source beyond Recanati, fol. 12va, where the Zohar is quoted:

text: Wirszubski says the source of the thesis (a king of the earth is not punished on earth unless the host of heaven is first humbled) is a commonplace of the Midrash, quite likely reached through Recanati, with Gicatilla's Portae Iustitiae as an alternative source in which the nation's archangel must fall first.

Wirszubski says the Bahir passage in which the archangel Michael on God's right hand of water and hail and the archangel Gabriel on his left of fire make peace between them lies behind another thesis of the first set, and that Pico could have read it in three of his manuscripts.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum secretam doctrinam (the passage on Michael and Gabriel, bohu and tohu)

text: Wirszubski says that the order of the theses of the first set often reflects the order of Recanati's book, three blocks of theses following their sources in Recanati exactly, and that the placement of Conclusio XXIX between two theses about angels reflects Recanati's arrangement even though its phrasing is from the Bahir.

Wirszubski says the symbolic language of the ten sefirot is sometimes transformed in Mithridates's translations almost beyond recognition, names of divine manifestations or properties being replaced by symbolic numbers, as in the Ma'areket ha-'Elohut, and that the Kabbala of the sefirot is thereby given a twist toward magic.

Wirszubski says that, unless he is mistaken, Pico's notion that numbers are proper to the work of Kabbala is for the most part out of tune with the Hebrew originals of his sources but in keeping with their Latin translations, which shift emphasis from language symbolism to number symbolism.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Magicae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio 25 (numeri sunt proprii operi cabalae)

text: Wirszubski says Mithridates preached his Sermo de Passione Domini before the pope and cardinals on Good Friday 1481, some five years before the Kabbalistic translations, adducing what he presented as secret Jewish evidence for Christ's Passion, and that interpolations linking Kabbala with Christian dogma occur in his translations.

Wirszubski says the Latin translation adds a Trinitarian clause that the Hebrew lacks, connecting the three superior sefirot with the Trinity, and that in the case of the word 'az the effect can be seen in Pico's twentieth Kabbalistic thesis.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio xx ('az) and Conclusio xlvii of the first set (Amen)

text: Wirszubski says a Latin glossary passage was tampered with so as to link 'homo id est tiphereth' with Jesus Christ, to whom all power was given, a link the translator himself supplies by quoting Matthew 28:18 in the margin.

Wirszubski says that Mithridates, on his own showing, interpolated a Christianizing interpretation at Genesis 1:26, but that it does not follow that all the Christianizing interpolations are his, since authorship of each must be established independently and at the present state of research cannot be.

Wirszubski says the similarity between Pico's symbolism of the kiss and two Zohar passages on the kiss of spirit is striking and, unless he is mistaken, the only instance of similarity between Pico and an identifiable Zohar passage not quoted in Recanati or another source Pico used, but that the balance of probabilities does not favour Pico's direct acquaintance with the Zohar.
loc: commento | Book III, chap. viii, Stanza 4 (binsica)

text: Wirszubski suggests, tentatively, that Pico's theologia inferior may have been conceived after pseudo-Dionysius's cataphatic theology of divine names, the superior way being the apophatic, so that the third Kabbalistic thesis would mean that practical Kabbala practises the formative principles and divine attributes.
loc: 900-conclusions | Conclusiones Cabalisticae secundum opinionem propriam, Conclusio iii (theologia inferior)

text: Wirszubski says that next to Flavius Mithridates the person who matters most for Pico's encounter with Kabbala is Johanan Alemanno, identified in a letter as Pico's teacher, and that it remains unknown what Johanan taught Pico and when their association began, though it is usually dated to 1488 in Florence.

Wirszubski holds that the balance of probabilities favours Garin's identification of 'Johanan et Manaen ebrei' in the Commento with Johanan Alemanno and Menahem Recanati, so that Pico already knew Alemanno when he wrote the Commento, dated by consensus in 1486, and that Alemanno may have been Pico's teacher in cabalisticis at the most decisive period, a possibility he calls fascinating.
loc: commento | Book III, on Solomon's Song (p. 535 ed. Garin): Johanan e Manaen ebrei

text: Wirszubski says the Hebrew terms of the fourfold interpretation of Scripture in Pico's Apology, sechel for tropological and cabala for anagogical, are unlikely to derive from any source but Bahya ben Asher, yet Pico's own marginal note in Levi ben Gershom's Latin commentary on the Song shows the terminology could travel without Bahya's text, so that Isaac of Acre is as good a source for the three worlds as Bahya.
loc: apology | the fourfold interpretation of Scripture among Christians and Jews (Opera p. 178)

text: Wirszubski says the Oration was meant as the opening address of the public debate on the nine hundred theses, that it was not delivered, and that Pico was summoned before an ecclesiastical commission appointed by Innocent VIII, which condemned thirteen theses, none of them a Kabbalistic thesis, though Kabbala is involved in the condemned magical thesis that no science certifies Christ's divinity better than magic and Kabbala.
loc: apology | the condemned magical thesis on magic and Kabbala (Quaestio Quinta)

text: Wirszubski says Pico's defence of the condemned thesis rests entirely on a distinction between revealed and nonrevealed science, and that his line of defense requires distinguishing the Kabbala which is the foundation of his Conclusiones Cabalisticae from the Kabbala involved in the condemned magical thesis.
loc: apology | Quaestio Quinta de magia naturali et cabala Hebraeorum

text: Wirszubski argues that behind Pico's picture of Kabbala as the divinely revealed explanation of the mysteries of the Law there is an intervening Kabbalistic source between the Talmud and Maimonides, on the one hand, and Pico, on the other, that Abulafia is the obvious and only choice, and that De Secretis Legis is the only book Pico is known to have read before the Apology that couples these ideas with divine names and combination of letters.
q: What makes me think of an intervening Kabbalistic source between the Talmud and Maimonides, on the one hand, and Pico, on the other, is the unerring judgment that singled out the "mysteries of the Law" as the heart of Kabbala. …

text: Wirszubski says that in the Latin quotation of Moses ben Nahman's preface in Abulafia's preface the statement that there are four names is an unnecessary and improper addition by Mithridates, since neither Moses ben Nahman nor Abulafia says four names and the obvious division is into three, and that italics there mark interpolations.
